item.title: 19-3 Economy as a Factor Across the Whole Business
item.description:
Part of 19 EconomyEvery other factor in this book has a name, an address and a phone number. You can renegotiate with a supplier, retrain a worker, redesign a product, re-site a shop. The economy has none of that. You can't ring it up, you can't switch to a cheaper one, and it will not take your call. It simply arrives — in your flour bill, your customers' confidence, your loan repayments and the wage you have to offer — whether or not you planned for it.So this subsection isn't about predicting it. Nobody reliably can, and the people who claim to are usually selling something. It's about seeing how it travels through a business, so that when it moves you already know where it's going to land.Here's the reframe worth carrying. Every factor you've studied in this book is priced inside the economy.Your suppliers buy their energy, pay their staff and borrow their money in the same economy you do — which means their costs move whether or not they change anything. Your customers earn, borrow and spend inside it. Your wages are set by it. The interest rate on your oven is decided by it. The Economy chapter isn't a topic that sits alongside suppliers, labour and financials; it's the weather all four of them live in.Which also tells you what you can and can't do about it. You cannot change the forecast. You can change how exposed you are to it, and that is a management decision — planning, organizing and controlling, from the opening chapter, applied to something you don't control.Macroeconomics has hundreds of variables. Four of them do most of the damage.Add a fifth if you buy or sell across a border: exchange rates. A currency that moves 10% changes your cost of goods overnight without a single supplier lifting a finger. Same logic, different dial.Notice something about that table. Growth and employment tend to help revenue; inflation and interest rates tend to hurt costs and cash. Most painful periods are a combination — which is exactly the scenario the worked example below walks through.Here's the shape of it. A single economic shift doesn't hit one chapter of your business. It fans out through all of them and meets again at the profit line.
That last arrow is the one to watch. When profit falls, businesses cut investment, hiring and stock — and if enough of them do it at once, that is the recession, feeding itself. You're not just standing in the weather; at scale, businesses like yours are the weather.Most economic shocks reach you first through what you buy. Commodity prices — wheat, steel, oil, cocoa — are set on world markets, which is the Raw Materials chapter's point about distance: you don't control the price, you inherit it.Three economic forces do the inheriting: Inflation raises your suppliers' own costs, and they pass on what they can. There's usually a lag of weeks or months between the world moving and your invoice changing — which is why watching the market beats watching your in-tray. Currency moves the price of anything imported, duties and freight included, long before your supplier bothers to reissue a price list. Growth cuts both ways. A boom can leave suppliers short of capacity, so lead times stretch and Distribution gets slower just when you need it most. The strategic move here is boring and effective: know which two or three inputs carry most of your cost, and follow them. Ignore the rest.The economy runs through your people and your machines too.Wages follow the labour market, as the Labour chapter set out. In a boom, skilled staff are scarce, your best baker gets poached by the café down the road, and the market rate for a replacement rises. In a downturn, applications flood in — but so do your customers' reasons to spend less.Interest rates decide your capital spending. A second oven, a bigger van, a second site — all of them are bets that only pay off at a certain cost of borrowing. The Manufacturing chapter's fixed-versus-variable arithmetic doesn't change with the interest rate, but the decision does. That's why the same investment can be sensible in March and reckless in September without anything about the oven changing.And the economy shifts the automation question. When wages rise and borrowing is cheap, replacing hours with a machine looks attractive. When wages are flat and money is expensive, flexible labour wins. The Costs chapter's fixed-versus-variable trade gets re-priced every few years by forces entirely outside your control.Then it reaches your customers — and this is where the Market chapter's elasticity stops being theory.In a squeeze, customers don't just buy less. They become more price-sensitive. The same loaf that sold comfortably at £4.40 last year may sit unsold at £4.20 now, because the alternatives — the supermarket meal deal, making it at home, skipping it — have all become more attractive. Your demand curve hasn't moved along; it has shifted. The Types of Competition chapter adds the second half of the story: when a whole market shrinks, rivals get desperate, and desperate rivals in an oligopoly start price wars. Margins get shredded for everybody.And the reverse is true in a boom, which is worth remembering because it's where the real mistakes get made. Demand is easy, so you stop being sharp. You hire in a hurry, you sign a long lease, you add capacity you'll regret. Booms don't just make businesses richer — they make them fragile.For most businesses, the economy shows up hardest in cash, not profit. Interest rates change what your overdraft, lease or loan costs — and a rate rise on a business with thin margins can be the difference between a small profit and a small loss. Inflation makes holding stock a hedge and makes borrowing expensive at the same time. The Stores chapter's carrying-cost arithmetic shifts, and with it your ideal stock level. The cash conversion gap — you pay your suppliers before your customers pay you — gets wider in a downturn, because your customers start paying late. The Financials chapter covers this properly; the economic version is that a squeeze squeezes twice, once on demand and once on cash. Nothing catastrophic happens to Priya's bakery. No fire, no lost contract, no rival opening next door. The economy just moves four dials a little.A £13,000 profit has become a £2,800 loss. Look at how modest each individual move was: 8%, 12%, 6%, 5%. None of them would make a headline. Together they wiped out a whole year's earnings and more — which is precisely why the economy is so easy to underrate until it's already happened.Now watch how she responds, because the shape of the response is the lesson: Cut waste. Her spoilage sits at 5% of materials. Getting it to 2% is worth about £1,100 — no negotiation, no customer needed. The cheapest profit in the building, exactly as the Raw Materials chapter argued. Raise one price, not all of them. She adds 15p to the counter loaf, where her regulars are least likely to switch, and leaves the wholesale price alone because the café contract is elastic. Worth roughly £2,000, and it's the same elasticity arithmetic from the Market chapter. Defer the second oven. The capex plan made sense at 5% interest. At 8%, the break-even volume — 25 extra loaves a day, in the Manufacturing chapter's sums — looks a lot further away. Hold less stock. Freeing cash out of the storeroom is worth more, not less, when borrowing is dear. Renegotiate. She asks the mill for a committed-volume price, and gets a little, because she's a predictable customer. Those two small operational moves recover about £3,100 — enough to get back to roughly break-even, not back to profit. Full recovery needs the structural decisions. That's honest, and it's typical: the economy takes a year off you, and it takes more than one clever fix to get it back.Two businesses on the same street can have completely different economic exposures, and knowing which one you run is strategy. Cyclical businesses sell things people can postpone — holidays, new kitchens, cars, weddings. They swing hard with growth. Defensive businesses sell things people can't skip — bread, electricity, basic healthcare, repairs. They barely move. Elastic products (commodity bread, budget hotels) lose volume fast when customers have less to spend. Inelastic products (a unique prescription, the only bakery in a village, a specialist tool) hold up far better. If your product is cyclical and elastic, you are running a business that will be tested hard roughly every decade, and your cost structure needs to reflect that. If you're defensive and inelastic, your risk is complacency, not collapse. Know which two dials move you most. A bakery watches wheat prices, local wages and consumer confidence. A van hire firm watches fuel and interest rates. Write yours down. Build buffers before you need them. Cash reserves, a second supplier, a flexible layer of labour rather than all-permanent contracts. Buffers cost a little every good year and save the business in a bad one. Watch leading signals, not headlines. Your own sales pipeline, job adverts in your sector, commodity prices, rate announcements, your suppliers' lead times. These are controlling, from the management loop — and they arrive weeks before your accounts do. Match your cost structure to your volatility. The more the economy can swing your sales, the more you want costs that move with them. Don't over-react to one quarter, and don't ignore three. Two data points in a row is noise; a trend across several is a signal. Use downturns as well as surviving them. Good staff become available, premises get cheaper, weaker rivals exit. The Competitors chapter's advice holds: a market shake-out is a repositioning opportunity for whoever is still standing. And the thread that runs through all of it: the economy is the factor you can't manage, which makes it the factor that defines good management. Anyone can run a business through easy conditions. The strategist's edge is being positioned for the other kind — with a margin that can absorb a shock, cash that can wait out a bad quarter, and a set of numbers honest enough to tell you it's coming.
Photo by Vladimir Srajber on Pexels The economy is the weather every other factor in this book operates inside. You can't change it; you can only change your exposure to it. Four dials do most of the work: growth (your volume), inflation (your costs), interest rates (your investments and cash) and employment and wages (your wage bill). Add exchange rates if you trade across a border. A single economic shift fans out through suppliers, labour, market and financials at once, meeting again at the profit line — and your resulting cutbacks become part of the economy itself. It reaches you upstream through input prices and currency, in the middle through wages, hiring and the case for capital spending, and downstream through demand, elasticity and the behaviour of desperate rivals. It hits cash harder than profit: interest costs, the stock-holding trade-off, and customers who start paying late. Small numbers compound — in the worked example, moves of 8%, 12%, 6% and 5% turned a £13,000 profit into a £2,800 loss. Businesses differ enormously in exposure: cyclical vs defensive, elastic vs inelastic. Know which you are, and set your cost structure accordingly. The strategist's habit: know your two key dials, hold buffers, read leading signals, keep costs flexible where sales are volatile, and treat a downturn as a repositioning opportunity — all while running the same plan–organize–lead–control loop you'd use on anything else.

item.title: 19-1 What Economy Really Means
item.description:
Part of 19 EconomyYou've heard the word a thousand times this week. "The economy's slowing." "We need to grow the economy." "That's not economical." It gets used as though everyone agrees what it means — and in practice, most people are quietly talking about three different things.Getting this straight matters more than it sounds, because the economy is the single largest thing acting on your business that you will never be able to control. It changes what your customers can afford, what your suppliers charge, what your staff expect to be paid, and what your borrowed money costs. The better you understand what it actually is, the less it feels like random weather and the more it looks like something you can prepare for.An economy is the whole system a society uses to produce, distribute and consume goods and services — and the economy is that system, running, right now, everywhere at once.Read that slowly, because it's far bigger than it sounds. It isn't a building, a government department or a stock market. It's the total of every decision made by every person and every business about what to make, what to buy, what to charge and what to do with the money afterwards.Your bakery is in it. Your supplier's mill is in it. Your customers' wages are in it. The whole thing is not designed or run by anybody — it's the sum of millions of independent choices, all happening simultaneously, mostly without anyone coordinating them.That's the first surprising thing about an economy. It has no manager. And yet, as the Market chapter showed, prices emerge, goods flow, and strangers manage to trade. Nobody is in charge, and somehow it works.Before going further, untangle the senses. "Economy" does at least three jobs in everyday speech: A system. "The German economy is export-driven." A particular country's arrangement of production and trade. Aggregate activity. "The economy grew 2% last year." Here it usually means total output — how much got made and sold, added up. Thrift. "That's an economical way to do it." Nothing to do with nations at all; it means not wasting resources. The third one is a nice reminder that the word's root is about household management. Which is exactly the right instinct: an economy is a household, scaled up to millions of people.Here's the bridge from what you already know. In the Market chapter, you met a market as the set of buyers and sellers who could trade a particular thing, plus the channel and rules that let them do it.Now multiply. An economy is all of those markets, running at once, feeding each other. The labour market, the market for flour, the market for coffee, the market for second-hand vans, the market for money itself. They're not separate — they're wired together. A rise in the price of fuel pushes up the cost of flour, which pushes up the price of bread, which changes what customers can afford to buy, which changes how many staff a bakery needs.That's the whole point. An economy is what you get when you connect thousands of markets and let them affect each other.Once you see the wiring, a simple picture emerges. It's usually called the circular flow, and it explains where money actually goes.
Read it as a loop rather than a list. Households supply labour and spend their wages. Businesses buy that labour and sell goods back. Government taxes both and pumps money back out as services, contracts and infrastructure. Nothing in this picture sits still — which is why it's called flow.Two consequences fall straight out of that loop:Everyone is both a buyer and a seller. This is the point from the Labour chapter: you rent people's effort in the labour market, and they spend the wages back into the product markets. Your customer is somebody else's employee. When wages rise across a town, your customers have more to spend — and so do your rivals, who can now outbid you for staff.Money leaving your business is somebody's income. Your flour bill is the mill's revenue. Your wage bill is your staff's spending power. An economy is a chain of consequences, and every decision you make sends a ripple both ways.Since aggregate activity is invisible, we measure it with a handful of dials. These get quoted constantly, so it's worth knowing what each one actually says.None of those numbers will ever tell you what to do on a Tuesday afternoon. What they do is tell you which way the wind is blowing — and the businesses that read them early get to make their decisions while there's still time to make them.Economies don't grow in a straight line. They expand, slow, contract, and recover. That rhythm is the business cycle, and it has one feature that every owner should internalise.When demand rises, your revenue rises — but so do your costs, because suppliers, landlords and staff all want a share of the good times. When demand falls, your revenue falls immediately, and your costs don't. The rent is fixed. The salaries are fixed. The lease on the van is fixed.So the good times make you a bit more money, and the bad times take a lot of it away. The Costs chapter called this the fixed-versus-variable split. In an economy, it's the difference between surviving a downturn and joining the statistics.Priya runs her bakery with roughly £230 a day of fixed costs — wages, rent, energy — and £1.20 of ingredients per loaf. Watch three versions of the same week.Look at the downturn column, because that's the lesson. She loses 20% of her sales and 112% of her profit. The recipe didn't change, the staff didn't get worse, and she didn't make a single bad decision — the economy simply turned, and her fixed costs refused to turn with it.And notice the boom column is no free lunch either. She sells 30% more but only doubles her profit, because wages and energy rose too. Good times are good; they're just not as good as the revenue line suggests.Now watch what a strategist does differently in each. In the boom, she doesn't assume it lasts — she uses the fat months to build a cash buffer and get her suppliers onto longer contracts at fixed prices. In the downturn, she can't cut the rent, but she can flex the hours she buys, shift her range towards cheaper loaves that still sell, and lean harder on the customers she already has. Because she saw the signals early, she made those changes while they were choices rather than emergencies.Here's where a lot of business writing goes wrong, and where you should be sceptical.It's tempting, in a bad year, to say "the economy did this to us" — as though nothing could have been done. Sometimes that's true. Often it isn't.The economy sets the conditions. It doesn't decide who wins inside them. As the opening chapter of this book argued, management is the multiplier — and the same downturn that bankrupts one bakery feeds the one next door, because the survivors pick up the customers, the staff and the premises of the ones that fold. Two businesses can live through an identical recession and end in opposite places.What you control is modest but real: whether you see the shift early, whether your costs are flexible, whether you have cash in reserve, and whether you keep the customers you already have. The Financials chapter and the Customer Service chapter are, in a downturn, worth more than any clever marketing. The economy is not one thing — it's every market, wired together, with no manager. Understanding it means understanding how those markets feed each other. Read the dials as signals, not instructions. GDP, inflation, interest rates and unemployment tell you which way the wind is blowing, months before the effects reach your till. Respect the asymmetry. Revenue falls fast in a downturn; costs fall slowly. The gap is what kills businesses, so build a cash buffer in the good years and keep some cost flexibility in reserve. Treat the economy as weather. You can't change it, and you shouldn't plan as though you can. You can decide how much shelter you've built before it arrives. Watch the chain. Your suppliers' costs, your customers' wages, your lenders' rates and your government's taxes are all the same system, and all of them arrive at your door eventually. An economy is the whole system a society uses to produce, distribute and consume goods and services — and it's simply running, everywhere, all the time. It has no manager. It's the sum of millions of independent decisions, coordinated by prices rather than by anyone's plan. An economy is every market stacked together and wired up — the labour market, the product markets, the money markets — each one feeding the others. The circular flow connects households, businesses and government: wages, spending, taxes and public services moving in a loop, with everyone both a buyer and a seller. We describe it with a few dials — GDP, growth, inflation, unemployment, interest rates — each of which tells you about demand, costs, or the price of money. Economies move in a cycle, and the cycle is asymmetric: revenue rises gently and falls sharply, while fixed costs refuse to move at all. The economy sets the conditions, but it doesn't decide who wins inside them. Management, cash reserves and flexible costs are what turn a downturn into somebody else's opportunity. Next, we'll look at the very different ways societies choose to organise that system — from free markets to central planning — and at what each one means for the business running inside it.

item.title: 18-4 Costs vs. The Other Factors
item.description:
Part of 18 CostsCosts are strange company among the business factors. Almost every other factor on the list is something you acquire — a market, a product, a store, a member of staff. Cost is what every one of those decisions leaves behind. It is the receipt. Which means you can't really understand cost by looking at cost alone; you understand it by putting it next to everything else and asking the only question that matters: is this worth what it takes?That's what this subsection does. We'll walk the full list of factors and, for each one, look at the two-way relationship — how that factor drives costs, and how your cost position changes what you can do with it. Hold one idea in your head the whole way through: every factor is a cost decision wearing a costume.Before the factor-by-factor tour, here's the mental model. Your operating factors push costs up. The market and your competitors set the price you can charge. Profit lives in the gap.
If your floor rises above the ceiling, you don't have a business — you have a hobby with invoices. Everything below is really about managing that gap.Start with the container. The form a company takes is itself a cost decision before a single product exists. A sole trader has almost no compliance overhead; a limited company adds accounting, filing, audit and insurance costs, but gains limited liability and cheaper access to capital. A group with five subsidiaries carries administration costs that a single trading company never sees.Company size matters just as much. Bigger companies spread fixed costs — rent, software licences, a finance team, a warehouse — across more units, so cost per unit falls. That's an economy of scale, and it's one of the most reliable sources of competitive advantage there is. But it isn't free: past a certain size, coordination costs, management layers and bureaucracy start pushing unit costs back up. This is why "just get bigger" is not a strategy. Remember the Foundations chapter's point that good management makes or breaks a business — the difference between scale that helps and scale that bloats is management, not ambition.For most businesses selling anything other than pure software, people are the largest controllable cost line.Labour is where the crudest mistake in business gets made: assuming the cheapest worker is the cheapest labour. Labour cost is not a wage; it's a cost per unit of output. A skilled machinist at £25 an hour who produces 30 good parts costs you 83p a part. An untrained worker at £12 an hour producing 8 parts, half of which get scrapped, costs you £3 a part. Add recruitment, training, sick pay, employer taxes, and the turnover cost of hiring again in four months, and the "cheap" option is often the expensive one. The genuine trade-off is labour versus machinery: replacing people with equipment converts a variable cost into a fixed cost, which lowers cost per unit at high volume and destroys you at low volume.Staff — the salaried, ongoing layer of the business — behaves differently again. Staff costs are largely fixed and largely invisible to the person making the decision to hire. The tell-tale metric is revenue per employee: how much output each person's cost is buying. If that number drifts down for two years while headcount grows, you have a cost problem hiding inside a growth story.Management is the meta-factor. Managers don't just incur costs; they decide them. A budget is a management document. A make-or-buy call is a management call. A decision to accept a 2% defect rate is a decision to carry the cost of rework forever. Poor management doesn't show up on the P&L as a line called "bad management" — it shows up as overtime, waste, rework, refunds, and customers who leave. Good management, by contrast, is the only factor that can reduce several cost lines at the same time.This trio is the physical cost base.Suppliers look like pure cost — their invoice is your cost. But the purchase price is only part of the story. Total cost of ownership includes delivery reliability, defect rates, lead times, and how much stock you have to hold because you can't trust them. A supplier 6% cheaper who misses one delivery a quarter may cost you far more in expedited shipping and lost sales. Payment terms are a separate lever again: 60 days to pay doesn't lower your cost, it lowers your cash requirement — a distinction we'll return to under Financials, and one that trips up a surprising number of otherwise competent owners. Meanwhile, a single-source supplier is cheap and fragile; dual-sourcing costs a little more and buys resilience.Raw materials are the most volatile factor on the list. Commodity prices move for reasons entirely outside your control, and a 30% rise in your main input can wipe out a thin margin in one quarter. Your weapons here are substitution, buying forward, careful specification, and yield. That last one is underrated: cheap material that generates 12% scrap is more expensive per finished unit than good material with 3% scrap. Buying in bulk lowers unit price and raises storage cost and cash tied up — a cost you've moved, not removed.Manufacturing is where all of this gets converted into unit economics. Cost per unit falls as volume rises, because setup time, machine depreciation and factory rent get spread across more items. Run a plant at 60% capacity and your unit costs are dreadful; run it at 95% and they're excellent — until a breakdown stops everything and you start paying overtime at a premium. The make-versus-buy question lives here too, and it's never just arithmetic: making it yourself gives you control and absorbs fixed costs; buying it in gives you flexibility and someone else's fixed costs to worry about.Now the offer and the route to the buyer.Product is where costs are designed in. Every feature, every material choice, every packaging flourish is a cost committed months or years before the customer ever sees it. Two products can look nearly identical on the shelf and differ by 40% in cost, purely through design choices. This is why value engineering — stripping cost without stripping what the customer actually values — is one of the highest-leverage skills in business. The Product Life Cycle chapter adds a timing dimension: unit costs are highest at introduction (low volumes absorbing fixed costs), fall through growth, and then in maturity the price starts eroding faster than costs fall. Maturity is when a comfortable business quietly becomes an unprofitable one.Distribution is a cost-structure choice disguised as a logistics question. Sell direct and you take on warehouses, delivery vans, drivers and a website — high fixed costs, but you keep the whole margin and own the customer. Sell through wholesalers and retailers and you swap fixed costs for a big chunk of margin given away on every unit. Neither is right; they suit different volumes. Below a certain volume, direct distribution's fixed costs will crush you; above it, third-party margins become an expensive habit.Stores are the purest fixed-cost commitment in retail. Rent is due whether anyone walks in or not, which means a store's whole economics come down to footfall per pound of rent — or in the online equivalent, sales per pound of fulfilment cost. Two shops can pay identical rent and one is a goldmine and the other a slow bleed, based entirely on what walks through the door. Fixed costs are wonderful when volumes are high and merciless when they aren't, which is why downturns kill retailers faster than almost anyone else.Here's the demand side, where your costs meet reality.Market sets the ceiling. In a price-sensitive market, a high-cost operator simply cannot compete — buyers will take the cheap option every time. In a market that values quality, speed or brand, a higher cost base is survivable because the price ceiling is higher too. The size of the market matters for a subtler reason: a small market may never give you enough volume to absorb your fixed costs, no matter how good you are. Entering a market is a cost decision before it's a revenue decision.Competitors turn cost from a number into a relative number. You don't need low costs; you need costs that let you survive at the price your rivals set. A price war is a contest of cost positions — the firm with the lowest cost per unit can hold a lower price for longer, and eventually the higher-cost firm runs out of cash. This is why cost advantage is one of the few genuinely durable moats: brand can fade, features can be copied, but a structural cost advantage is very hard to dislodge. Rivals also affect your costs directly, by bidding up the wages and materials you both need.Sales is where cost has a per-customer flavour. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) — everything you spend to win one customer — must be covered by what that customer is worth over their life. A sales team on salary is a fixed cost; a commission-only team is variable. Both are legitimate, but a business that grows its headcount of salaried sellers before proving the CAC-to-value maths is buying revenue at a loss and calling it growth.Customer Service is the classic "cost centre" that isn't. On the surface it's pure expense: staff, systems, refunds. Underneath, it's the thing that stops the customer leaving, and acquiring a replacement customer usually costs several times more than keeping the one you have. The strategic move is not to cut service costs but to find their root cause: a great deal of service cost is really the cost of a product defect, a confusing instruction, or a broken process. Fix those and service costs fall while revenue rises.Financials are the scoreboard that reveals cost at all. Without accounting you don't know your costs — you feel them. Financial statements turn the physical reality of wages, rent and materials into numbers you can compare, trend and act on. Two cautions. First, depreciation and accruals spread a cost across time, so profit and cash tell different stories. Second, allocated overhead can mislead: a product shown as "profitable" after overhead allocation may still be consuming cash. Also note that a cost incurred is not a cost paid: the timing of payments is a cash question, not a profit question, and confusing the two is one of the most common ways profitable businesses go bust.Revenue is the other half of every cost decision. Revenue without reference to cost is a vanity number. The joining concept is contribution margin: price minus the variable cost of delivering one more unit. That single figure tells you whether extra volume helps or hurts, and how much you must sell before fixed costs are covered. A business can grow revenue, celebrate, and go bankrupt — because it bought each sale for more than it earned. Costs are finite; there's a floor to how much you can cut. Revenue has no such ceiling. That asymmetry is the reason a good strategist treats cost cutting as damage control and growth as the mission.Three external forces that reshape your cost base without asking permission.Economy. Inflation raises input costs, often faster than you can raise prices. Interest rates change the cost of borrowing and therefore whether that new machine or store is worth financing. Exchange rates change the cost of anything you import. Recessions hit the revenue side and the cost side simultaneously — volumes fall, so your fixed costs get spread over fewer units and unit costs rise just as buyers become more price-sensitive. That double squeeze is why timing matters so much when you commit to fixed costs.Tax. Tax is a cost, but a strange one: it's a share of your success, not a hurdle you must clear before you can trade. That matters strategically. Tax-deductible business costs are effectively cheaper than they appear, because part of the expense is shared with the government — which is one reason decisions made on headline price alone get it wrong. Watch the distinction between taxes on profit, which only bite when you're winning, and taxes on employment or consumption, which are real operating costs you build into your price from day one.Regulations. Compliance is a cost with no revenue attached — and its cost scales with size, which means it hurts small firms more per pound of revenue. Oddly, that's a competitive advantage for established players: regulation is a wall that keeps newcomers out. But regulation also raises genuine risks, since the cost of getting compliance wrong (fines, shutdowns, lawsuits) dwarfs the cost of getting it right. Treat compliance spend as insurance with a legally mandated premium.Picture a small roastery selling bags at £22 each, mostly through its own shop and website. Incremental cost per retail bag — beans, bag, label, power, packing time — is about £6. Nice contribution margin.A local café chain offers to take 400 bags a month on a wholesale basis at £9 a bag. New incremental cost per bag for the wholesale format: plainer packaging, larger bags, bigger roast batches, a bit less labour per kilo — call it £6.50. Contribution: £2.50 a bag, or £1,000 a month. Not exciting.Now put it next to the other factors: Manufacturing and Stores: the roaster already sits half-idle on weekday mornings, and the rent is fixed. Those 400 bags use capacity that currently earns nothing. The relevant comparison isn't £2.50 versus £16 — it's £2.50 versus £0. Labour: the wholesale run adds packing hours, pushing one part-timer from 16 to 22 hours a week — cheap, because no new hire or training is needed yet. Competitors: the café is also quoting a roaster across town at £8.50. Undercutting to win would shave contribution to £2, and if the rival pushes to £8, Ember & Oak still survives where the rival — newer, higher rent, less efficient — does not. Raw materials and Economy: green bean prices jump 30%. Retail price can rise £1 with a shrug. The wholesale contract is fixed at £9 for twelve months — contribution drops to well under £1 a bag. Suddenly 400 bags of low-margin work is crowding out the higher-margin retail roast. Customer Service and Sales: wholesale accounts complain less and reorder without marketing spend, so CAC is near zero. But losing the account later costs a fifth of revenue in one email. Financials: the £1,000 a month is profitable in the accounts but arrives 45 days after invoicing, while the beans are paid for on delivery. Profitable and cash-hungry at the same time. That's the whole discipline in one decision. Not "is £2.50 enough?", but "enough compared to what, in light of everything else, and what happens if the world moves?" Cost is the receipt for every other factor. To judge a cost properly, you have to judge it against what it buys. Company form and size decide your fixed-cost base and how thinly you can spread it. Labour, Staff and Management are usually the biggest controllable cost — and cheap labour is often the expensive option. Management doesn't just incur costs, it decides them. Suppliers, Raw Materials and Manufacturing are the physical cost base: purchase price is only part of total cost, and yield, reliability and utilisation matter as much as price. Product, Distribution and Stores are where cost is designed in, channels are chosen, and fixed costs are committed. Design and channel decisions are cost decisions in disguise. Market, Competitors, Sales and Customer Service set the ceiling your costs must fit under. Cost matters relative to rivals, and service is revenue protection dressed as a cost centre. Financials and Revenue are the measurement layer. Contribution margin is the bridge; remember that a cost incurred is not a cost paid, and that revenue has no ceiling while cost cutting does. Economy, Tax and Regulations reshape your cost base from outside — through inflation, interest rates, deductibility, and compliance walls that hurt small firms most. The strategic takeaway: cost is the factor you control most directly and the one most easily mismanaged, because the cuts that look best on this month's P&L are often the ones that quietly drain next year's revenue. Cut what doesn't create value. Protect what does. And never lose sight of the gap between the floor and the ceiling — that gap is the business.
item.guid: Business Management/18 Costs/18-4 Costs vs. The Other Factors.md

item.title: 18-3 Costs as a Factor Across the Whole Business
item.description:
Part of 18 CostsCosts have an image problem. Revenue is exciting, profit is the scoreboard, and costs are the boring line in the middle that everyone wants to shrink and nobody wants to talk about. That reputation is undeserved, because costs are where strategy actually gets decided.Here's the uncomfortable truth: you don't get to choose what you charge. The market does — buyers, rivals, substitutes, whatever the customer's next-best option happens to be. Remember the two sandwich shops from the opening of this book: same street, same footfall, same prices, same wholesaler, and one owner keeps $170 a day while the other keeps $30. Nothing about their revenue explains the gap. Their costs do.That's why costs deserve to be treated not as a list, but as a factor running through the entire business. Every decision you've met in this book — which supplier, how many staff, whether to buy the second oven, where to put the shop, which channel to sell through, how fast to promise delivery — eventually arrives on your cost sheet. Nothing escapes it. So let's pull back and see how it all connects.Start with the loop you've seen throughout this book, and notice what feeds it.
Read the two arrows arriving at margin. One is the price, which the Market and Competitors chapters showed you rarely control. The other is cost per unit, which is largely yours. In a competitive market, cost is the lever you can actually pull — which is why the Types of Competition chapter kept pointing out that commodity producers compete almost entirely on efficiency.That's not a small point. It means cost isn't an accounting chore sitting at the end of the year. It's the half of the profit equation you own.You've already met the fixed-and-variable split in the Types of Costs section. What matters here is what that split does strategically.Variable costs rise and fall with what you sell. Flour, packaging, hourly labour, delivery fuel. They're forgiving: sell nothing, and they mostly disappear.Fixed costs don't move. Rent, salaried managers, machine leases, insurance, software subscriptions. They're a bet on volume — and the bet cuts both ways. Run a lot of volume and each unit carries only a sliver of them, which is why scale is such a powerful cost lever. Run too little and every unit carries a crushing share.This is operating leverage, and it's the single most useful idea in this subsection. A business with high fixed costs and low variable costs makes beautiful money above its break-even point — and bleeds catastrophically below it. A business with mostly variable costs survives a quiet quarter but never gets rich on scale.You've met this trade disguised in several places already: the second oven in the Manufacturing chapter, the shop lease in Stores, the automated production line in Types of Manufacturing, the permanent-versus-casual ladder in Labour. Every one of them swaps flexibility for a lower cost per unit at volume.And it's why the product life cycle matters so much to costs. Investing in fixed capacity makes brilliant sense for a product in growth and terrifying sense for one in decline. The kit doesn't care which stage you're in.If costs were just numbers, you could only stare at them. But they have causes, and every cause is a lever. The main ones: Scale. Spreading fixed costs over more units, plus better terms from suppliers as your volumes grow. Straight from the Suppliers chapter — volume is your strongest negotiating chip. Utilisation. An oven running half-full, a van making one delivery, a shop assistant standing idle at 2pm. Underused capacity costs the same as full capacity and earns nothing. Learning and design. People get faster at repeated work, and — more powerfully — most of a product's cost is locked in by how it was designed. The Product chapter's warning that product decisions lock in costs belongs right here. Technology. Better tools turn variable labour hours into fixed investment. Whether that's good depends entirely on your volume. Input prices. Flour, fuel, energy, wages — set by markets you don't control, as the Raw Materials and Economy chapters make clear. Waste. Spillage, rework, spoilage, downtime, mistakes. Money already spent, generating no revenue. It's the cheapest saving in any business, because it needs no negotiation and no extra customers. Priya is offered a contract to supply 200 loaves a week to a café chain at £2.60 each. Revenue is easy: £520 a week.Now watch where the costs actually land.The contract contributes £80 a week. Notice what happens if Priya only counts what most people count — the flour. She'd have told herself this was a £280-a-week contract. The difference between £280 and £80 lives entirely in cost lines that never appear on the ingredients invoice: labour, energy, packaging, Distribution, and the admin that Sales quietly generates.That's the whole point of treating costs as a factor across the business. The visible cost is rarely the whole cost. The Suppliers chapter's total cost of ownership idea, and the cost to serve idea from Customer Service, are the same lesson wearing different hats.There's a cash dimension too. To serve this contract Priya needs a bigger flour buffer — say £600 of stock sitting in the back room — and the café chain will pay her on 30-day terms. So she funds a month of £440 weeks before a penny comes back. That's not a cost on the profit statement; it's a cash squeeze that can still sink her. Costs are a Financials question as much as a profit question.When money gets tight, the instinct is to cut costs. It's a good instinct pointed in a dangerous direction, because not all costs are equal.Waste — the loaf that gets binned, the hour lost to rework, the insurance you're paying on a machine you sold — is pure loss. Cutting it is unambiguously good.But plenty of costs are actually investments in disguise: staff training, machine maintenance, quality ingredients, marketing, decent wages. Cut these and the savings arrive this month, while the damage arrives over the next year — higher turnover, more breakdowns, worse reviews, fewer customers. You saw that spiral in the management chapter: cuts to training raise turnover, turnover raises mistakes, mistakes lose customers, lost customers force more cuts.The test to apply to any cost line is simple: does this buy something the customer is paying for? If yes, it's an investment and you should be asking whether it earns its keep, not whether it can be trimmed. If no, cut it today.A durable cost advantage is one of the best assets a business can have, because it gives you choices a rival doesn't have: charge less and win on price, or charge the same and bank a fatter margin. That fatter margin funds the reinvestment arrow in the diagram — better equipment, better people, better terms — and the advantage compounds exactly as the management loop described.But two warnings.An advantage you can't defend isn't an advantage. If your only edge is buying more cheaply this month, a rival can match it next month. Real cost advantage comes from hard-to-copy things: scale, a better-designed product, a smarter process, a location, a relationship.Cost-cutting races hurt everyone. When rivals in an oligopoly all cut to win share, prices fall faster than costs can, and the whole industry's margins get shredded — the price war from the Types of Competition chapter. Being the low-cost producer is a strategy. Being one of five firms all trying the same trick is usually just a way to work harder for less.Some of your biggest cost movements aren't decisions at all. They're weather. The economy. Inflation lifts input prices and wage expectations; interest rates decide what that new oven or shop lease really costs you over five years. High-fixed-cost businesses feel this hardest, because their commitments are locked in while prices move. Tax. Payroll taxes, sales taxes, property taxes and duties all sit on your cost base. Two employees on the same salary can cost very different amounts once the full picture is counted — the Tax chapter's point about the true cost of a hire. Regulations. Compliance, safety, labelling, environmental rules — each one adds cost, and each one raises the bar for newcomers, which quietly protects whoever's already in. Suppliers and raw materials. A harvest, a shipping route, a currency swing. The Economy chapter explains the ripples; your job is planning for them rather than being surprised by them. You can't control these. You can choose how exposed to them you are — which is a cost-structure decision, made in advance. Know your structure, not just your total. Fixed versus variable, direct versus indirect, cost per unit and break-even volume. Those four numbers tell you how hard a quiet month hits and how much volume you need to be safe. Follow the cost of a decision all the way through. Every choice has cost consequences in several places — labour, energy, packaging, delivery, admin, stock, cash. Count them before you commit, not after. Manage by driver, not by total. Totals tell you what happened. Utilisation, waste, yield, scale and lead times tell you why, and they're the things you can actually change. Separate waste from investment. Cut waste ruthlessly. Test every other cost against whether the customer is paying for it. Remember costs are cash. Money goes out early and comes back late. Growth is the time when a profitable cost structure can still kill you. Treat it as a control loop. Plan the cost base, organise the resources that generate it, lead the people who spend it, then check it on a rhythm — weekly for materials and labour, monthly for overheads. Budgets set in January and unopened until December aren't control; they're archaeology. And keep your eye on the point of it all. Costs aren't the enemy. Unnecessary costs are. The goal was never a cheap business — it was a profitable one, and profit is what's left when the market has set your price and your costs have done their worst. Profit is revenue minus costs, and the market sets the revenue. Costs are the half of the equation you actually control — which is why they're strategic, not administrative. Costs have two dimensions: how much, and how they behave. Fixed costs are a bet on volume; variable costs are flexibility at the price of a higher cost per unit. That trade-off — operating leverage — is why scale makes money above break-even and bleeds below it. Costs are driven by scale, utilisation, learning, design, technology, input prices and waste. Each driver is a lever; waste is the cheapest one to pull. Every decision carries costs in several places at once. The visible cost — flour, components — is rarely the whole cost. Count labour, energy, packaging, distribution, admin, stock and cash too. Not all costs are equal. Waste should go; training, maintenance and quality are investments that pay back over time. Cutting them saves money this month and costs more next year. A defensible cost advantage is a genuine competitive weapon that compounds through reinvestment — but cost-cutting races between rivals destroy everyone's margins. Outside forces — the economy, tax, regulation, input markets — move your costs whether you plan for them or not. What you control is how exposed your cost structure leaves you. The strategist's habit: know your structure and break-even, follow each decision's full cost, manage by driver, cut waste not capability, watch the cash, and check the numbers on a rhythm.
item.guid: Business Management/18 Costs/18-3 Costs as a Factor Across the Whole Business.md

item.title: 18-2 Types of Costs
item.description:
Part of 18 CostsLook at a business's costs and they seem like one big pile — money out, listed in a column. But that pile is doing at least four quite different things at once, and the differences decide almost everything: what happens to your profit when sales dip, whether a new order is worth taking, where your break-even sits, and how badly a price war hurts you.Sorting costs into types is the most useful half-hour of arithmetic a manager can do. Get it right, and your accounts stop being a record of the past and start being a tool for decisions.Every cost in your business can be interrogated with a single question: If I sold one more unit tomorrow, would this number change? Answer that honestly for each line and you've already done most of the work. The rest of this subsection is about naming what you find — and knowing which type of cost you're looking at is what tells you whether a decision will help or hurt.Direct costs can be traced to a specific thing you sell. The flour in a loaf, the steel in a bike frame, the card-processing fee on one transaction. If you stopped selling that item tomorrow, the direct cost would vanish with it.Indirect costs — usually called overhead — keep the place running but belong to no single unit. The rent, the insurance, the accountant's fee, the cleaner, the wifi. Sell a thousand loaves or none, the bill arrives the same.You've met this split twice already in different clothes. The Raw Materials chapter separated direct materials (which become the product) from indirect materials like machine oil and cleaning fluid. The Labour chapter did the same for people: direct labour touches the product, indirect labour supervises, cleans and files. Same distinction, three costumes.It matters because it decides where a cost sits — in the cost of goods sold, right next to the product, or up in overhead. That affects how you price, how you compare products, and which products turn out to be quietly losing you money.Now the big one. This is the split that decides your break-even, your risk and, frankly, whether your business survives a bad quarter.Fixed costs don't move with how much you sell in the short run. Rent, business rates, insurance, a salaried manager, the machine lease, the website subscription. You pay them whether you sell a hundred units or a thousand.Variable costs rise and fall with each unit. Flour, packaging, hourly wages, delivery charges, a platform's commission. Sell nothing and they're near zero; double your output and they roughly double.Stepped costs are the awkward middle. Fixed up to a point, then they jump. Your oven bakes 200 loaves a day; want 400 and you need a second oven, which is a whole new lump of fixed cost. A second delivery van, a second supervisor, an extra warehouse — these are steps, not slopes.
Here's the strategic punchline. Fixed costs are a bet; variable costs are a tax. Every pound you convert from variable to fixed — automating a task, hiring a permanent employee, signing a warehouse lease — is a bet that volume will come. Win the bet and your cost per unit falls. Lose it and you're paying for capacity that isn't working. Remember the Manufacturing chapter's furniture workshop: the automated line only wins above about 1,000 units a month, and bleeds badly below it.It's also why the Labour chapter's ladder of commitment matters so much. Every rung you move down — permanent, part-time, fixed-term, casual, agency — shifts labour from fixed to variable. You buy the ability to shrink your wage bill when demand does, and pay for it in consistency, skill and loyalty.Once you know what's fixed and what's variable, three numbers fall out of them: Total cost = fixed costs + variable costs. The whole bill. Average cost per unit = total cost ÷ units produced. This falls as volume rises, because the fixed costs get spread over more units. It's why factories chase scale. Marginal cost = the cost of producing one more unit. Usually it's just the variable cost — the oven's already hot, the rent's already paid. That third one sounds technical and is actually the most useful. Decisions are made at the margin. If Priya's marginal cost of a loaf is £1.20, then any sale above £1.20 adds something, even one that looks "too cheap" against her average cost.Which is exactly where a lot of businesses get themselves into trouble — because they price against average cost and turn down work that would have made them money.The gap between the price of a unit and its variable cost has a name.Contribution = selling price − variable cost per unit.It's called contribution because that's what it does: it contributes towards your fixed costs, and once the fixed costs are covered, it becomes profit. It's the number you met in the Suppliers, Manufacturing and Sales chapters, and here's where it comes from.Priya's bakery makes it concrete. Her loaf sells for £4.00. Ingredients cost £1.20. Her daily fixed costs — rent, salaries, energy — are £230.Contribution per loaf is £2.80. So her break-even is £230 ÷ £2.80 ≈ 82 loaves a day. Below 82 she loses money; above it, every extra loaf drops £2.80 straight onto the bottom line. That's the whole logic of scale in one sum.Now watch it earn its keep. A café offers to buy 50 loaves a day at wholesale — £2.60 each, well below her counter price. Bad deal?Not necessarily. Contribution is £1.40 a loaf, so 50 loaves adds £70 a day. Her fixed costs are already covered by her counter trade. If the run can be done with the van already going that way, that £70 is nearly pure profit — a 40% jump on her £50 a day.But if the order needs a dedicated morning delivery run at £80 a day, the answer flips: £70 of contribution against £80 of new cost is a loss. That's the difference between a relevant cost (the new delivery) and an irrelevant one (the rent she's paying anyway). Which brings us neatly to the trickiest type of all.A sunk cost is money already spent and impossible to recover. The market survey for a product you've now shelved. The £8,000 spent developing a feature nobody wants. The deposit on a venue you've outgrown.Here's the rule, and it's a hard one to follow: sunk costs are irrelevant to the next decision. The only question that matters is what happens from here — what you'll spend next and what you'll get back.That sounds obvious and almost nobody does it. You'll hear it in every boardroom: "we've put so much into this already, we can't stop now." That's the sunk-cost fallacy, and it's how businesses throw good money after bad for years. The £8,000 is gone either way. Spending £20,000 more to "justify" it doesn't recover anything — it just adds £20,000 to the loss.The discipline is simple: cross out every cost that's already been paid, and decide on what's left.Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you gave up when you made a choice.Priya's back room holds the flour. It could hold something else — a bigger counter, a small seating area, a second fridge of cakes. Whatever she gives up by using that space for flour is a real cost of keeping flour, and it appears on no statement anywhere.This idea runs through the whole book once you start looking: Shelves. Every square metre given to slow-moving stock is a square metre not given to something that sells — the Stores chapter's core problem, measured in stockturn rather than rent. The owner's time. The Labour chapter's blunt lesson: a business that only looks profitable because the owner is quietly donating fifty hours a week isn't profitable, it's subsidised. Those hours had an alternative use. Channels. Selling through a platform that takes 25% isn't just a fee — the Distribution chapter's question is what the next best channel would have earned. Cash. Money sitting in stock is money that can't buy an oven, pay down debt, or sit in the bank — the Financials chapter's working-capital squeeze, arriving from a different direction. Opportunity cost is invisible to accounting and decisive for strategy. If you only ever count the money that left, you'll systematically overvalue the status quo and undervalue change.One last cut, and it's about attention as much as money.Controllable costs are the ones your decisions move: what you buy, who you buy it from, how much you waste, how you schedule staff, what you pay for a delivery.Uncontrollable costs arrive from outside: business rates, interest rates, the world price of flour, wage inflation, a change in tax or regulation. The Economy, Tax and Regulations chapters all deliver these straight to your door.The point of the split isn't to shrug at the uncontrollable ones — it's to stop wasting management energy arguing with the weather and point it at what you can actually move. Remember the Suppliers chapter's test: how easily could I walk away? A cost you can switch supplier on is controllable. A cost set by a world market is not, and your only real responses there are to reduce how much you need of it, substitute something else, or redesign the product so the cost matters less.One quiet caveat hangs over all of this. In the short run, many costs are fixed. In the long run, almost none of them are.This month, Priya's lease is fixed — she signed it. Over three years, it isn't: she can renegotiate, move, or go smaller. The oven is fixed today; over five years it's a decision.That's why a choice that makes no sense right now can make perfect sense on a longer view, and vice versa. It's also why fixed costs feel so heavy in a tough quarter: you're stuck with a decision you made when things looked different. The product life cycle chapter makes the same point from the other direction — dedicated equipment is comfortable in growth and terrifying in decline. Ask one question of every cost: would this change if I sold one more unit? The answer sorts the pile. Direct costs trace to a specific product; indirect costs (overhead) keep the business running. The same split appears in materials and labour. Fixed costs don't move with volume; variable costs do; stepped costs are fixed until they jump. Converting variable to fixed is a bet on volume. Total, average and marginal are three views of the same money. Average cost falls with scale; decisions are made at the margin. Contribution (price − variable cost) is what each sale hands over to cover fixed costs. Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit — the single most useful sum in this chapter. Sunk costs are already spent and must be ignored in forward decisions, however much they hurt. Opportunity cost — the value of the best alternative forgone — never appears on an invoice and shapes every real strategy choice. Separate controllable from uncontrollable costs, and spend your energy on the first. In the short run many costs are fixed; in the long run almost none are. Match the decision to the horizon. Sort your own costs into these types this week. The exercise is dull, takes an afternoon, and will tell you more about your business than any report you could buy — because it tells you exactly which levers make you money, and which ones you're only arguing with.
item.guid: Business Management/18 Costs/18-2 Types of Costs.md

item.title: 18-1 What Costs Really Mean
item.description:
Part of 18 CostsAsk most business owners what something costs them and you'll get a number off the top of their head. "Flour's about a pound twenty a loaf." That number came off an invoice, and it's not wrong — it's just roughly a third of the answer.Costs are the least glamorous subject in this book and the one that decides whether you have a business at all. Every chapter so far has quietly been spending money: suppliers, raw materials, labour, manufacturing, stores, distribution, sales, service. This chapter is where all that spending gets named, added up, and — if you're any good at this — reduced. But before we can sort costs into types, we need to be precise about what a cost actually is, because the everyday meaning is narrower than the real one.A cost is the value of the resources a business gives up in order to get something.Three phrases in that sentence are carrying the weight.Value of the resources. Costs are measured in money, but they aren't always paid in money. The fifty unpaid hours Priya works every week have a cost — the Labour chapter was blunt about this. So does the stock that spoiled in the back room, and so does the wear on an oven that nobody invoices you for.Gives up. Cost is the sacrifice side of every decision. You hand over something — cash, stock, time, a machine's working life — and you get something back. Cost is what it took.In order to get something. This is the phrase people skip. A cost doesn't exist on its own; it exists against a purpose. Spending £40 on a second-hand display case is a cost if it sells more buns and pure waste if it doesn't. The money looks identical in both cases.Which leads to the reframe that runs through this whole chapter: every cost is a decision made visible. A cost line isn't an abstract number that happens to you. It's the footprint of a choice somebody made — to buy, to hire, to build, to discount, to keep something too long. When you look at your costs, you're not auditing arithmetic. You're auditing decisions.Here's the muddle that catches nearly everyone. The price you pay a supplier is not the cost of what you bought. It's the first instalment of it.The Suppliers chapter made this point with total cost of ownership, and it's worth one line here because it's the same idea wearing different clothes. A cheap flour has a price of £17 a sack. Its cost includes what you pay for delivery, what you lose to damp in the back room, the cash tied up in having bought a month's worth at once, and the batch that turns out wrong and has to be binned.
Photo by Chris Spain on PexelsSo when someone says "our costs went up", always ask which one they mean: the price you were quoted, the spend you actually handed over, or the cost you truly incurred to get the thing and have it ready to use. They're three different numbers, and only the middle one shows up on a receipt.This is where cost and cash part company, and it trips up beginners constantly.Timing. You pay for a machine today and use it for ten years. The cash left in one go, but the cost arrives slowly, in small slices, as the machine wears out. Accountants call those slices depreciation, and the Financials chapter will show you why it matters. The same is true in reverse: buy flour now on 30-day terms and you've incurred the cost today but parted with no cash at all.Non-cash costs. The owner's unpaid labour. A spoiled pallet nobody invoiced you for. The value of a van quietly losing worth every month. Real costs, no bank transfer.That's why a business can be profitable on paper and out of cash, or flush with cash and losing money. Both happen, both are dangerous, and both are invisible if you only ever look at one column. Costs and cash are two views of the same business, and you need both.Nobody prices "total costs". You price a loaf, a haircut, an hour of advice. So the cost that matters is almost always cost per unit.And here's the twist that makes costs so interesting: cost per unit depends on how many units you make. Some costs rise every time you bake another loaf — flour, bags, gas. Others sit there regardless: the rent, the insurance, Dario's wage whether the ovens run or not. Spread those fixed costs over 100 loaves and they're small; spread them over 30 and they're crushing. Same recipe, same suppliers, wildly different cost per loaf — purely because of volume.We'll sort those two behaviours properly in the next subsection. For now, hold onto the shape of it:
Each arrow widens the number and narrows what you can do with it — until, at the end, you have the only figure that tells you whether a sale is worth having.Sunk costs are behind you. Money already spent, already gone, unrecoverable. The oven you bought last year. The stock that didn't sell. Here's the discipline: sunk costs should have no vote in what you do next. The only question that matters is whether what's ahead of you earns more than what's ahead of you costs.The trap is emotional, and it's everywhere: "we've put £8,000 into this, we can't stop now." You can. The £8,000 is gone either way. Continuing because of money you've already lost just adds a second loss on top of the first — which is precisely the spiral from the Why Good Management Makes or Breaks a Business section, where each bad turn makes the next one worse.Opportunity costs are beside you. This is the value of the best thing you gave up. When Priya spends Saturday morning running the market stall, the cost isn't just the stall fee — it's the wedding-cake consultations she didn't hold, and the rest she didn't get. Opportunity cost never appears in any account, and it's often the largest cost in the building.That's why strategy is mostly a series of noes. Every yes commits resources that can't be somewhere else: the oven's hours, the owner's attention, the £4,000 of spare cash. The Competitors chapter called choosing which fights to enter the biggest decision management makes. Opportunity cost is the price tag on that decision.Revenue minus costs is profit. That's the whole income statement in five words, and the Revenue chapter took one half of it. This chapter takes the other.Here's why this half deserves the attention. Revenue is largely what the market allows you — the going price, the elasticity of demand, what the shop down the road is charging. Costs are largely what you allow yourself. One is negotiated in a market you don't control. The other is a set of decisions you make in your own building.That asymmetry is the whole reason costs reward study. When the Market chapter said "you don't argue with the market price — you lower your costs," this is what it meant.And one caution, because cost-cutting has a bad reputation for good reason: costs are not the enemy. A business with no costs is a business with no product, no staff and no customers. A cost that buys more than it costs is the entire mechanism of profit. The goal was never the lowest cost — it's the best ratio of cost to value delivered. A £45 tasting session that wins an £180 wedding cake is expensive and worth every penny. A £2 saving on packaging that loses you a café contract is cheap and ruinous.Let's put it together. Priya sells a counter loaf for £4.00 and a wholesale loaf to a café for £2.60.Look at the two ends of that table. The invoice says £1.20. The real cost of getting a loaf into a customer's hands is £1.65 over the counter and £1.77 to the café — between a third and a half higher.Now the consequences. The counter loaf leaves about £2.35 after its direct costs; the wholesale loaf leaves about £0.83. That's the Sales chapter's arithmetic, and now Priya can see exactly where the gap comes from — not from the recipe, which is identical, but from the delivery and the lower price. It also tells her something the invoice never would: the wholesale loaf is worth keeping anyway, because it's 400 units a month on a repeat contract with one conversation, and it uses capacity she'd otherwise waste.And notice what isn't in that table: the rent, the insurance, the till system, Dario's wage for the hours the shop is empty. Those don't rise with a loaf. Tuck them into the per-loaf figure and it changes depending on whether she bakes 30 that day or 100 — which is exactly the fixed-versus-variable question the next subsection takes on.One more thing. Last spring Priya bought £600 of proving baskets, because a supplier talked her into them. They're in the loft. That £600 is sunk — it should have no say in anything she decides now. What should have a say is the opportunity cost of her own Saturday, which she currently spends on the market stall. It appears nowhere in her accounts, and it's a real cost every single week. Count the whole cost. The invoice is the beginning, not the total. Add waste, storage, handling, delivery, the cash tied up and the cost of things going wrong. Keep cost and cash separate in your head. Both matter, they move on different timetables, and confusing them is how profitable businesses run out of money. Work in cost per unit, at your real volume. A number that assumes a busy month will mislead you in a quiet one. Ignore sunk costs; watch opportunity costs. The money behind you is gone. The thing you gave up to be here is the one nobody puts on a spreadsheet — which is exactly why it's so often missed. Remember that yes has a price. Every decision commits oven hours, staff attention or cash that can't be used elsewhere. Strategy is the art of spending those on purpose. Ask what each cost bought. A cost is a decision made visible, and decisions can be checked. Run the management loop on it — plan what you expect to spend, organise so it happens, and control it by comparing the bill against what it delivered. Then check the cheapest costs most carefully. A cost that buys less than it costs is the easiest money in the business to find, and the easiest to miss. A cost is the value of the resources a business gives up in order to get something — the sacrifice side of every decision, and a decision made visible. Price is not cost. The price you pay is the first instalment; the real cost adds waste, storage, handling, risk and tied-up cash. Cost is not the same as cash leaving the building. Depreciation, unpaid owner labour and spoiled stock are all real costs with no bank transfer — which is why profit and cash can point in opposite directions. Cost per unit is the number decisions are made with, and it depends on volume, because some costs rise with each extra unit and some don't. Sunk costs are behind you and should have no vote in what happens next. Opportunity costs sit silently beside you and are often the biggest costs of all. Profit is revenue minus costs. Revenue is what the market allows; costs are what you allow yourself — which is why this half of the equation rewards attention. Costs aren't the enemy. A cost that buys more than it costs is the mechanism of profit; the aim is the best ratio of cost to value, not the lowest number. Next, we'll take the cost base apart and sort it into types — direct and indirect, fixed and variable, and the ones that catch businesses out precisely when they can least afford it.
