item.title: 14-2 Types of Staff Roles
item.description:
Part of 14 StaffAsk a small business owner to describe their team and you'll get a list of names. Ask what each of them is actually for — what they decide on their own, what they're measured on, what breaks if they leave — and the list suddenly gets shorter.That gap is what this subsection is about. Not job titles, but roles.A role is the bundle of work, decisions and expectations attached to a position in a business — independent of whoever happens to be filling it.Break that open and three things are inside: Tasks and duties — what actually gets done. Bake the bread. Ring the customers. File the return. Authority — what this person may decide without asking. Refund £20? Yes. Refund £2,000? Not alone. Expectations — the standard it's held to, and how anyone would know. On time, no waste, no complaints, under budget. Two people with the same job title can hold completely different roles. Plenty of bakers bake; one of them is also the person who decides the morning's production quantities. And two people with different titles can hold the same role: at a three-person firm, the "office manager" and the "operations lead" are often doing one job between them.This is the same distinction the Labour chapter drew between people and effort. Staff are the people; labour is what they supply; a role is what you've agreed the effort is for.Why bother sorting roles into types at all? Because the type predicts three things you care about: What it costs — and whether that cost rises with sales or sits there in a quiet month. How easily it's covered — could you replace it next week, or not for six months? How it's managed — what you can honestly measure it on. Get the type wrong and you'll measure a creative role on output, a production role on charm, and a support role on nothing at all. That last one is how headcount quietly creeps.You can slice a workforce a dozen ways. Four cuts do nearly all the work, and every real role sits at a point on all four at once.
Change any one and you change the cost, the hiring pool and the management style.This is the cut most people mean when they say "what do you do?" And it's the same set of parts you met in The Parts of a Company, now with names attached.Two reminders from earlier chapters. Core and support is not a ranking — it's a statement about whether the role touches the product or the customer directly. In a bank, IT is core; in a bakery, it's a laptop somebody sorts out on a Sunday. And support roles grow in steps, not smoothly. A firm with three people needs no finance function. A firm with thirty needs a person doing nothing else.Here's a wrinkle worth knowing, partly because it's a genuine piece of management vocabulary and partly because it's a delightful accident that it appears in a chapter called Staff.Line roles produce or deliver the thing the customer pays for, and they carry authority over the chain of work. The head baker is a line role. So is the salesperson and the van driver. Line managers can direct the people below them.Staff roles — in this specific sense — advise, support and check. The bookkeeper, the HR adviser, the health-and-safety officer, the in-house lawyer. Their authority comes from expertise, not command. An accountant can tell you that your margins are heading the wrong way; they can't order the bakery manager to change the recipe.So "staff" is doing two jobs in this book. In everyday use it means the workforce — all the people. In organisation theory it means the roles that support the line. A line baker and a staff accountant are both "staff" in the first sense and on opposite sides in the second. If a consultant ever looks at you oddly when you use the word, that's why.Why it matters practically: line roles tend to grow with volume; staff roles tend to grow with complexity — new regulations, new tax rules, new systems, new risks. That's a legitimate reason for them to exist, and it's also why they can multiply faster than revenue unless somebody owns the headcount decision. This is the Costs chapter's fixed-cost problem in human form: a salaried support role is a cost you carry whether you sell one loaf or a thousand.Sort roles by how far their decisions reach and you get four levels. The Core Jobs Every Manager Does section showed that the mix of planning, organizing, leading and controlling shifts as you climb. Here's the same shift from the role's point of view.Notice what this table quietly says: a promotion changes the job, not just the pay. The best baker in the building is not automatically a good shift lead, because the shift lead's day is mostly other people's problems. Firms get this wrong constantly, and it costs them a good baker and a bad manager.Which is why most growing businesses need somewhere for excellent doers to go that isn't management. An individual contributor track — senior baker, principal engineer, lead designer — lets someone get better and better at their craft without being pushed into a role they'll hate. That's not kindness; it's the same talent-market logic the Competitors chapter applies to customers. You compete for good people against the firms on your own street, and the ones who can offer a real future keep them.Some roles meet the customer. Some meet the customer's problem second-hand.Customer-facing roles carry the promise your brand made — the augmented product layer from the Product chapter, delivered live by a human being. Counter staff, drivers, support agents, account managers. These roles are where satisfaction is won or lost, which means their skill, training and mood are strategy, not sentiment.Back-office roles serve the people who serve the customer. A production planner, a bookkeeper, a warehouse picker. Their "customers" are internal — and internal service is just as real. A credit controller who takes three weeks to answer a query creates two angry customers, only one of whom is external.And there's the honest complication: almost everyone is customer-facing sometimes. The baker who steps out to explain why the order is late is doing front-line service that day. This is the same seam problem flagged in The Parts of a Company: from inside, six teams are doing six jobs; from outside, it's one experience with your name on it.Two shorter cuts to finish.How the role is attached to the business. Employee, contractor, agency temp, apprentice, volunteer, family member, owner. You've met the full ladder in the Labour chapter — from commitment and consistency at one end to flexibility and variable cost at the other — so we won't re-teach it here. The role-design question is simply: which attachment does this particular job actually need? A role that carries your quality standard needs someone with a reason to still be there next year. A role that covers a summer rush doesn't.Specialist or generalist. A specialist does one thing deeply; a generalist does many things adequately. Small firms are built on generalists, because ten hats can't be filled by ten people. Growth changes that, for exactly two reasons the Parts of a Company section named: volume (one person can no longer hold the work) and conflict (sales wanting speed and finance wanting control need separate owners). The moment your generalist "person who does everything admin-y" splits into a bookkeeper and a receptionist, you've paid for specialism with coordination — a new seam to manage.Before you post a job advert, a role needs answers to three questions: Purpose — what is this role for? One sentence, in terms of the business outcome, not the tasks. Measure — how will we know it's going well in a month? One or two numbers, from the table above. Boundary — what can this person decide alone, and what must come to someone else? Miss the third and you get either paralysis — everyone asking permission — or chaos, with a counter assistant refunding £200 because nobody said not to. Miss the second and you get the classic complaint: "they're lovely, but I've no idea if they're doing a good job." Miss the first and you've hired a set of tasks with no owner.This is the organizing job from the management cycle, applied to people: clear roles, clear responsibility, clear authority. When two people each think the other is ordering the flour, that isn't a personality clash. It's a role-design failure.One person. Priya holds every role at once — production, sales, procurement, finance, cleaning. She isn't a generalist by preference; she's a generalist by arithmetic. The Labour chapter's point applies: she supplies an enormous amount of effort with no staff at all.Three people. Dario bakes (operations, line). Mel bakes and covers the counter (operations plus customer-facing). A freelance bookkeeper files the returns (finance, staff role, contracted). Note what just happened: the first role Priya bought in was a support role, not a production one — because the bookkeeping was the work she was worst at and most likely to get wrong.Eleven people. Now roles have split and become visible.Six roles, six different measures — and note that the shift lead produces nothing at all. That's indirect labour in the Labour chapter's language, and it's the first role a small business resists hiring. So here's the arithmetic Priya runs when she finally takes one on.A shift lead costs about £2,200 a month, fully loaded with tax and contributions — call it £2,800. That's a pure cost, twelve months a year, whether the oven is hot or not. What it buys is roughly 25 hours a month of Priya's own attention: she stops covering shifts, stops fixing rota gaps, stops being the person who unlocks the door. She spends that attention opening a second site, which — on the numbers in the Manufacturing chapter — contributes around £1,600 a month once it passes break-even.So the role isn't justified by what the shift lead produces. It's justified by what Priya can now do instead. That's the same "hire, automate or outsource" trade-off from the Labour chapter, and it's why a role's value has to be judged against the alternative — not against a wage bill sitting alone in a spreadsheet.Forty people, two sites. Now there are functional heads, a named finance person, a part-time HR role handling rotas and hiring, and — Priya's new problem — a shortage of generalists. Everyone is a specialist, and nobody knows how the whole thing fits together. That's the seam problem arriving with a payroll attached, and her fix isn't a new role. It's a person whose role is to sit across the boundaries.Promoting your best doer into a role they don't want. The craftsperson and the supervisor are different jobs. Offer a path that doesn't require leaving the craft.Letting support roles grow unwatched. Every staff role is a fixed cost, and each new rule, system or regulation spawns a plausible reason for one. Justify each by what it prevents or enables, not by how busy the person looks.Designing roles around people rather than work. It's comfortable in the short term and disastrous in the long term, because when the person leaves the role leaves with them and nobody can say what's missing. Design the role, then find the human — not the other way round. Think in roles, then in people. A role is what the business needs; a person is who supplies it. Confusing the two is how you end up with a job nobody can describe. Use the four cuts as a checklist every time you create, review or replace a role: what work, how far it reaches, who it touches, how it's attached. Sort line from staff, and know which one grows with volume and which with complexity. Both are legitimate; only one tends to creep. Build a path for specialists. If your best doer has nowhere to progress except management, you'll lose a good doer or create a poor manager — sometimes both. Match role types to demand certainty. Permanent where demand is steady, flexible where it isn't. The Costs chapter's fixed-versus-variable split, applied to headcount. Give every role a purpose, a measure and a boundary. That's the organizing half of the management cycle, and it's the cheapest performance improvement available to you. Watch the seams, not just the boxes. Most staffing problems show up as friction between roles — Sales promising what Operations can't deliver — not as failure inside one. Measure the mix, not just the headcount. Wage cost as a percentage of revenue, output per labour hour, revenue per front-line role. A team whose shape drifts out of step with the strategy will look busy and quietly lose money. A role is the bundle of tasks, authority and expectations attached to a position — separate from the person filling it, and more useful than a job title. Four cuts sort every role: by function (operations, sales, finance, people, procurement, admin), by level (front line, supervisory, functional, senior), by contact (customer-facing or back-office), and by attachment (employee, contractor, agency, volunteer, owner). Line roles deliver the product and carry authority down the chain; staff roles advise, support and check, wielding expertise rather than command. Both are "staff" in the everyday sense — a word doing two jobs. Line roles grow with volume; support roles grow with complexity, which is why they need watching. Every one is largely a fixed cost. Promotion changes the job, not just the pay. Excellent doers need somewhere to go that isn't management. Specialists and generalists suit different stages of growth. Roles split because of volume and conflict — and every split creates a new seam to manage. Every role needs a purpose, a measure and a boundary. Most staffing failures are design failures, not people failures. The strategist's habit: choose the type of role deliberately, price it against the alternative rather than in isolation, and review whether your mix still matches what the business is trying to be.

item.title: 14-3 Staff as a Factor Across the Whole Business
item.description:
Part of 14 StaffStaff, so far, has been the people who supply the effort your business runs on. That framing is useful up close — it tells you what you're actually buying when you hire someone. But pull the camera back and something bigger appears.Every other factor in this book is inert until a person picks it up. Raw materials sit in a warehouse. Machines wait for somebody to switch them on. Money does nothing in an account. Even your systems and processes are just documents until a human being follows them. Staff aren't one factor sitting alongside the rest — they're the factor that operates all the rest. Which means a decision about your people is really a decision about your costs, your quality, your service, your cash and your competitive position, all at once.Here's the picture worth holding.
Notice that staff points at both sides of the income statement at the same time — payroll is a cost, and everything else in that list generates revenue. That double role is exactly what makes people decisions so strategically interesting, and it's why "how much do they cost?" is such a bad opening question.Notice something else too. None of those boxes is a department. A single person on a single shift might be doing three at once: making the product, serving the customer, and quietly carrying the know-how of how the place actually works. From the inside, staff looks like a function. From the customer's side, your staff are the company. Every seam the Parts of a Company section warned about is a place where two members of staff hand work to each other.Look at a wage bill and you see hours. That's the Labour chapter's view, and it's a useful one — hours are perishable and they can be measured. But what you actually lose when someone leaves is far more than hours. Tacit knowledge — the know-how that was never written down. Which oven runs hot. Which supplier's delivery arrives early, and why that matters. Which customer wants their loaf sliced. Relationships — with customers, suppliers, the bank, the inspector. These belong to a person, not to your business, however much you'd like to believe otherwise. Judgement — the accumulated sense of when to bend a rule and when not to. It's what separates twenty years of experience from twenty years of attendance. The training you already paid for — every hour you invested, walking out of the door. None of that appears on a balance sheet. All of it lands in the profit and loss account eventually, usually at the worst possible moment. Which gives you the staffing version of the Suppliers chapter's test: if this person left on Friday, what would I lose by Monday?Here's where the Product chapter pays off. A brand is a promise; the product is the keeping of it. Somebody keeps that promise every day, and it's a person, not a machine.Two things follow. Your ceiling — how good the product can be — is set by what your people can do. The finest oven in the world is useless to a baker who can't tell when dough is ready. And your floor — how bad it gets on a bad day — is set by how well trained and well supported they are. A strong team at 90% effort beats a weak team at 100%, every week of the year.Consistency is the harder half. Customers forgive an average product far more readily than an inconsistent one, and inconsistency is rarely a machine problem. It's a training problem, a rota problem, or a management problem wearing overalls.Then there's the service side. The Customer Service chapter argued that satisfaction lives in the gap between what a customer expected and what they got. That gap is closed or opened by a person, in a two-second window, with no manager present, every single time. And here's the uncomfortable bit: people serve customers roughly the way they're treated themselves. Under-trained, over-stretched staff who get hung out to dry do not walk into a customer's day and make it better.Cost. For most service businesses and plenty of others, payroll is the largest single cost line. Remember the split from Costs: salaried staff are broadly fixed (you pay them whether it's busy or not), hourly staff are more variable. And the honest figure isn't the wage — it's the fully loaded cost: wages plus payroll taxes, training, equipment, uniforms, insurance, and the productivity dip while someone learns. Two people on identical salaries can cost you very different amounts.Revenue. Staff don't only cost money, they earn it. Revenue per head is one of the bluntest and most useful numbers in business — Priya's bakery turning over £156,000 with four staff is earning £39,000 per person. Track it over time. Growth that doesn't move it usually means you're adding people simply to stand still.Timing. This is the part that catches people out. Wages go out on a fixed rhythm — weekly, fortnightly, monthly — with no flexibility whatsoever. Your customers pay you whenever they get round to it. That mismatch is the working-capital squeeze the Financials chapter describes, and payroll is the least forgiving bill a business has, because it cannot be delayed and everybody notices immediately when it is.There's a quiet symmetry that beginners miss. The Market chapter described a labour market with employers as buyers and workers as sellers, and the Competitors chapter warned that you're fighting the same firms on that street. Put them together: your best candidate is usually somebody else's employee, and your best employee is somebody else's candidate.A rival who pays more, trains better, or offers flexibility can drain your team without ever taking a single customer from you — and when your head baker leaves for them, your product quality follows. Meanwhile the wider weather is set by others: inflation pushes wage expectations up, the Economy chapter decides whether your inbox is full or empty of applicants, and Tax and Regulations quietly attach employment law, minimum wage, working time and health-and-safety duties to every hire you make. There's no hire without those strings attached.Dario has been Priya's head baker for four years. A café chain two streets away offers him £2,000 a year more, and he takes it. Watch what actually walks out of the door.And that's before you count the six weeks Priya spent doing the 4am bake herself, on top of everything else she was already doing.Now the uncomfortable question. Would a £2,000 pay rise have kept him? Probably. Which means Priya spent £8,600 avoiding a £2,000 conversation — roughly four pounds for every one she saved.Two honest caveats, because this isn't an argument for simply paying everybody more. You can't always keep people with money, and a business that pays above market for every role eventually prices itself out of its own market. But the arithmetic of replacement is almost always worse than the arithmetic of retention, and most owners never actually run the numbers.Look at where those costs fall: Costs (recruitment, training, waste), Manufacturing (the ramp-up lag), Product (quality), Customer Service (complaints), Revenue (drifted regulars), Financials (the cash hit), and Competitors (the rival who hired him). One person, seven chapters.Put it all together and you get the same reinvestment cycle that has run through this whole book, with people at the centre of it.Invest in staff — decent pay, proper training, enough people on shift, the authority to solve problems — and they deliver better product and better service. Better service keeps customers, and keeping customers is far cheaper than winning them. That shows up as revenue and profit, which funds the next round of investment in staff. Turn by turn, it gets stronger.Run it backwards — squeeze the training, stretch the rota, ignore the rota requests, hire in a panic — and it unwinds just as reliably. It's slower, which is precisely why it's harder to spot. This is the management loop from the opening chapter, and it's why leading deserves a job of its own: it's the one that leaves no paper trail, and the one employees notice most when it's missing.One genuinely cheering consequence. Culture is the one competitive advantage a small business can build that a bigger rival can't simply buy. A competitor can clone your prices this afternoon and your product by next season. Copying the way your people treat each other, and therefore your customers, takes years — and by then you've moved on. Ask what each person is worth, not what they cost. The question isn't the salary; it's the contribution they generate and the knowledge they hold. Count the replacement cost before you need it. Recruitment, training, ramp-up, waste and drift usually add up to several times the pay rise that would have prevented it. Measure revenue per head. It's the simplest productivity signal you have, and it works at every size of business. Remember payroll's timing. You pay your people on a schedule that doesn't wait for your customers to pay you. That's a planning problem, not a surprise. Build the culture on purpose. How staff are treated is how customers get treated, and the chain runs through every seam in the company. Plan capacity ahead of demand. Hiring, training and reaching full productivity all take weeks — the same lag that applies to machines and deliveries applies to people, and it bites hardest when you're busy. Watch the market you're hiring in. Wages, rival employers, demographics and employment rules all move, and none of them consult you first. Staff are the factor that operates every other factor — materials, machines, money and systems are all inert until a person acts on them. Staff drive both sides of the income statement: payroll is a cost, and product, service, sales and relationships all generate revenue. People carry tacit knowledge, relationships and judgement that never appear on a balance sheet but leave with them — so ask what you'd lose by Monday if someone walked out on Friday. Staff set the quality ceiling and the consistency floor, and they are the service: satisfaction is a gap closed or opened by a person every day. How you treat staff is how they treat customers. The money has three faces: payroll's cost, the revenue staff generate, and the timing mismatch between paying wages and being paid. You compete for people against the same rivals you compete for customers against — and wage expectations, employment law, tax and the wider economy all move the goalposts. Replacing someone usually costs many times more than retaining them; retention isn't sentiment, it's arithmetic. Culture is the one advantage a smaller business can build that a larger rival cannot simply buy — and it's the management loop from the opening chapter, turning steadily in either direction.

item.title: 14 Staff
item.description:
Part of Business Management
14-1 What Staff Really Means
14-2 Types of Staff Roles
14-3 Staff as a Factor Across the Whole Business
14-4 Staff vs. The Other Factors

item.title: 14-1 What Staff Really Means
item.description:
Part of 14 StaffAsk a bakery owner how many staff she has and she'll answer instantly: "three, plus me." Ask her who works in the building on a Saturday morning and the number jumps. Ask her who she's legally responsible for and it changes again.So before we go any further in this chapter, let's pin the word down — because "staff" gets used for at least three different things, and the answers only diverge exactly when it starts to cost you money.Staff are the people who work inside a business and supply its labour — employed, contracted, volunteering, or family helping out.Four pieces of that are doing real work.People. Not hours, not roles, not headcount on a spreadsheet. Actual humans with names, lives, ambitions and a Monday morning. This is the whole reason the word exists separately from labour.Work inside the business. They're part of your operation, not standing outside it doing deals with you.Supply its labour. Being there isn't enough — they're there to contribute effort, physical or mental. That's the thread running back to the Labour chapter: labour is the effort; staff are the source of it.Employed, contracted, volunteering, family. That last phrase is deliberately loose, because the everyday meaning of "staff" is looser than the legal one. Hold that thought — we'll come back to it.If you've read the Labour chapter, you've already met this triangle. It's worth one more look from this side, because almost every muddle about workforce management starts here.Dario is staff. His Tuesday is labour. What Priya does about it — the rota, the target, the quality standard — is management.Two wrinkles worth noticing, because they're where the tidy version breaks down.Managers are staff too. A supervisor on a payroll is a member of staff who happens to spend their day doing the four management jobs from the opening chapter. So "management versus staff" is a real distinction within an organisation — it's how we talk about who decides what — but it isn't a distinction between two kinds of human being.Owners might be staff, or might not. Priya owns the bakery and bakes in it, so she's both. A shareholder who never visits isn't staff in any sense. And here's the trap: when the person who owns the business also works in it, that fact can hide for years — fifty unpaid hours a week quietly propping up a business that looks profitable on paper. The Labour chapter's worked example found exactly that.This is the boundary question, and there's no single clean answer — which is precisely why it's worth thinking about rather than assuming.The honest summary: "staff" is a role inside the business, not a legal category. In everyday speech, anyone who turns up regularly and works under your direction is staff. In law, that's decided by employment law — not by what you call them, what their contract says, or how you think of them.Which matters, and not in an abstract way. The legal line decides who you withhold tax for, who has employment rights, who you must insure, and who you owe health-and-safety duties to — the whole apparatus of the Regulations chapter. Call someone a contractor because it's cheaper and simpler, while actually treating them as staff, and you haven't simplified anything. You've stored up a problem.The practical test, if you want one: does this person work inside my business, under my direction, on an ongoing basis? If yes, treat them as staff in every sense that matters, whatever the paperwork says.Here's the idea that makes staff strategically interesting rather than just administratively fiddly.Everyone else your business deals with stands outside it. Customers buy from you and leave. Suppliers sell to you and leave. Lenders, regulators, landlords — all outside, all at arm's length. Staff are the only group on the inside.
Two consequences fall out of that.First, staff are the only people who see the mess. A customer sees one bad experience. A supplier sees one late payment. Only staff see the whole thing — the broken process, the supplier who's always late, the product everyone complains about, the shelf nobody ever restocks. That's intelligence sitting inside your building, and most businesses never ask for it.Second, staff carry your promises. Everything the Product and Customer Service chapters insisted on — consistency, the brand as a promise, service that happens at every touchpoint — is delivered by a person. Nobody buys a promise from a company. They buy it from whoever is standing in front of them.Back to the bakery. Priya says "three staff." Let's write out who actually works in her business in an ordinary week.Now look at the consequences of that blur. Her obligations, her insurance, her tax paperwork and her right to tell someone what to do are all different across those rows. Her rota is one thing; her legal exposure is another; her actual "team" in the everyday sense is a third.And notice the strategic shape underneath. She has a core of two permanent people who hold the recipes and the standards, a flexible fringe of temps and freelancers for the spikes, and a grey zone of helpers and relatives. That's not sloppiness — it's a sensible response to demand that rises and falls. It just needs to be a deliberate response, not an accidental one.One more thing, and it's the reason this chapter exists separately from Labour.Machines wear out. A delivery van depreciates from the moment it's driven off the forecourt. Flour goes stale. Every other thing a business owns gets worse over time, or at best stays the same.Staff are the exception. A trained baker who's been in your kitchen for three years is not just an older version of the person you hired — she's a faster, more accurate, more confident one. Her judgement has improved. She spots problems earlier. She can train the next person. She is, quite literally, an asset that appreciates.That's the productivity loop from the Labour chapter, seen from the other end: good staff get better, get better at making things, and make the business better at everything downstream. And it runs in reverse just as easily — a demoralised team, a stretched rota, a training budget cut to save a few pounds this quarter, and your only appreciating asset quietly starts depreciating instead. Count people, not just posts. Headcount tells you about cost; knowing who these people are tells you about capability, risk and loyalty. They're different questions. Be precise about the boundary — for the right reason. The everyday sense of "staff" is generous; the legal sense is not. Know which one you're talking about, because Tax and Regulations deal in the second. Never treat the owner's labour as free. It's the most common hidden subsidy in small business, and it makes weak businesses look strong. Ask your staff what's broken. They're the only people who can see the seams between your departments — the handoffs the Parts of a Company section warned about. Treat retention as strategy, not sentiment. Staff are the one input that can leave and take what they know to the competitor down the road. That's the Competitors chapter and the Labour chapter meeting on the same street. Remember what you're actually managing. You can schedule labour and you can budget headcount. You can only ever lead people. That's why the four management jobs include one that has nothing to do with numbers. Staff are the people who work inside a business and supply its labour — whether they're employed, contracted, volunteering, or family helping out. Three words that get muddled: labour is the effort, staff are the people who supply it, management is what directs it. Managers are staff too, and owners may or may not be. "Staff" is a role inside the business, not a legal category. The legal line — employment rights, payroll tax, insurance, safety duties — is set by law, not by what you call someone. The test: does this person work inside my business, under my direction, on an ongoing basis? If so, treat them as staff regardless of the contract label. Staff are the only internal party a business has — everyone else (customers, suppliers, owners, regulators) stands outside. That's why staff see the mess others never see. Their work reaches every other chapter: they build the Product, deliver the Customer Service, make the Sales, run Manufacturing and Distribution, and make up the largest cost line in most service businesses. Staff are the only input that improves with use. Every other asset depreciates. Invest in the one that doesn't. Next, we'll sort staff into their main role types — from the front line to the back office — and see why a business needs a mix of them rather than a single kind of person.

item.title: 13-4 Customer Service vs. The Other Factors
item.description:
Part of 13 Customer ServiceCustomer service is strange among the twenty factors in this book, because it is the only one your customer experiences personally and directly. Everything else — your raw materials, your distribution network, your financial statements — is something your business does. Customer service is something the customer feels. That makes it less a spoke in the wheel and more like the hub that touches nearly every other spoke.So when we compare customer service to the other factors, we are really asking three questions about each one: what does this factor do to customer service, what does customer service do back to it, and what does customer service teach it? Keep those three questions in mind as we work through the list.Think about the last time you were delighted by a company. Chances are you cannot describe the product in detail, but you can describe exactly how you were treated. And when you were annoyed, the same is true.Customer service sits at the point where the whole business meets a human being. That gives it a unique double role: It consumes everything the business produces — good products, bad products, late deliveries, well-trained staff. It produces the things the business ultimately lives on — loyalty, repeat purchases, referrals, price tolerance.
These factors decide what your service team actually has to work with. Service can polish a good operation and it can paper over cracks in a mediocre one, but it cannot manufacture quality that was never there.Product and service are almost never separable in the customer's mind — they are one bundle. A great product with terrible support feels like a bad product. A mediocre product with excellent support feels acceptable, at least for a while.The relationship runs in three directions: Complexity creates service demand. Every feature, option and setting is a future support ticket. A product designed with a clear setup guide and sensible defaults costs less to serve than a clever one nobody understands. That is a product decision with a service bill attached. Defects create service volume. Faults arrive at the service desk before they arrive anywhere else in the accounts. The defect rate and your service cost are close cousins. Service buys time. If a product is flawed but fixable, brilliant service can hold customers long enough for the fix to land. This is a genuine strategic option — but it is a bridge, not a destination. Customers eventually reach the far bank and judge the product on its own merits. One more product–service link worth carrying forward: as a product moves through its life cycle into maturity, products in a category start to look alike, and service becomes the main thing left to compete on. That is why mature industries — banking, airlines, telecoms — talk about service so much.Manufacturing quality and service cost are locked together. Every defect that leaves the factory becomes a return, a repair, a complaint call and a refund, and each of those costs more than fixing the defect would have.Manufacturing decisions also shape your capacity to serve. Lean operations with thin buffers are wonderfully efficient in normal conditions, but when demand spikes, there is no slack left, and the customer sees it as a delay. Location matters too: a spare-part warehouse on the other side of the world turns a two-day repair into a three-week one.The traffic is not one-way. The service desk is the best defect-detection system a factory can have, and it is free. Feeding complaint data back into manufacturing is one of the cheapest quality improvements available to you.Your suppliers' failures arrive at your service desk wearing your logo. A late delivery, a batch of faulty material, a substitution made during a shortage — all of it becomes "your company let me down."This is why supplier relationships are, in practice, customer service policy by proxy. Service-level agreements, quality checks and dual sourcing are really promises about what your customers will experience. If you skip the due diligence in choosing suppliers, you are outsourcing your reputation to someone who has no reason to protect it.Raw materials sit one step further upstream but work the same way: the quality of the input caps the quality of the output. No amount of warm reassurance fixes a shirt that shrinks after one wash. And when shortages force a substitution, customers notice — the complaint "it's not the same as it used to be" is a raw-materials problem wearing a service costume.Distribution is where the promise meets the doorstep, and the last mile is often the first impression. Delivery speed, packaging condition, tracking updates and what happens when nobody is home are all customer service moments — usually delivered by a third party carrying your brand.Channel choice matters enormously here. Sell direct and you own the customer relationship and every service failure with it. Sell through a retailer and you may lose control of the experience while keeping the blame. Either way, the customer does not distinguish between you and your courier.The single most valuable service feature in most businesses is not a friendly voice — it is availability. "Can I get it, and when?" beats "how nice were they?" for most purchases. That makes inventory and distribution decisions service decisions.Stores are the physical stage for all of this: queue lengths, staffing levels, opening hours, layout, the state of the toilets. Store staff are the company's face. And returns handled in-store are a genuine service touchpoint that also happens to be a reverse-logistics cost — a neat example of the cost and revenue sides meeting in one interaction.Service is labour-intensive and stubbornly resistant to automation in its most valuable moments. That means people factors are not adjacent to service — they are service.In a service business, your staff are not delivering the product, they are the product. The old idea known as the service–profit chain captures the sequence neatly: internal service quality (how well the business treats its people) drives employee satisfaction, which drives productivity and care, which drives the value customers receive, which drives loyalty, which drives profit and growth. Break any link and the chain drags.Practically, this means hiring for temperament as well as skill, training beyond the script, and — the big one — giving frontline people enough authority to fix things without a manager's permission. A refund rule that requires three approvals is a service failure with paperwork.Labour is the raw capacity underneath everything described above. Wage levels decide who you can hire; the labour market decides how long they stay. High turnover is the quiet killer of service quality, because consistency is what customers actually trust, and consistency is the first thing to go when the team changes every four months.Notice that service work is unusually hard to measure. "Average call time" is easy to count and actively harmful as a target. Labour productivity in service is real, but it lives in resolution rates and repeat contacts, not minutes.Management sets the standard and, more importantly, the trade-offs. If service appears nowhere on the scorecard, it will not appear in behaviour. If the manager's bonus depends on cutting headcount, the queues will grow.Three management levers matter most: empowerment (can staff act?), measurement (do we know how we are doing?), and escalation (what happens when it goes wrong?). Management also owns the culture question — whether the organisation treats a complaint as a threat to be minimised or as information to be welcomed.The market defines what "good service" even means. A luxury buyer expects a named contact and a same-day answer; a discount buyer expects speed and low friction and will forgive almost anything else. Service that ignores its market is just expense.Two useful ideas from the market chapter apply directly. First, service quality is part of your value proposition, so improving it shifts demand in your favour — the same way price or product quality does. Second, in markets with few alternatives, customers tolerate poor service; in crowded ones, they do not. Competitive intensity is what turns service from a nice-to-have into a requirement.There is a feedback role too: complaints, questions and returns are the market talking to you. This is the cheapest market research you will ever get, and most businesses throw it away by treating it as an annoyance.Service is the classic escape hatch from a price war. When products converge, service is often the only thing left that a customer can feel — and the only thing worth paying a premium for.Two cautions. First, expectations are set by the best competitor in your customers' experience, not by your industry average. If a customer's bank answers in thirty seconds, they will wonder why their insurer takes three days. Second, service is easy to copy in appearance and very hard to copy in substance, because it rests on staff, culture and management — all slow to build. That combination — visible value, invisible effort — is exactly what you want in a differentiator.Sales makes promises; service keeps them. The friction between these two is one of the oldest tensions in business. A commissioned sales team is rewarded for the first order; a service team inherits whatever was oversold.The strategic fix is to remember that sales sells the first order and service sells the rest. If your incentive structure pays only for new business, you are systematically starving the function that produces repeat business. The best service teams are also sales channels — renewals, upgrades, referrals and reviews all originate in a good support conversation.Customer service affects revenue through four doors, none of which appear in a sales forecast: Retention. The classic Bain finding is that a five-point improvement in retention can raise profits by roughly a quarter to nearly all of it, depending on the industry. Retention is largely manufactured in the service function. Price tolerance. Customers who trust you complain less about price and switch less when a cheaper option appears. Referrals. Word of mouth is free customer acquisition, and it is overwhelmingly driven by how people were treated, not by what they bought. Direct sales. Support plans, extended warranties, service contracts and premium tiers turn service itself into a product line with its own revenue. There is also the service recovery paradox: a customer whose problem was handled brilliantly can end up more loyal than one who never had a problem. Treat it as a real effect with limits — it works for small, well-handled failures and does not survive repeated ones.Service is simultaneously a cost centre and a cost reducer, and confusing the two is expensive. As a cost: wages, training, technology, premises, tools. As a reducer: fewer returns, smaller warranty bills, less churn, lower acquisition costs, fewer legal disputes.The right lens is the cost of poor service, not just the cost of service. A business that strips its support budget to protect margin usually finds the savings reappear as customer churn, discounts to win replacements and warranty claims — often multiplied. There are diminishing returns in both directions: spending more on service past a point buys little, and cutting past a point costs a great deal. The strategic job is finding where service stops paying for itself, and that answer differs by segment. Not every customer deserves the same cost-to-serve.Here customer service has a genuine visibility problem. Its value hides inside other numbers: revenue growth (retention), lower marketing spend (referrals), reduced warranty provisions (fewer defects), and goodwill that never shows on the balance sheet at all. Its costs, meanwhile, are perfectly visible.That asymmetry creates a well-known bias: service looks like an expense and behaves like an investment, and accounting systems are better at showing the first. As a strategist, you have to correct for it deliberately, using something like customer lifetime value to connect a service cost today to revenue over years.The company is the container that decides how much service is even possible. Its structure determines who has authority to resolve a complaint; its policies determine what staff may promise; its culture determines whether customers are seen as a nuisance or an asset. A company's mission statement is not what is written on the wall — it is what happens at the counter when something goes wrong.Size matters too. For a small company, service is often the only factor where it can beat a larger rival, because personal attention does not scale and does not need to.Economic conditions change both the cost of service and its value. In a boom, customers are forgiving and spending is easy, so it is tempting to let service standards drift — a mistake, because that is exactly when you are quietly losing the habit. In a downturn, service becomes decisive: customers scrutinise every purchase, churn risk rises, and service becomes a cheaper way to defend margin than discounting.The economy also moves your inputs. Inflation raises service wages faster than most businesses can raise prices. Interest rates change how easily customers buy big-ticket items they may then need servicing. Currency swings affect imported spare parts and therefore repair times.Tax rarely shapes service directly, but it shapes its economics. Employment taxes sit on the largest service cost. Sales tax or VAT may apply to service bundles, support plans or extended warranties, changing what you can profitably sell. Import duties slow down spare parts. Compliance itself consumes management attention that could be spent on customers. None of these are reasons to change your service strategy — but all of them are reasons to check the numbers before pricing a service promise.Regulation sets the floor; service sets the ceiling. Consumer protection law defines refund rights, warranty periods and cooling-off windows. Privacy rules govern how you store and use customer data in your CRM. Accessibility standards apply to digital service channels. Some industries impose formal complaint-handling deadlines and require licensed staff for advice.The strategic point is simple: complying with the law is the minimum standard and offers no advantage, because your competitors must comply too. Your opportunity lies above the floor — in the discretionary effort that regulations can never mandate.Imagine a mid-sized bike shop that sells a £1,200 electric bike. Three weeks in, the motor fails. Watch how many factors converge on one service conversation.The product was designed with a motor that runs hot; the manufacturing batch had a weak seal; the raw materials in that seal came from a supplier who was swapped in during a shortage. The distribution partner left the box in the rain, and the store had one mechanic on duty. The staff member knows the fix is a £90 part, but management policy caps goodwill spending at £50 without approval. Labour turnover means this is her second week.Now the forks in the road. If sales over-promised a two-day repair, the customer's anger is already primed. If competitors nearby offer a free loan bike, the customer knows what good looks like. If the market is a wealthy commuter segment, they will pay for quality — but only once. If the financials show the shop has no provision for returns, the manager will resist. The costs of refusing are invisible: no churn line, no referral line. The revenue consequences are real: a repaired customer buys accessories for five years and refers three friends.Then the outer frame. A regulation gives the customer a statutory repair right, so the shop will pay either way — the only question is whether it pays gracefully. A tax change raised the price of imported motors last quarter, squeezing the repair margin. And the economy has tightened, so the customer is unusually ready to walk. In a boom, they might have shrugged.One broken motor, and the outcome was decided by nineteen factors — most of them long before the phone rang.A handful of heuristics fall out of all these comparisons: Fix the product before scaling the service. Service is a multiplier; multiplying a weak product multiplies your problems. Match the service level to the market. Luxury, mid-market and discount customers need different service, and paying for the wrong one is pure waste. Measure the cost of poor service, not just the cost of service. Churn, returns and warranty are service costs wearing other labels. Read complaints as data. The service desk is your cheapest, fastest source of product and market intelligence. Never promise what the supply chain cannot deliver. Suppliers, distribution and manufacturing are the physical limits of your service promise. Remember that regulation sets the floor. The advantage is always above it. Customer service is the hub of the business: it consumes everything the other factors produce and produces loyalty, revenue and reputation in return. Product, manufacturing, suppliers, raw materials, distribution and stores determine what your service team has to work with — and set the ceiling on what it can promise. Staff, labour and management are not adjacent to service; in most businesses they are the service. The market and competitors define what good service means, and set the expectation bar ever higher. Service drives revenue through retention, referrals, price tolerance and paid support, and reduces cost through fewer returns, warranties and churn — but its value hides on the financial statements while its costs are perfectly visible. The economy, tax and regulation shape the economics and the legal floor of service, without changing the core principle: compliance is mandatory, excellence is voluntary — and only the second one is a competitive advantage.

item.title: 13-3 Customer Service as a Factor Across the Whole Business
item.description:
Part of 13 Customer ServiceEvery chapter so far has asked you to look at one part of the business at a time. The product, the price, the stock on the shelf, the van, the wage bill. Customer service refuses to stay in its lane.It's the one factor that runs through all of them, because it's where every promise your business made gets tested against what actually happened. Your brand is a promise, your product is the keeping of it — and service is what you do on the days when the keeping doesn't go to plan. A business that only serves customers well when nothing has gone wrong isn't offering service. It's offering luck.So let's do what we've done with raw materials, labour and distribution: pull back and watch where service shows up across the whole business — and what it quietly costs and earns.Remember the three levels of a product from the Product chapter: the core benefit the customer actually wants, the actual product they receive, and the augmented product wrapped around it. Service is the augmented layer. Delivery speed, returns, how easy it is to ask a question, whether anyone picks up the phone.That's not a soft point. In any market where rivals have converged — and in most markets they do — the actual products are nearly identical. Two loaves of sourdough, same flour, same oven, same price. The fight moves upstairs to the augmented layer, which is where service lives. This is the Types of Competition chapter telling you why: in monopolistic competition, rivals are close substitutes, not identical goods. Service is one of the cheapest ways to stop being a substitute.Here's the idea that makes service a financial topic rather than a nice-to-have. The Sales chapter put it bluntly: one sale is a transaction, a customer is an asset. The first sale costs money to win — advertising, an introductory offer, hours of somebody's time. The second one costs almost nothing.
Run that loop in reverse — service failures, lost regulars, a reputation that slips — and it compounds just as reliably downwards. Which brings us to the arithmetic.Priya sells a loaf at £4.00 that costs her £1.20 in ingredients, leaving £2.80 of contribution toward rent, wages and profit.Now meet Sam, a regular. She buys one loaf a day, five days a week, forty-eight weeks a year.Priya's whole bakery turns over enough to leave her roughly £50 a day — about £18,000 a year. Twenty-five regulars like Sam are worth £16,800 of contribution. In other words, her regulars are the business. Everything else — the market stall, the delivery app, the café contract — is how she finds more of them.Now run the other direction. Suppose indifferent service drives away five regulars over the year. That's £3,360 of contribution gone. At £2.80 a loaf, Priya would have to bake and sell an extra 1,200 loaves — twelve full days of production — just to get back to where she started. And that's before counting the bad reviews, which the Competitors chapter reminds us are public signals that steer the next customer away before she ever gets the chance to serve them.Set that against what fixing it costs. Replacing a stale loaf costs £1.20. A £1-an-hour pay rise for the person on the counter — the one who remembers Sam's name and slices her loaf without being asked — is about £1,400 a year. That's less than the contribution from three Sams.She can replace a stale loaf for £1.20. She can't replace Sam for anything close to that.Service sits on both sides of the income statement, exactly like labour.Revenue. Repeat purchases and referrals, obviously. But also pricing power — the Market chapter's elasticity. A customer who trusts you compares you less on price, which makes your demand less elastic, which means you can nudge prices without losing the queue. Service is a pricing strategy wearing an apron.Costs. Note the counter-intuitive bit: good service is usually cheaper than bad service. It costs less to answer the phone than to handle the complaint it became. Less to replace one stale loaf than to lose a regular. Less to train a counter assistant properly than to hire her replacement twice a year. Only a fraction of service cost appears as a "service budget" — most of it is hidden in the returns, refunds, remakes and goodwill discounts that never needed to happen.Financials. Refunds, credits and warranty claims are all working-capital events, and every one of them is a service failure that got invoiced. The Financials chapter will tell you how to account for them; the strategist's job is to notice how many of them are self-inflicted.Front-line staff are the brand as far as most customers are concerned. Which makes service a Labour problem and a Management one, not a communication exercise.Two consequences:Service quality follows staff quality, and staff quality follows how you treat them. The Labour chapter made the point that labour is the only input that can choose, learn and leave. Service is where that bites hardest. A rival paying more, training better, or rostering more humanely drains your service quality along with your people — and the customers follow a little later. Staff turnover shows up in your reviews about six months before it shows up in your sales.Service also needs authority, which is an organizing problem. If every exception has to be approved by a manager, your service runs at the manager's walking speed. Deciding who can say yes to what — a free replacement, a small refund, a swapped shift — is exactly the organizing job from the management cycle. So is the planning half: what standard are you actually promising? And the controlling half: repeat-purchase rate, complaint volume, response times, review scores. Pick three or four and check them monthly, like any other control measure. Stores. Layout, queue length, opening hours, whether anyone makes eye contact. Availability is service — the third level of the product, again. Distribution. Delivery windows, tracking, and returns — reverse logistics, often the most expensive leg of all. Most "where is my order?" calls are a distribution failure wearing a service costume. Sales. Every promise made at the point of sale becomes a service commitment. Over-promising in sales is the single most common cause of a service crisis. Product. Complaints are free market research. The complaint that recurs is a product brief. Suppliers. A supplier who lets you down becomes your service failure in your customer's eyes. They will never blame the flour mill. Regulations. Consumer rights, returns, refunds, complaint handling and data protection all set a floor beneath your service promise. You can exceed the rules, never fall short of them. The Economy. In a downturn, customers scrutinise every purchase and switch more readily after one bad experience — yet service budgets are usually the first thing cut. That's backwards, for the reasons in the tables above. Service can't rescue a bad product. A sincere apology and a painless refund are still a refund. If the thing doesn't work, fix the thing. Service keeps the promise; it doesn't make one.And you can over-serve. Gold-plating service for customers who don't value it burns the same money that could have gone into product or price. Match the service level to what buyers will actually pay for — the same contribution logic that runs through the Costs chapter. A luxury showroom experience on a commodity product is a cost with no revenue attached. Treat service as a product decision, not an afterthought. It's the augmented layer, and it's where converged markets are actually won. Price the loop honestly. Know what a regular is worth over a year, then compare that with the cost of retaining them. The gap is usually enormous, and it's almost always in service's favour. Look for it in the wrong places. Returns, remakes, refunds and walkouts are service costs hiding in your cost lines. Invest in the people who deliver it. Pay, training and hours are service strategy. Turnover is a leading indicator of service decline. Give the front line the authority to fix things. Every exception that needs a manager's signature is a service delay with a price. Watch your competitors, because this ratchets. Once a rival offers free returns or next-day delivery, it becomes the expectation — and you must match it or explain why not. Close the loop. Set a service standard, organise so it can be delivered, lead the people delivering it, and control it with a few honest numbers. Customer service is the one factor that runs through the whole business, because it's where every promise made elsewhere gets tested. It is the augmented product — the layer where competition happens once actual products converge. Service turns a transaction into a customer, and the retention loop compounds: repeat revenue, referrals, contribution, reinvestment. The arithmetic is brutal and one-sided. A regular is worth many multiples of a single sale, and good service is usually cheaper than bad service — it just hides its costs in avoided refunds rather than in a budget line. It appears on both sides of the income statement: it drives revenue and pricing power, and it shows up as returns, remakes, credits and lost regulars. Delivery depends on people and management: staff quality, staff retention, and how much authority the front line actually has. It surfaces everywhere — Stores, Distribution, Sales, Product, Suppliers, Regulations, the Economy — and it ratchets upwards as rivals raise the floor. Two limits: service can't fix a bad product, and over-serving customers who don't value it is just an unmeasured cost. The strategist's habit: price the retention loop, then spend on service up to the point where the next pound earns more than a pound back.

item.title: 13-2 Types of Customer Service
item.description:
Part of 13 Customer ServiceCustomer service comes in more shapes than most owners realise. The bakery owner who knows your usual order, the chatbot that resets your password at 2am, the account manager who rings to check the last delivery landed properly, the self-checkout till that made you do the work yourself — all four are customer service, and they cost wildly different amounts to deliver.That's why sorting service into types is worth your time. The type you choose decides who you hire, what your rota looks like, where your costs land, and — crucially — which customers you're actually building a relationship with. Pick the wrong type for your product and your prices, and you'll either burn money on service nobody valued or lose customers over a problem you never saw coming.You can slice customer service in a dozen ways. Four cuts explain nearly everything that matters, and most real service sits at a position on all four at once — a bit like the four cuts in the Types of Sales section, which this one deliberately mirrors. Service is, after all, the other half of the same transaction.
Change any cut and you change your costs, your staffing and the kind of relationship you end up with.In person. The oldest channel, and still the richest. A person reads your face, hears your tone and fixes things on the spot. It's also the most expensive, because it consumes someone's hour.By phone. Faster than writing, warmer than a form. Voice carries reassurance, which is why anything emotional — a complaint, a refund, a bereavement — usually ends up on a call.By message. Email, live chat, text, WhatsApp, a support ticket. Cheap, written down, and easy to track. Slower, and hopeless at conveying sincerity.Self-service. The customer does it themselves: FAQs, tracking links, kiosks, self-checkout, a returns portal, an app that lets you rebook. Almost free per use — and the type most likely to leave someone furious if it's badly designed.Automated and semi-automated. Chatbots, IVR menus, auto-replies, and now AI assistants. They handle the predictable volume so humans can handle the difficult remainder.Social and public. Answering a complaint in the open. Higher stakes, because everyone else is watching — which is both the risk and the opportunity.Notice these aren't alternatives so much as a ladder of cost. Every rung up costs more per contact, and every rung up buys you more warmth, more nuance and more recovery power when something has gone wrong.The figures are illustrative, but the order is real, and it's the same fixed-versus-variable logic you met in Costs. Self-service costs you once to build and almost nothing to use. A person costs you an hour every time.The customer serves themselves. Underrated, and quietly the most common type in modern business. A tracking link, a clear instruction sheet, a well-signposted returns process — these are service, even though nobody from your company is involved.Front-line staff. The default. Whoever the customer meets first is doing customer service, whether or not that's in their job title. This is the Staff and Labour chapters arriving at the counter.A dedicated service team. Call centres, support desks, account managers. They exist because service needs specialist skill and constant availability, and because letting the whole company answer the phone means nobody is ever actually listening.Outsourced partners. Agencies and contact centres who handle it for you. Cheap and scalable, and dangerously easy to let drift out of line with what your brand promises — remember the Suppliers test: how easily could you walk away?Systems and automation. The chatbot, the confirmation email, the "your parcel arrives Thursday" text. Service with no payroll attached.Third parties you don't control. The courier who delivers late, the platform who takes your order, the supplier whose fault it really was. Your customer will hold you responsible regardless, which makes this the most frustrating type of all — and the one that most needs managing upstream.This cut is about timing, and it's where the real strategy sits.Reactive service waits for the customer to raise a problem. A complaint, a return, a "this doesn't work". Necessary, but it's the most expensive kind, because the customer is already unhappy and you're paying to repair damage rather than to build goodwill.Proactive service goes and looks. A follow-up call after a big order. A note telling customers about a delay before they notice it. A check-in from an account manager. You spend the same hour, but you spend it before the problem hardens.Service designed into the product happens before the customer needs anything at all. Clear instructions. A returns label already in the box. A simpler product that breaks less often.That last one is worth pausing on, because it connects straight back to your other chapters. Every quality problem you prevent is a service contact you never pay for. The Manufacturing chapter's consistency is really a customer service strategy — variation is what generates complaints. And the Product chapter's augmented layer — delivery, guarantees, returns, support — is customer service, built into the offer rather than bolted on afterwards.
Self-service and transactional service are about speed and resolution. Scripts, targets, quick answers. Perfect for a £4 purchase.Relationship service is a person who recognises you and remembers your history. This is where loyalty is built and complaints are forgiven.Advisory service goes further: you're not just fixing things, you're helping the customer do their job better. Suppliers of specialist equipment, accountants, and good software firms all sell this way — and it's often the non-price competition from the Types of Competition chapter in its most durable form, because a relationship is far harder for a rival to copy than a discount.Deeper isn't automatically better. Advisory service is expensive, and if you're selling loaves of bread, nobody wants it. Depth should follow the value of the customer's lifetime of purchases, not the size of today's order.Consumer service deals with individuals buying for themselves. Emotional, fast, and heavily shaped by consumer protection rules on refunds and returns — the Regulations chapter, wearing a complaints policy.Business service deals with firms buying to operate. More measured, more contractual, more likely to run through a named account manager and a service-level agreement with response times written into it.Internal service is department serving department. The IT team helping the warehouse, the finance team paying the sales team's expenses. It never touches a paying customer, and yet a bad internal handoff is one of the most common reasons a customer's problem takes a week to fix. That's the seam problem from the Parts of a Company chapter.Same ovens, same counter, six different service types in a single day.The £4 counter sale needs the cheapest service in the table — a smile and a paper bag. The café contract, worth £1,040 a month, can justify a phone call and a relationship. And the delayed delivery is the one that could cost her the account, which is why the Suppliers chapter argued that a supplier's failure is never really theirs alone.Match the service type to the value of the relationship. That single sentence is what this whole subsection is for. Service that outruns the margin on a product is generosity you can't afford; service that undershoots it is a customer you'll lose to someone who bothered. Design the ladder, don't drift onto it. Decide which channels you offer, in what order, and at what volumes. A self-service FAQ plus a phone line for the hard cases often beats an expensive call centre doing both jobs badly. Push volume down the ladder, keep judgement up it. Let the website handle "where's my order" and let your people handle "I'm disappointed". Same logic as routing stock — the cheap path takes the routine, the expensive path takes the exception. Count the cost-to-serve. Service is a cost, and it lands in the Costs and Financials chapters alongside everything else. Two customers paying the same price can cost you wildly different amounts to look after. Remember that service closes the trust gap. The Market chapter explained that strangers trade because of trust. At scale, brands and reviews carry it; at the point of contact, service does. Treat service as a sales channel. A service contact is the cheapest moment you will ever get to sell again — and the Revenue chapter will back you up: keeping a customer costs far less than winning a new one. Staff and train for the type you chose. Advisory service needs judgement and time; transactional service needs speed and scripts. Rostering the wrong people onto the wrong type is a Labour problem disguised as a service problem. Close the loop. Pick two or three numbers — response time, first-contact resolution, repeat complaints — and check them on a rhythm. That's the controlling job from the opening chapter, pointed at your customers. Customer service sorts along four cuts: where it happens, who delivers it, when it happens, and how deep it goes — plus who the customer is. Channels run from self-service at pennies per contact up to in-person at the cost of an hour. Higher rungs buy warmth and recovery power; lower rungs buy volume and reach. Service is delivered by customers themselves, front-line staff, dedicated teams, outsourced partners, automated systems, or third parties you don't control. Timing splits into reactive — after the problem, the most expensive kind — proactive — before the customer notices — and designed into the product, which prevents the contact altogether. The best service is often the service you never have to give. Depth runs from self-service and transactional through relationship to advisory. Deeper service is not automatically better; it should match the value of the relationship. Consumer, business and internal customers each need a different style, shaped by contract, regulation and handoff. The governing rule: match the service type to the value of the relationship. Cheapest service for routine, high-value contact for the relationships that pay for it.
