item.title: 08-1 What Distribution Means
item.description:
Part of 08 DistributionHand someone a perfect loaf of bread and ask what it's worth. In a locked cupboard, nothing. On a counter with a customer standing in front of it, four pounds. Same loaf, same recipe, same baker. The only thing that changed is where it was and who could get to it.That gap — between a product being made and a product being bought — is what distribution exists to close.Distribution is everything that happens to a product between it leaving production and a customer using it: the moving, storing, splitting, sorting, informing and handing over that puts the right goods in the right place at the right time.Three things are worth pulling out of that sentence.It's an activity, not a place. A shop is a place. Distribution is the work — the van route, the warehouse, the wholesaler breaking a pallet into singles, the website that takes the order, the app that tracks the parcel.It starts when the product is finished and ends when the customer has it. Everything before that is covered elsewhere in this book — raw materials, manufacturing, suppliers. Everything after is customer service, repeat purchase, and revenue. Distribution is the middle act.It's deliberately broad. Most people hear "distribution" and picture a delivery van, the same way they hear "market" and picture a fruit stall. Both pictures are true and both are about a tenth of the story.If you've met the classic four Ps of marketing — product, price, place, promotion — distribution is place. It's the one people forget, and often the one that decides whether the other three make any money.Here's why distribution has to exist at all. Making and buying don't naturally line up. They're mismatched in four ways, and each one is a job somebody has to do. Place. Production happens in one spot, or a handful of spots. Consumption happens in thousands of streets, kitchens and offices. Time. Your oven runs at 4am; your customers want bread at 8am. A farmer harvests in August; people eat in February. Quantity. A mill wants to sell flour by the tonne. A customer wants one loaf. Somebody has to split the difference. Assortment. Nobody wants everything from a single maker. A shopper wants bread from one baker, milk from a dairy and coffee from a roaster — and wants all three in one trip and one payment.
Every distribution system ever built — a Roman road, a corner shop, a courier network, a vending machine — exists to shrink one or more of those four gaps. This is the same idea you met in the Market chapter, where buyers and sellers are separated by space, time, quantity and trust, and a market is the arrangement that bridges them. Distribution is that bridging, viewed from the seller's side.Strip away the specific businesses and the same handful of functions show up in every distribution system: Moving — physically getting goods from one place to another. Storing — holding them until someone wants them, which is how you beat the time gap. Breaking bulk — turning a pallet into a case, a case into a loaf, a loaf into a slice. Sorting and combining — gathering many producers' goods into one place so a buyer can shop once. Informing — letting buyers know what's available, and letting producers know what's selling. Transferring ownership and taking payment — the boring, essential plumbing that makes a sale a sale. This links straight to the Financials chapter. Supporting after the sale — delivery, returns, installation, replacement. Now the part that trips people up. You can outsource these functions, but you cannot delete them. If you don't store your own stock, someone stores it for you. If you don't deliver, the customer travels instead. If you don't sort an assortment, the buyer makes four trips to four shops and pays for it in time.That's the honest version of the "middleman" question from the Market chapter. A wholesaler, a distributor, a delivery app or a retailer charges you money — but only earns it when the function they perform costs you less than doing it yourself. Remove them and the work doesn't vanish. It just moves, often onto your customer, who is less willing to do it than you'd hope.It isn't just transport. Driving goods about is one function out of seven. A business that moves things brilliantly but stores them badly, prices them badly or runs out of them constantly has a transport business, not a distribution system.It isn't just shops. A shop is one route to a customer. So is a website, a market stall, a wholesaler, a vending machine, a courier, a locker, a phone call and a van in a lay-by. Which route you pick is the subject of the next section; here, just note that a shop is a type of channel, not a definition.It isn't the same as inbound logistics. Bringing materials in from suppliers is upstream work — covered in the Suppliers and Raw Materials chapters. "Distribution" is usually used for the outbound half: getting your finished product out to buyers. The two halves are mirror images, and the same four mismatches apply to both.And it applies to services, not just goods. A plumber's van, a salon's location, a barber's booking system and a consultant's video call are all distribution decisions. Services can't be stored, so the time gap has to be closed by appointment systems and capacity planning instead of inventory. That's the Product and Customer Service chapters knocking on the door.placeholder
Photo by Pavel Danilyuk on PexelsTake Priya's sourdough and follow it from the oven to somebody eating it.Priya's loaf costs her £1.20 in ingredients. She sells it to the café at £2.60. The café sells the equivalent onward at around £4.00 once it's on a plate with coffee. So the loaf nearly doubles in price between the oven and the customer — and Priya keeps almost none of that increase.It's tempting to see that as someone taking a cut. Look again at the table. The café moved it across town, stored it, broke a baker's batch into single servings, combined it with everything else the customer wanted, took the risk that it might not sell, and handled the payment. That work is distribution, and the price gap is what the market pays for it. Remember the loop you've seen throughout this book — every function a business performs has to be paid for by somebody, out of the price the customer agrees to.Now try a second example, because it makes the point even harder to ignore. A bottle of water. Extracting, treating and bottling it costs a few pence. The bulk of the price you pay is packaging, transport, shelf space and someone's willingness to keep it cold and handy. For gravel, cement, bottled soft drinks and bread, distribution often costs more than production. That's why industries built on cheap, heavy, bulky things — brewing, quarrying, soft drinks — tend to cluster their plants near their customers rather than their ingredients. Raw materials set the quality ceiling; distribution sets the reach.placeholder
Photo by Tom Fisk on PexelsMost business decisions can be reversed next quarter. Distribution decisions are different. Sign a shop lease, buy a van, appoint an exclusive distributor, list on a platform that takes 25% of every sale, or commit to a cold chain — and you've made a decision for years, not weeks.And it doesn't just decide your costs. It quietly decides five more things: How much of the customer's price you keep — the more hands between your oven and the customer, the more mouths sharing the money. Who your competitors are. This is the point from the Competitors chapter worth repeating: the same product sold wholesale competes with industrial bakers on price and reliability; sold over a counter it competes with the café next door on atmosphere. Different channel, different fight. How much you know about your buyers. Sell direct and every conversation teaches you something. Sell through three layers and you're managing a relationship with a distributor, not a customer. How fast you can grow. Every channel has a ceiling — a counter serves a street, a website serves a country. How much cash is tied up. Stock sitting in a warehouse or in transit is money you've already spent and can't use yet, which is exactly the working-capital squeeze the Financials chapter warns about. One more thing, and it's the cheerful version: distribution doesn't only serve demand, it can create it. Deliver to villages that never had a shop, open a website that serves a country, put a coffee machine where no café would survive — and you've made a market that didn't exist before. Distribution is one of the few functions that can genuinely enlarge the pie rather than just slice it differently.placeholder
Photo by Frans van Heerden on Pexels Availability is part of the product. Remember the three levels of a product: the augmented layer — delivery, returns, convenience — is where most competition actually happens. Distribution builds that layer, so it isn't an afterthought, it's the offer. Run the four mismatches as a checklist. Place, time, quantity, assortment. For each one, decide: do we close this ourselves, or pay somebody else to close it? Write down the cost of both. That single exercise usually reveals where your margin is leaking. Don't try to delete a function. If you stop storing, splitting or informing, somebody still does it — your supplier at a price, or your customer at the cost of a lost sale. Back-of-envelope it before you commit. Every channel has a cost per unit sold. Compare them like-for-like, including commissions, delivery, packaging and the cost of holding stock. Then check it against what customers will actually pay — the same discipline you'd apply to any other price decision. Manage it like the loop from the opening of this book. Plan the route and the volumes, organise the vans, warehouses and people, and then control it with two or three numbers: cost per delivery, on-time rate, and stock-turn. Distribution is the easiest part of a business to run blind, and the most expensive when you do. Treat the channel as strategy, not plumbing. It's the single biggest lever on your margin, your reach, and who you're up against. Distribution is everything that happens between production and the customer using the product — moving, storing, breaking bulk, sorting, informing, transferring ownership and supporting after the sale. It exists because making and buying are mismatched in place, time, quantity and assortment. Every distribution system ever built closes one or more of those gaps. It is not just transport and not just shops. Transport and retail are single functions and single routes within a much wider activity — and services need distributing too. Functions can be outsourced but never deleted. A middleman is worth paying only when they close a gap more cheaply than you could. Distribution often costs more than making the product, especially for cheap, heavy or bulky goods — which is why plants cluster near customers, not ingredients. Channel decisions are sticky and structural: they set your margins, your cash, your reach, your knowledge of customers, and who your competitors are. Distribution can also create demand, not merely satisfy it, by putting goods where no market existed before. The strategist's habit: ask how your product gets from where it's made to where it's wanted, what that costs, and what would happen if it stopped.

item.title: 08 Distribution
item.description:

item.description: Part of 07 Raw Materials
item.guid: Business Management/07 Raw Materials/07-4 Raw Materials vs. The Other Factors.md

item.title: 07-3 Raw Materials as a Factor Across the Whole Business
item.description:
Part of 07 Raw MaterialsRaw materials sit at the far end of the business — furthest from the customer, least visible on the shop floor, and easiest to treat as somebody else's problem. That's exactly why they deserve their own lens. You can run a beautiful operation and still watch your profit evaporate because the price of flour moved, because a harvest failed, or because a batch arrived a shade too damp. Nobody outside your business ever sees your raw materials. Everybody inside it feels them.This subsection zooms out. Rather than looking at raw materials as a purchasing task, we'll follow the threads that run from them into every other part of the business — cost, product, operations, risk, people, rules — and see how each thread changes what a good strategist should do.Start with the blunt truth: you cannot make a better product than your inputs allow. No amount of skill in the bakery makes a poor flour into good bread. No amount of polish on the shop floor makes up for a component that fails after six months.This puts raw materials directly underneath the Product chapter. Remember the three levels of a product — core benefit, actual product, augmented product? Raw materials decide the quality and consistency of the actual product, and that in turn decides whether the promises wrapped around it hold up. A brand is a promise; the product is the keeping of it. A raw material that varies batch to batch quietly breaks that promise, and the customer experiences it as a complaint — which lands in Customer Service, not in the purchasing ledger where it started.Two consequences follow: Consistency beats brilliance. A predictable material lets you promise a predictable product. That's why the boring supplier with reliable spec control often beats the exciting one with better samples. New materials create new products. Tastes and markets don't only pull products into existence; materials push them too. Cheaper solar cells, lighter alloys, better batteries — each one opened a market that couldn't have existed before. Watching materials is one way to spot a product opportunity before your rivals do. For most product businesses, raw materials are the largest single line inside cost of goods sold. That's the costs that rise with every unit you sell, as opposed to the fixed ones — rent, salaried staff, insurance — that you pay whether you sell anything or not.Costs come off profit pound for pound, which means a small change in material cost has an outsized effect at the bottom of the page. Watch what happens to a bakery with £1,000 of daily sales:*Assuming flour is roughly a fifth of the ingredient bill.A 6% rise in total costs wiped out the entire profit. That's the leverage: material costs are paid by the business, but only the profit line suffers. This is why purchasing is a profit centre, not an admin chore — and why the Costs and Financials chapters keep circling back to it.There's a cash dimension too. Materials you've bought but not yet sold are money sitting in a warehouse doing nothing — stock, which is cash you can't spend on anything else. Raw materials are unusually demanding here: they tie up cash, they may need paying for before you've sold the finished goods, and if you don't use them, they rot, rust or go out of fashion. A material price rise you can usually survive. A material price rise during a cash squeeze is how businesses die.Here's the pattern in one picture. Raw materials don't have one consequence; they have four, and all of them land on profit.
Note that last arrow. Profit funds the next round of buying — better materials, bigger volumes, keener terms — so advantages and disadvantages compound, exactly as the management loop in the opening chapter described.Manufacturing. The material dictates the process. Flour needs ovens and proving time; steel needs furnaces and presses; chemicals need tanks and precise temperatures. The whole vocabulary of the Manufacturing chapter — job, batch, mass, continuous production — grows out of what you're working with. Change your raw material and you may have to rebuild your factory.Stores. Materials carry their own storage rules. Grain keeps for months; milk keeps for days. Bulk materials need space, dangerous ones need containment, valuable ones need security. Every gram that spoils or walks out the door is a material cost with no revenue attached — pure loss, invisible in the accounts unless somebody is counting.Distribution. Weight and volume are paid for twice. A cheap heavy material can cost more to move than to buy, which is why businesses that make weight-losing products historically located near their source — mills by rivers, breweries by water. Add long lead times from overseas and your Distribution planning gets longer, and the stock you must hold gets bigger.Labour. Materials decide who you need, what you must train them to do, and how safe the work is. Hazardous inputs mean protective equipment, procedures, insurance and Regulations compliance. Fine tolerances mean skilled hands. This is the Labour thread running straight out of the material you chose.Raw materials are where the wider world reaches directly into your cash flow. Almost every big swing has an external cause: Harvests, weather and geology. A bad season lifts prices for everyone, including your rivals — but not equally, because the well-supplied firm has stock and contracts while the other one is buying at the spot price. Commodity markets. Materials traded in bulk get a going price set by supply and demand, exactly as the Market chapter described. You're a price taker. Currency. Buy in a foreign currency and an exchange rate move can change your material cost without a single supplier lifting a finger. Tariffs, duties and taxes. Goods crossing borders pick up charges, dealt with in the Tax chapter. Regulation. Restrictions on hazardous substances, sourcing rules, sustainability requirements and labelling all sit on materials rather than on finished products. If regulators ban an input, your production line stops until you reformulate. Interruption. Strikes, port closures, a fire at a supplier you've never met. This is the Suppliers chapter's tier problem: your Tier 2's disaster is delivered to you as your Tier 1's apology. And the quiet one: a rival who locks up supply. Control a scarce input — the best site, the only licensed processor, an exclusive contract — and you've built a barrier your competitors can't cross. In the language of the Competitors chapter, that's a structural advantage, and a durable one.Priya's bakery, from earlier in the book, sells 100 loaves a day at £4. Ingredients cost £1.20 a loaf; everything else — wages, rent, energy — comes to £230 a day.A 3% rise in costs cut her profit by a quarter. Now watch her think. Raising the price to £4.10 would recover £10 a day if the same 100 customers stayed — but as the Market chapter showed, her bread has close substitutes and her demand is elastic, so some of them walk to the café next door. So instead of one blunt move, a strategist plays several small ones: Cut waste. She counts what she throws away, finds 4% of her flour going in the bin, and gets it under 1%. Worth a few pounds a day, permanently. Reformulate. One of her six lines moves to a cheaper blend of the same quality grade. The customers don't notice; the margin does. Negotiate. She asks the mill for a small discount on a committed weekly volume — and gets it, because she's now a predictable customer. Adjust selectively. She puts 5p on the sourdough, where she has the most loyal buyers, and leaves the everyday white loaf alone. No single lever saves the day. Together they more than cover the £12. That's what raw materials as a factor across the business looks like in practice: not one heroic decision, but four ordinary ones in different corners of the company.You can apply this to any material, in any business, in about ten minutes: How much of my cost is it? A material that's 2% of your costs can be ignored; one that's 30% is a board-level topic. Know which is which. Could I substitute it? Flexibility — a second material, a second grade, a second specification — is insurance you buy before you need it. How easily could it be cut off, and by whom? One supplier, one country, one mine? Then you're managing risk, not price. How much do I lose? Waste, spoilage, shrinkage, over-ordering, expired stock. This is the cheapest saving available, because it needs no negotiation and no customer. Could it be an advantage rather than a cost? Better material, or exclusive access to it, can be the thing customers pay a premium for. That's a Product decision financed by a purchasing one. Raw materials set the quality ceiling on your product and the consistency your brand depends on — no amount of downstream skill fixes bad inputs. They are usually the biggest part of cost of goods sold, and because costs come off profit pound for pound, a small material price change swings profit hard. They tie up cash in stock, which links them directly to the Financials chapter and to survival during a squeeze. Materials shape your manufacturing process, storage needs, transport costs and labour requirements — they're an operations decision disguised as a purchase. The biggest shocks are external: weather, commodity markets, currency, tariffs, regulation and interrupted supply chains. Most of them are predictable, which means most of them are planable. The strategist's toolkit is a set of small moves — reduce waste, substitute, negotiate, design around the material, adjust prices selectively, hold buffer stock — rather than one heroic fix. Finally, ask whether a material is a cost to be minimised or a capability to protect. Sometimes control of supply is the advantage your rivals can't copy.

item.title: 07-2 Types of Raw Materials
item.description:
Part of 07 Raw MaterialsHere's the thing about raw materials: the word "raw" makes them sound uniform, like a single sack of stuff sitting at the back of the warehouse. In reality, a business's raw materials might be iron ore, live cattle, fresh basil, sand, crude oil, and recycled cardboard — all at once. Grouping them isn't academic box-ticking. Each type behaves differently, and that behaviour ripples straight through your costs, your suppliers, your factories, and your bottom line.Think of it like sorting a crowd of people. You can sort by age, by job, by hometown, or by how early they wake up. None of those is the right answer — each one tells you something different, and which lens you reach for depends on the question you're asking. The same is true here. Let's walk through the most useful lenses.This is the most intuitive way to carve things up, and it's a good starting point.Plant and agricultural materials. Cotton, timber, wheat, cocoa, rubber, sugar beet, palm oil. They're grown, and growth depends on weather, seasons, and soil. That means supply wobbles — a drought in one region moves prices worldwide. (Your Market chapter explained how supply and demand set price; agricultural raw materials are the clearest, most brutal example of that mechanism in action.)Animal materials. Hides and leather, wool, dairy, tallow. Niche but important for fashion, furniture, food, and some cosmetics.Mined and mineral materials. Iron ore, bauxite, copper, lithium, cobalt, potash, gravel. You can't grow more of these on a useful timescale, and they tend to sit in specific countries — which is exactly why so many Regulations and trade disputes revolve around them. Note the weight consideration here too: nobody ships gravel across an ocean to save a few pennies, because the Distribution cost dwarfs the material cost.Fossil and energy-derived materials. Crude oil, natural gas, and coal aren't just fuels — they're the starting point for plastics, fertilisers, synthetic fibres, and a huge range of chemicals. Buy a plastic bottle and you've indirectly bought petrochemicals.Water and industrial gases. Easy to forget, but breweries, soft-drink makers, and food processors treat water as a primary raw material, and they care enormously about its quality and consistency. Welders and hospitals buy oxygen and nitrogen by the tank.
Photo by Kefentse Molotsane on PexelsA second lens, and one that now carries real commercial weight: Renewable — timber, crops, wool. Replaceable within a human lifetime, if managed well. Non-renewable — metals, minerals, fossil feedstocks. Use it and it's gone. Secondary (recycled) — scrap steel, recovered paper, recycled plastic, reclaimed glass. That third category is the fastest-growing one in many industries, and it's a beautiful illustration of how chapters interlock. A recycled input can cut raw material Costs, reduce exposure to commodity price spikes, and satisfy tightening environmental Regulations and packaging rules. It can also become a marketing asset that lifts Revenue — customers will pay more for a product whose story they like. Skipping this category isn't just old-fashioned; it's ignoring a lever.Ask a simple question: does this material end up inside the thing we sell?Direct materials do. Flour in bread, steel in a bicycle frame, cotton in a T-shirt, glass in a bottle.Indirect materials don't, but production grinds to a halt without them — machine lubricants, cleaning chemicals, welding gases, safety gloves, replacement drill bits.Why care? Because this split maps almost perfectly onto the direct and indirect Costs you met earlier, and it shapes how you track inventory in your Financials. Direct materials scale with output: make twice as much, buy twice as much. Indirect materials often behave more like fixed overhead — a factory uses roughly the same drum of lubricant whether it runs at 70% or 100% capacity. Get that distinction wrong in your costing and you'll misjudge which products are actually profitable."Raw" is a matter of where you stand on the supply chain. The same substance is raw material to one business and finished input to another.
A bakery typically buys at the "commodity" or "intermediate" rung — flour and sugar are already refined. A carmaker buys at the "component" rung — stamped panels, wiring looms, tyres. A mining company sells at the very first rung.Where you choose to buy isn't a detail. It decides which Suppliers you deal with, how much of the Manufacturing work you take on yourself, and what your cost structure looks like. Buying lower down the ladder is usually cheaper per unit but demands more capability; buying higher up costs more but is faster and simpler. That's a genuine strategic choice, and it's one Competitors are making at the same time — often in the opposite direction.Finally, sort by how the material forces you to handle it. This is where raw materials meet your Stores and Distribution chapters.Perishable. Fresh milk, cut flowers, berries, live yeast. They have a shelf life measured in hours or days, which forces fast production, cold chain logistics, and ruthless stock rotation — first in, first out. Waste here is pure lost margin.Bulky or heavy. Sand, cement, gravel, coal. Low value per kilogram, so transport distance is the enemy. Plants that use them tend to sit right next to the source.Hazardous. Acids, solvents, flammable liquids. Extra storage rules, extra insurance, extra regulation, extra cost — but unavoidable in many chemical and metalworking businesses.Standardised vs critical. A standardised commodity like copper wire trades on global exchanges; you can buy it from almost anyone and hedge the price. A critical material — a rare-earth element, a specialised alloy, a single-origin botanical — might come from two suppliers on one continent. There, your supplier relationship is your risk management.
Photo by Willians Huerta on PexelsA small bakery. Direct materials: flour, butter, sugar, eggs, yeast, salt. Indirect materials: oven cleaner, pan grease, parchment paper, gloves. Classification by origin: mostly agricultural, highly perishable, water is a key input. By stage: buying at the intermediate rung. What should the owner worry about? Flour price volatility (a Market issue), spoilage (Stores and Distribution), and butter costs, which swing with dairy markets. Cheap, fast, simple — but not risk-free.A phone assembler. Direct materials: aluminium, glass, copper, gold traces, lithium. Indirect: solder flux, cleaning solvents, isopropyl alcohol. Classification by origin: mineral-heavy. By renewability: almost entirely non-renewable, with a growing recycled stream. By criticality: cobalt and rare earths sourced from a handful of regions, exposed to geopolitics, tariffs, and conflict-mineral Regulations. Same word — "raw materials" — but the second business lives in a totally different world of risk.
Photo by Marcelo Solis on PexelsRaw materials come in types, and the type tells you where you're exposed: By origin — plant, animal, mineral, fossil-derived, water and gases. By renewability — renewable, non-renewable, or secondary/recycled, with growing regulatory and reputational weight. By role in the product — direct materials become the product; indirect materials keep the machines running. By stage of processing — the ladder from extracted commodity to finished part, and the strategic choice of where you buy. By behaviour — perishable, bulky, hazardous, or critical, each demanding different storage, transport, and supplier tactics. Here's the payoff. Every one of those labels points to a lever you can pull: price risk points to contracts and hedging; perishability points to logistics and stock rotation; criticality points to supplier relationships; renewability points to regulation, cost savings, and brand. You don't need to memorise the categories — you need to look at your own material list and ask, honestly, which types am I actually dependent on? That question is where good business strategy starts, and it's the thread we'll pull on next, when we look at raw materials as a factor across the whole business.

item.title: 06-4 Suppliers vs. The Other Factors
item.description:
Part of 06 SuppliersSuppliers are the only factor in this entire book that lives outside your company's walls but inside your cost structure. That single sentence explains almost every relationship in this section.Think about what you learned in the Company chapter: a company is a legal and organisational boundary — a "we" with a bank account, staff, and a set of things it chooses to do itself. Everything on the other side of that boundary has to be bought. And nearly everything you buy arrives through a supplier. Pull the supplier away and the other factors don't politely stand still: your Manufacturing line stops, your Product's quality story collapses, your Sales team starts quoting lead times it can't hit, your Financials show inventory you can't sell, and your Customer Service team spends its week apologising for someone else's failure.So "Suppliers vs. the Other Factors" isn't a list of twenty tidy comparisons. It's a question of position. Where does the supplier sit relative to each of the others — upstream, downstream, or wrapped around them?
The dotted lines matter as much as the solid ones. Suppliers sit at the point where the outside world — market prices, competition, cash — leaks into your operating chain. Let's walk the whole map, cluster by cluster.The relationship here is the make-or-buy decision, and it's one of the most consequential choices a manager ever makes. Every supplier relationship is a deliberate statement: we don't need to own this capability.Take Bean & Brook, a small coffee roastery. It doesn't grow coffee, doesn't own farms, doesn't run container ships. It buys green beans from importers and does the one thing it has decided is its core competency: sourcing, roasting, and brand. Northern Italy's packaging-machine makers, Apple's contract assemblers, and your local bakery buying flour from a mill are all making the same trade.The upside is enormous — you rent capability without buying it. The downside is that anything you outsource, you no longer control. If your coffee importer switches farms without telling you, your "single-origin Ethiopian" claim becomes a lie, and you find out from a customer, not a spreadsheet. The strategic rule of thumb: outsource what is not your differentiation; own what is. A company that outsources its point of difference has quietly become a reseller.Look back at the Competitors chapter — you learned to size up rivals on price, product, and brand. Here's the missing lens: your competitors are often bidding for the same suppliers you are.In a shortage, supplier capacity is a zero-sum prize. When semiconductors dried up in 2021–22, carmakers didn't lose sales because demand vanished. They lost sales because a handful of fabs allocated scarce chips to whoever had signed long-term agreements — and the carmakers who had treated chips as a cheap commodity to be bought at the last minute were at the back of the queue. The bill ran into billions.Three practical consequences: Exclusivity is a competitive weapon. Locking a key supplier into a supply agreement starves rivals of the same input. Supplier strength is competitive intelligence. Your supplier sells to your competitor too — they know the market's volumes, lead times, and pricing pressure better than anyone. Suppliers can become competitors. A supplier who forward-integrates (the importer starts selling roasted beans under its own label) is now on both sides of your value chain. The Market chapter taught you that supply and demand set the price. Suppliers are where that theory becomes a bill you actually pay.Your supplier operates in their market — the green coffee market, the steel market, the freight market — and that market's price becomes your cost of goods. When the coffee "C price" spikes because of a drought in Brazil, Bean & Brook's margin compresses long before its own customers notice anything. This is why the supplier relationship is a transmission belt for the market: commodity cycles, currency swings, and freight rates arrive at your door through it, usually with a lag of one contract cycle.The strategist's move is to know which market your supplier is exposed to, and how much of that exposure you're willing to absorb.Product and supplier are handcuffed together, and the Product chapter's lesson on quality applies with brutal directness: your product's quality ceiling is set by your inputs. Design is constrained by supplier capability. A bike maker that designs a frame around a carbon layup no supplier can produce has designed a fantasy. Features depend on suppliers. Electric-vehicle range is largely a battery supplier's spec sheet. Phone camera quality is a sensor supplier's roadmap. Co-development is a competitive advantage. The best suppliers aren't order-takers; they're engineering partners who tell you what's possible before you commit to a design. Getting them in early shortens new-product development and prevents expensive redesigns. The life-cycle link is real. In the Product Life Cycle, growth phases demand volume, and volume demands supplier capacity. A product that takes off with a single-source supplier often stalls exactly when it should be scaling. Notice the pattern across all four of these: the supplier determines what you can be, not just what you can spend.This is the closest, most-confused pairing in the book, so let's draw the line cleanly.Raw materials are things. Suppliers are entities. You buy raw materials from a supplier — but not everything a supplier sells is a raw material. Suppliers sell components, sub-assemblies, finished goods, services, software licences, and labour. An IT contractor is a supplier with no raw material in sight.The dependency runs deeper than vocabulary. Your supplier choice determines which raw materials you can even access, at what grade, and at what price. Suppliers also stack in tiers — the tier 1 supplier you invoice sits on top of tier 2 suppliers and tier 3 raw-material producers you've never met. When a fire hits a single chemical plant three tiers down, your line stops anyway. That's why "know your supply chain" means knowing past your immediate counterparties.Manufacturing is where the classic make-vs-buy question gets its sharpest edge. Every factory you don't build is a supplier doing it for you. Contract manufacturing lets you scale without capital. A clothing brand can go from 500 to 50,000 units without owning a sewing machine. But you inherit their limits. Their defect rate becomes your warranty cost. Their capacity becomes your growth ceiling. Their quality system becomes your brand risk. Vertical integration is the reverse bet — more control, better margin potential, far more capital and rigidity. It's the same trade-off you saw in the Company chapter, expressed in machinery. A useful test: If this supplier doubled its price tomorrow, would I be trapped or merely annoyed? Trapped means you've outsourced too deep.Distribution is the mirror image of supply: inbound logistics versus outbound logistics. Suppliers feed the front door, distribution moves things out the back. Some firms do both — Amazon is a supplier's customer and a distributor simultaneously.The supplier relationship defines where your distribution responsibility begins. Under DDP terms a supplier delivers to your warehouse; under FOB you own the goods from the moment they're loaded onto a ship, and the freight, insurance, and customs work becomes yours. Suppliers who drop-ship directly to your customers blur the two factors into one — convenient, until a customer's experience depends on a partner's packaging.Physical stores are the visible end of a supply chain that starts with a supplier — and the place where supplier failure becomes most embarrassing. Lead times set reorder points. If your supplier needs eight weeks, your store must carry eight weeks of cover, which is eight weeks of cash sitting on a shelf. Stockouts are usually supply-chain stories. The empty shelf in the Customer Service chapter's complaints is frequently a supplier's late shipment wearing a store's uniform. Vendor-managed inventory and consignment reverse the burden: the supplier watches your shelf and replenishes it. You get less cash tied up; they get more visibility. Direct-to-consumer suppliers compete with your stores. If your supplier starts selling the same goods online, your shelf space is now a showroom for their brand. Labour touches suppliers twice.First, labour is itself a purchased input. Staffing agencies, freelancers, and contractors are suppliers in the ordinary sense — you're renting hours instead of hiring them. That's the fixed-versus-variable cost trade-off you met in Costs: outsourcing turns a salary you pay in a bad month into a cost you only pay when you need it, at a higher unit rate.Second, your supplier's labour is your risk. A strike at a port, a shortage of welders at a fabricator, or a labour-law violation in a tier 2 factory becomes your delay and, increasingly, your legal liability. Your supplier's workforce is invisible on your org chart and entirely real on your P&L.Staff are your internal people; suppliers are your external capacity. The bridge between them is the buyer.A skilled procurement person is worth multiples of their salary. They negotiate terms, spot concentration risk, build relationships that get you priority in a shortage, and know when a "cheaper" supplier is actually a more expensive one. This is why supplier management sits inside the Staff and Management chapters too: relationships don't manage themselves. In small businesses, buying is often the owner's job by default — and it's one of the highest-leverage hours in the week.There's also a knowledge angle. Good suppliers train your staff, share technical expertise, and act as an extension of your team. Bad ones teach your staff to work around problems.Suppliers are a management discipline, not a purchasing transaction.The classic framing — the Kraljic matrix — sorts purchases into four boxes: strategic (high value, high risk — partner closely), bottleneck (low value, high risk — secure supply above all), leverage (high value, low risk — squeeze on price), and non-critical (low value, low risk — automate it). A single roastery might treat specialty green beans as strategic, replacement gaskets as bottleneck, packaging as leverage, and cleaning supplies as non-critical. Same company, four entirely different relationships.Management also decides risk appetite: single-source for efficiency or dual-source for resilience? That's not a procurement question — it's a strategy question, and it belongs in the boardroom.Sales promises what suppliers can deliver. The two are locked together by lead time. Quote a two-week delivery and your supplier takes five weeks, and Sales becomes the department that lies to customers. Sell a large order before confirming supplier capacity, and you've sold something you may not be able to make. Exclusivity and territory arrangements are jointly negotiated with suppliers and shape what Sales can offer. A healthy business gives Sales a live view of supplier lead times and stock. A fragile one lets Sales discover the constraint at the same moment the customer does.Customer Service is where supplier failures are felt, and it's the factor that pays for them in reputation rather than cash. Warranty and returns costs are often supplier defects in disguise. Track them to the source and you have a negotiation lever, not just a complaint queue. Service recovery depends on supplier responsiveness. A customer waiting on a replacement part is waiting on your supplier's dispatch desk. SLAs cascade. The commitments you make to customers must be mirrored by commitments your supplier makes to you. If your supplier has no obligation to respond in 48 hours, you cannot honestly promise one. The suppliers who make Customer Service easy are usually the suppliers who were chosen with Customer Service in mind — which is a decision made long before any complaint arrives.Suppliers show up on your balance sheet in three places, and each is a cash decision. Payables are the mirror image of the Revenue chapter's receivables. Stretching payment terms from 30 to 60 days is effectively an interest-free loan from your supplier — one of the cheapest sources of working capital a small firm has. Inventory is cash you've converted into goods. Every extra week of safety stock is money that isn't funding growth. Concentration risk is a footnote investors read carefully. A business where one supplier provides 70% of inputs is a business with a single point of failure baked into its valuation. You cannot sell what you cannot get, so supplier capacity is a revenue ceiling — and revenue growth plans that ignore it are fiction.If demand doubles and your supplier can only deliver 30% more, your revenue grows 30% and your disappointed customers go to competitors. The strategic move is to align supplier capacity planning with sales forecasting before the growth push, not after. And watch for supplier-side revenue levers too: volume rebates and annual bonuses reduce your effective purchase price, which shows up as margin rather than revenue — but it's real money either way.This is the most direct relationship in the whole book. Cost of goods sold is mostly supplier price.But unit price is a trap. The useful number is total cost of ownership: price, plus freight, duties, quality failures, rework, inventory carrying cost, and the management time spent firefighting. A supplier 10% cheaper who delivers 5% defective can easily be more expensive than the incumbent. This is exactly the Cost chapter's hidden-cost lesson, applied upstream.The profitability insight is simply this: every pound saved on a purchased input drops straight to the bottom line, while every pound of extra sales contributes only its margin. In low-margin businesses, procurement is often the fastest route to profit that exists.Suppliers are the shock absorber between the macroeconomy and your P&L. Inflation arrives as a supplier price increase, usually with a justification letter attached. Interest rates change the cost of the inventory you're funding. Currency moves change the price of anything imported, even if the supplier's own price hasn't budged. Recessions do the opposite work: demand falls, suppliers' spare capacity rises, and suddenly your negotiating position improves. The strategist's question is where your supplier is exposed — one country, one commodity, one currency, one shipping lane — because that's where the economy will hit you.Tax quietly rewrites supplier economics. Import duties make a nearby supplier competitive against a cheaper distant one. VAT/GST on purchases is usually recoverable, but it's a cash-flow event between payment and reclaim. Transfer pricing rules govern what you may pay an overseas supplier you also own — and getting it wrong is expensive. Withholding tax on cross-border payments can push an offshore supplier to charge more to compensate. Tax is also a reason suppliers cluster geographically: free ports, export-processing zones, and duty-drawback schemes all exist to make certain supply routes cheaper than others.Here the relationship turns from commercial to legal, and the stakes are the highest they get.You increasingly inherit liability for your suppliers' behaviour. Labour-law breaches, environmental damage, sanctioned trading partners, conflict minerals, forced labour in tier 2 factories — regulators now expect you to know and to act. Supplier codes of conduct, audits, and traceability systems are the cost of doing business in regulated markets.Regulation cuts both ways, though. A supplier holding a patented process or a licence can be a moat. A regulation that raises the bar for entry can protect your supplier relationships from new rivals. And when rules change, your supplier is often the first to tell you what's coming.The supplier factor is the seam where the outside world enters your business, and that's why it touches all nineteen others. Strategically, suppliers define what your company chooses not to own, shape your competitive position, transmit market prices, and cap what your product can ever be. Operationally, they feed raw materials into manufacturing, hand off to distribution and stores, and are staffed, managed, sold through, and serviced by people. Financially, they are your cost of goods sold, your payables, your inventory, and your revenue ceiling. Externally, they are the channel through which the economy, tax rules, and regulation arrive at your door. If you take one habit from this section, take this: treat every significant supplier as a strategic relationship, not a transaction. Ask what breaks if they fail, what happens if they raise prices, who else is bidding for their capacity, and whether what you outsource is something you should own. Suppliers look like a cost line. Managed well, they are one of the most reliable levers on profitability a business has.

item.title: 06-3 Choosing and Managing Suppliers
item.description:
Part of 06 SuppliersPicking a supplier is one of those decisions that looks small and turns out to be enormous. Get it right, and your shelves stay stocked, your products hold up, and your costs behave. Get it wrong, and you'll spend the next two years apologising to customers for something a stranger did three countries away. This is the practical half of dealing with suppliers: how to choose one, and how to keep the relationship healthy once you have.Think of it as marriage with better paperwork.The rookie mistake is to run a beauty contest on price alone. Price is what you pay today; total cost of ownership is what you actually pay over time — the price, plus shipping, duties, storage, defects, rework, delays, and the customers you lose when a delivery doesn't arrive.That's why the cheapest quote is so often the most expensive supplier. A supplier who is 8% cheaper but late one delivery in five will cost you more in expedited freight and angry emails than you ever saved.Here are the criteria that genuinely matter:Notice how many of these are borrowed from other parts of the business. "Price and terms" is a Costs and Financials question — a supplier offering 90-day payment terms is quietly lending you working capital. "Compliance and ethics" is a Regulations issue, and a supplier caught using illegal labour becomes your reputational problem, not theirs. "Capacity and lead time" connect straight to Distribution and to how much stock you must hold. And "quality" flows into Product, which flows into Customer Service. Nothing here happens in isolation.
Photo by Pavel Danilyuk on PexelsGood supplier selection follows roughly the same path every time, whether you're buying industrial bolts or basil.
A few notes on the steps that people rush:Define the need properly. If you can't describe what "good" looks like in measurable terms — 5,000 units a month, delivered by the 3rd, meeting this spec, at this tolerance — you can't evaluate anyone. Vague requirements are how you end up with a supplier who is technically compliant and practically useless.Trial before you commit. A sample order is the cheapest due diligence available. It reveals their quality, their packaging, their paperwork, and how they behave when you're a small customer rather than a hypothetical big one.Score, don't vibe. Give each criterion a weight and mark candidates against it. This forces you to be honest about what you actually value, and it gives you a defensible answer when someone asks why you didn't pick the cheapest bid.
A tempting shortcut is single sourcing — one supplier for everything. It's simpler to manage, and you get volume discounts and a closer relationship.The risk is obvious once you say it out loud: if they fail, you fail. A fire, a strike, a bankruptcy, or a ship stuck in a canal, and your business stops.Multi-sourcing — spreading the work across two or three suppliers — costs you some scale discount but buys resilience and a permanent benchmark. If you can't compare one supplier's prices to another's, you have no idea whether you're being treated well. A common middle path is the 70/30 split: one main supplier, one backup who stays warm and ready.There's also sole sourcing, where only one supplier in the world can make what you need. That's not a choice, it's a constraint — and it means your job becomes managing risk rather than managing price: longer contracts, buffer stock, and a genuine relationship.Choosing a supplier is a one-off project. Managing one is a permanent habit. And like most habits, it decays the moment you stop paying attention.
Set expectations in writing. A simple agreement covering price, lead times, quality standards, minimum order quantities, payment terms, and what happens when things go wrong. This isn't about distrust — it's about making sure nobody is guessing.Measure with a small number of numbers. On-time-in-full delivery, defect rate, and responsiveness will catch most problems. Track them in a simple supplier scorecard and share it. Suppliers improve fastest when a customer is quietly counting.Review on a rhythm. A short quarterly conversation — here's what went well, here's what didn't, here's what we need next quarter — prevents small irritations from calcifying into a broken relationship.Plan your exit before you need it. What would you do if this supplier vanished tomorrow? Could you switch in a week, a month, a year? Knowing the answer is what lets you sleep.Imagine a small bakery chain deciding on a flour supplier. Supplier A quotes the lowest price but delivers on a "roughly Thursday" basis and has missed two orders this year. Supplier B charges 6% more, delivers every Tuesday before 7am, and offers 45-day payment terms. Supplier C is mid-priced and can supply organic and specialist blends that Supplier B can't. The naive answer is A. The better answer is B as the main supplier, C for the specialist lines, and A kept as an emergency backup for shortfalls. The 6% premium buys reliable opening hours, fewer wasted staff mornings, and 45 days of free cash flow — which, as the Financials chapter will tell you, is worth real money to a business with thin margins and rent due every month.Supplier management is a hinge between several chapters, and a good strategist notices the swing: Raw Materials — the quality of what you buy sets the ceiling on the quality of what you make. Costs — supplier prices are usually the largest single cost line, so this is where margin is won or lost. Product — consistency from suppliers is what lets you promise consistency to customers. Distribution — lead times and delivery reliability determine how much stock you must hold and how fast you can respond. Regulations and Tax — duties, tariffs, and rules travel with goods across borders. Economy — currency swings and inflation can turn a comfortable contract uncomfortable overnight, which is why long contracts sometimes include price-adjustment clauses. Competitors — a better supplier relationship can be a genuine advantage, especially if it locks up capacity others can't get.
That loop is the whole business in one picture — and the supplier sits at the top of it. If the flow into the loop is unreliable, everything downstream, right up to the cash in your account, inherits that unreliability.Choosing and managing suppliers comes down to a handful of durable ideas: Choose on total cost of ownership, not sticker price — reliability, quality, and payment terms are all part of the bill. Run a structured process: define the need, shortlist, sample, score, trial, then contract. Decide deliberately between single, multi-, and sole sourcing, balancing simplicity against resilience. Manage actively with clear agreements, a few tracked metrics, regular reviews, and a plan for if they disappear. Remember that a supplier is not an isolated transaction — it's the first link in the chain that ends in your customer's hands and your bank balance. Pick well, manage continuously, and your supply base becomes a quiet advantage. Pick carelessly, and it becomes the story you'll be explaining to customers for years.

item.title: 06-2 Types of Suppliers
item.description:
Part of 06 SuppliersA supplier is any business that provides goods or services yours needs in order to operate. That definition is deliberately broad — and that's exactly the problem. Calling a multinational chipmaker, the bloke who mows your yard, and a wholesaler of finished cushions all "suppliers" tells you almost nothing about how each one should be handled, what risk they carry, or how much of your money they swallow.So the useful next step is to sort suppliers into types. Not because labels are tidy, but because the type of a supplier predicts almost everything that matters: how easily you can replace them, how their failures land on you, where your costs sit, and what kind of relationship makes sense.There's no single official taxonomy — different businesses slice the same pie in different ways. Here are the five cuts that are most useful to a strategist.Direct suppliers provide things that physically become your product or are sold with it. Flour for a bakery. Timber for a furniture maker. Packaging that goes out the door with the goods.Indirect suppliers keep the business running but never touch the product: the accountant, the IT provider, the cleaning company, the firm that services the delivery van, the energy utility. These are often called MRO suppliers (maintenance, repair and operations), and managers have a bad habit of ignoring them until the day the only machine that matters breaks down.The distinction matters because direct suppliers shape quality and cost of goods sold, while indirect suppliers shape overhead — two very different lines on your cost sheet.
Raw material suppliers sell stuff that is processed or transformed: timber, steel, flour, cotton, crude oil. Their prices swing with global markets, which is why the Economy chapter matters here. Component suppliers sell parts you assemble rather than transform: hinges, bolts, circuit boards, zips, screens. Finished goods suppliers sell you something you resell unchanged — a wholesaler, importer or brand distributor. Retailers live almost entirely on these, which links straight to the Stores chapter. Service suppliers sell work rather than things: haulage, marketing agencies, IT support, security, and staffing agencies that provide Labour by the day. Capital goods suppliers sell big one-off items — machines, vehicles, shop fittings. These aren't daily costs; they're investment decisions that sit in your Financials. Every supplier has suppliers of its own. That chain is usually described in tiers.
Your Tier 1 supplier is the one you pay directly. Tier 2 supplies your Tier 1. Tier 3 supplies the Tier 2, and so on. You may never meet them — but they can still ruin your week: a fire at a Tier 2 sawmill becomes a shortage at your Tier 1, which becomes an empty workshop and an angry customer. Visibility gets thinner the further down you go, and that invisibility is one of the quiet risks of modern supply chains.This cut tells you who holds the power in the relationship. Sole-source (monopoly) suppliers. Only one realistic option exists — a patented component, a rare material, a specialist machinist. You have very little leverage, and switching is close to impossible. Oligopoly suppliers. A handful of big players dominate. Think of the few global makers of certain industrial chemicals or aircraft engines. Prices move together and negotiation is tough. Competitive suppliers. Many interchangeable firms offer much the same thing — stationery, basic haulage, generic packaging. Here you can shop around, switch easily, and squeeze on price. Spot suppliers. You buy when you need to, at whatever price is going that day. Flexible, but no loyalty and no guarantees. Contracted suppliers. Agreed prices, delivery terms and volumes over a set period. Predictable — which is exactly what your budgeting needs. Strategic partners. Long-term relationships where you share forecasts and plans, sometimes exclusively. More effort, but they'll often prioritise you when supply is tight. Local, national, or international. Local means short lead times, easy visits and sometimes lower transport cost; international means lower unit prices but longer lead times, currency swings, import duties and a longer list of Regulations to comply with.
Photo by Simon R. Minshall on PexelsRowan and Ash is a small furniture workshop. A quick inventory of its suppliers shows every type in action:That table isn't busywork. It instantly shows Rowan and Ash that FastFix is a low-risk convenience, while Kelmoor Timber is a single-source bottleneck whose own supplier could shut the workshop down.Classifying suppliers is the first act of strategy, because each type hints at a different decision: Risk. Sole-source and deep-tier suppliers are where a single failure can halt your Product. Competitive spot suppliers barely matter. Cost. Direct suppliers drive cost of goods sold; indirect suppliers drive overhead. Both end up in your Costs and Financials. Cash. Payment terms and lead times are the hidden difference between a service supplier paid monthly and a raw material supplier demanding cash up front — a working-capital question dressed up as a purchasing one. Quality and reliability. Components and finished goods flow into your Product, and Distribution depends on service suppliers turning up on time. Compliance and reputation. International and deep-tier suppliers drag labour, environmental and tax obligations into your risk register, even when they aren't legally yours. Negotiation posture. Knowing whether you're facing a monopoly or a crowded market tells you whether to push on price or invest in the relationship. None of this is about picking the cheapest option. It's about knowing what kind of supplier you're sitting across the table from — which is precisely what choosing and managing them depends on. "Supplier" covers a huge range, so sorting them by type reveals where risk, cost and leverage actually sit. Direct suppliers shape your product and cost of goods sold; indirect suppliers keep the lights on and add overhead. Suppliers also split by what they sell (raw materials, components, finished goods, services, capital goods). Tiers describe depth in the chain: Tier 1 is who you pay, Tier 2 and beyond are invisible but can still stop your business. The market structure — sole-source, oligopoly or competitive — decides who has the upper hand. Relationship and geography range from one-off spot buys to strategic partnerships, and from local firms to international ones with duties, currencies and regulations attached. Every one of these types feeds into other chapters — Costs, Financials, Product, Distribution, Labour, Tax, Regulations and the wider Economy all lean on how well you understand the suppliers behind them.

item.title: 06-1 What a Supplier Is
item.description:
Part of 06 SuppliersAsk most business owners who their supplier is and they'll name the firm that delivers their stock. That's right, as far as it goes — but the word covers far more ground, and getting the full picture straight now makes the next two subsections ("Types of Suppliers" and "Choosing and Managing Suppliers") much easier to use.A supplier is any organisation that provides something your business needs in order to operate.Notice how deliberately broad that is. Not "the firm that sells us stock" — anything your business needs. That pulls in a lot of people you probably don't call suppliers: the mill that sends you flour, or the wholesaler that sends you boxes, the electricity company keeping the ovens on, the accountant who files your returns, the bank that lends you money to buy the second van, the software platform that takes your card payments, the agency that sends you a temp when two staff are off sick. All of them supply something you can't operate without. All of them take money out of your business in return. If you only think of the first one, you'll miss where a surprising amount of your cost, risk and leverage actually lives.Here's the mental picture worth carrying. Your business sits in the middle of a chain. Things flow in from suppliers, you add value, and things flow out to customers — with money flowing the other way in both directions.
Two things follow from that picture, and both matter.First, the supplier is the mirror image of the customer. Your customers are the people who pay you for what you make; your suppliers are the people you pay for what you need. Same market, opposite side of the counter. That's exactly the point from the Market chapter about buyers, sellers and the space between them — and it means almost everything you know about looking after customers has a supply-side twin. You want your customers to come back, to trust you, and to give you a heads-up when something's wrong. Your suppliers want exactly the same from you.Second, nothing appears out of nowhere. The loaf on the counter is flour, water, salt, yeast, gas, packaging, a baker's time, a van, a card machine and a shop. Every one of those arrived via a supplier relationship, or several. Trace any product backwards and you'll find a chain of businesses, each one somebody else's supplier.Easy to forget: every business is on both sides of this at once. A bakery sells bread to a café — the bakery is the café's supplier. The same bakery buys flour from a mill — the mill is the bakery's supplier. The plumber who fixes the oven is a supplier; the office that hires the plumber is a customer of a different supplier.And sometimes the same firm is both. A café that buys Priya's bread and also sells her lunch is her supplier and her customer at the same time. Big firms live in these loops constantly, and they're worth protecting — being a reliable customer to your own customers is often worth more than any discount you could argue for. (The Competitors chapter makes the darker version of this point too: a supplier who could start making your product, or a big customer who could start making it themselves, is a rival in waiting.)Three consequences fall out of the definition, and each connects to a different part of the business.Suppliers are where most of your costs start. In a product business, the money you hand to suppliers is often the single biggest cost block — bigger than rent, bigger than wages in some trades. That's why the Costs chapter spends so long on direct versus fixed costs: a flour bill rises with every loaf you bake, while the accountant's monthly fee doesn't care how much you sold. Small improvements in what you pay suppliers land disproportionately on your profit, which is a theme we'll come back to. And where payment timing sits — paying a supplier in 30 days versus 60 — is a cash question belonging to the Financials chapter.Suppliers are where a lot of your risk sits. A supplier who fails, strikes, doubles their price, or disappears into administration mid-order is not a mild inconvenience — it can stop your business dead. You can't manage what you can't see, and the risk often arrives from a firm you've never spoken to. Remember Priya's flour mill buys wheat from farmers she'll never meet. If the harvest is bad, the price rise arrives at her counter anyway. That's a Raw Materials problem wearing a Suppliers costume.Suppliers are sometimes where your capability sits. Not everything you're good at has to be inside your four walls. Plenty of successful firms are essentially a small, sharp hub surrounded by suppliers who do the heavy lifting — the manufacturing, the warehousing, the accounts. Which raises the question the last subsection of this chapter will return to: should you make it yourself, or buy it in?Take one ordinary Tuesday at Priya's bakery and follow the money outwards.She opens at 7am. The ovens are already hot — gas, from a utility she has never spoken to and cannot negotiate with. The flour came from a mill forty minutes away; the yeast and butter from a cash-and-carry she visits herself; the cardboard boxes from a printer two towns over. The till takes card payments through a platform that skims a percentage of every sale before the money ever reaches her account. Her accountant will file her year-end figures in three months. A courier drops off a box of labels at 10am.Now notice something. Priya thinks of the mill as "her supplier" and thinks of the gas company, the card platform and the accountant as just facts of life. But they're all suppliers — they all provide something she needs, and they all take a cut. And the one she'd find hardest to replace isn't the mill she negotiates with every quarter. It's the payment platform, sitting invisibly on every single sale.That's the gap between how people use the word and what it actually covers, and closing it is the first real step towards managing suppliers rather than just paying them.
Photo by Othmane Ettalbi on PexelsIf you take a single idea away from this subsection, make it this one — because it sets up everything that follows:How easily could I walk away?Not "do I like them". Not "are they cheap". Could I replace them, and what would it cost me to try? If the answer is "there are six others who could do this tomorrow", that supplier competes for your business and you hold the cards. If the answer is "there is exactly one firm in the country who makes this", then they set the price, the lead time and the terms — and a piece of your margin belongs to them until you find another way.This is the Market chapter's supply-and-demand logic, viewed from underneath. A supplier with no rivals is a monopoly you have to live with, and that's just one of the shapes we'll sort suppliers into next. Recognition comes first. Write down everything your business actually needs to operate, and who provides it. Most owners find two or three entries on that list they'd never thought of as suppliers at all. Every supplier is a cost, a risk and sometimes a capability. Treating them as purely a price to be squeezed misses two-thirds of the picture. You're on both sides of the counter. The habits that make a good customer — paying on time, communicating, not vanishing when something goes wrong — are the habits that make a good buyer of supplies. Know where you can walk away and where you can't. That single judgement, applied supplier by supplier, is the foundation for choosing, managing and occasionally replacing the firms your business depends on. A supplier is any organisation that provides something your business needs to operate — not just the firm that delivers your stock. The list stretches well beyond goods: utilities, services, banks, software platforms, staffing agencies and advisers all supply something you can't run without. Your business sits in the middle of a chain — inputs flow in from suppliers, value gets added, products flow out to customers, and money flows the other way in both directions. The supplier relationship is the mirror image of the customer relationship, and every business is on both sides of it at once. Firms are sometimes supplier and customer — or supplier and future rival. Suppliers carry three things for you: a large share of your costs, a large share of your risk, and sometimes a chunk of your capability. The question that matters most about any supplier is simple: how easily could I walk away?
