item.title: 05-4 Product vs. The Other Factors
item.description:
Part of 05 ProductEvery chapter in this book so far has described a piece of the machine. Now we come to the piece that all the others are quietly serving. The product is where the business actually meets the world — the only one of the twenty factors a customer ever knowingly pays for. Everything else is either how you build the product, how you move the product, how you tell people about the product, or how you count the money the product brought in.That makes the product unusual, and it makes this comparison unusually important. Think of the other factors as spokes and the product as the hub. Spin the hub and every spoke turns with it.
There is a second reason the product deserves special treatment: it is the hardest decision to reverse. You can change a price on Monday and a promotion on Tuesday. You cannot un-design a product. Once you have chosen aluminium cans, a co-packer, a cold chain and a shelf-ready case size, you have committed suppliers, tooling, trucks and cash for years. Strategists call this path dependence. Practically it means the product decision is where the most leverage sits — and where the most expensive mistakes live. Get the product right and the other nineteen factors have a chance to work. Get it wrong and no amount of clever pricing, energetic sales or lean manufacturing will save you.So let's walk around the hub, one group of factors at a time.These are the factors that face outward, and the product is their common language.Market. In the Market chapter you learned that a market is buyers with a want and the ability to pay. The product is your answer to that want — and the market decides whether the answer was right. This is what people mean by product–market fit: not "do people like it?" but "does the market's definition of value match what I built?" A market also tells you how many variants are worth making. One national market with three clear buyer segments might justify three product versions; a fragmented market where every region wants something different may justify none, because complexity will eat the margin.Competitors. Competitors are the reason your product cannot be judged in isolation. A product has no inherent price — its price is set relative to what else the buyer could pick. The Competitors chapter gave you the tools for sizing up rivals; apply them directly to the product: which features are table stakes, which are differentiators, and which are expensive flourishes nobody pays for? Every unnecessary "nice to have" you add to match a rival is cost you carry forever. The competitor's product also sets your price ceiling, which is why a competitor's launch can wreck your unit economics overnight even if nothing about your own factory changed.Distribution. A product's physical nature dictates its route. Bulky, fragile, perishable, hazardous, digital — each one draws a different map. Water is heavy, so you don't ship it far. Ice cream needs a cold chain, which means distributors with freezer trucks. Software has near-zero distribution cost, which is why a digital product can reach a global market on a tiny budget. Read the Distribution chapter again with this in mind: channel choice is really a product design consequence, and changing the channel often forces a redesign (smaller pack, longer shelf life, tougher box).Stores. Shelf space is scarce, and it is rented by results. In a physical store your product must earn its slot against every other product competing for the same 30 centimetres, and it must sell itself off the shelf, because most shoppers decide in seconds. That is why packaging is sometimes called the silent salesperson. Store format also shapes the product: convenience stores push single-serve sizes, warehouse clubs push bulk multipacks, and a product designed for one often fails in the other. Add the private-label problem — the store's own version of your product competes with you on the same shelf, usually cheaper.Sales. Salespeople sell products, and the product's complexity sets the length and cost of the sales cycle. A product that's easy to demonstrate and easy to explain mostly sells itself; a complex one needs trained reps, long meetings and possibly a technical specialist riding along. Remember that sales can amplify a good product but cannot rescue a bad one indefinitely — word of mouth travels faster in reverse.Customer service. Service load is largely a product decision made months earlier. A product that breaks generates warranty claims. A product that confuses generates support calls. A product with a baffling manual generates returns. In the Customer Service chapter you saw that service can also be part of the product — a warranty, an installation visit, a subscription upgrade. Either way, the cost of service sits downstream of the design decision, which is why experienced managers budget service costs at the design stage, not the complaints stage.These factors face inward. The product is the specification they all have to hit.Suppliers. Your product's bill of materials picks your suppliers. Design a product around a rare component and you have just married yourself to whoever makes it. This is why smart firms involve suppliers early in design — not as vendors but as co-designers who can say "we can't hold that tolerance" or "there's a cheaper standard part that does the same job." Switching suppliers later often means redesigning the product, which is exactly the kind of hidden cost that kills a launch.Raw materials. Materials set a ceiling on quality and a floor on cost. Choose steel and you get durability and weight; choose plastic and you get cheapness and a different set of customer expectations. Commodity materials also import volatility: a cocoa or copper price spike arrives as an uninvited change to your product margin. The strategic response is usually a design response — lightweighting, substituting, or reducing waste per unit — which is why the Raw Materials chapter and this one are effectively the same conversation held twice.Manufacturing. Manufacturing constraints shape what the product can be. Tooling costs mean you need volume before a design makes sense. Minimum order quantities mean your "small trial batch" might not exist. The variety tax is real: every extra variant adds changeovers, setup time and quality risk, so a portfolio of forty SKUs can be measurably less profitable than a portfolio of eight. Design for manufacture is the discipline of shaping the product so the factory can make it cheaply and consistently — and it is usually worth far more than squeezing the factory to make a badly designed product.Labour. Product complexity determines the skill mix, and the skill mix determines your wage bill and your exposure to labour shortages. A product with heavy hand-work content is vulnerable to wage inflation and to losing key people; a highly automated product line is vulnerable to capital cost instead. There is no free option — only a choice about which risk you'd rather carry.Staff. Your staff are the product's first internal customers, and they need to understand and believe in it. A product nobody internally can explain will be explained badly to customers. Product changes also create retraining costs that rarely appear in the launch budget. And there's a quieter effect: the products a company makes determine who wants to work there. Interesting products attract good people, which loops straight back into Labour and Management.Here the relationships become arithmetic. Recall the shape of profit:Profit = (price − variable cost) × units sold − fixed costsLook at how many of those terms the product touches. It sets the price ceiling (via Competitors and Market), the variable cost (via Raw Materials and Manufacturing), the volume (via Stores, Sales, Distribution and Customer Service), and the fixed cost (via tooling, plant and development). Very few decisions move all four terms at once. This one does.Costs. Most of a product's cost is committed at design. Analysts sometimes say 70–80% of unit cost is locked in before the first unit ships, because after that you are only optimising within the design you chose. Value engineering — systematically stripping cost out of a product without stripping value out — is one of the highest-return activities in business.Revenue. Revenue is product × price × volume, but the quality of revenue matters as much as the size. One blockbuster product is efficient but terrifying; twenty small products are diversified but expensive to run. Subscription and consumable products shift revenue from one-off to recurring, which is worth far more than the same money earned once.Financials. This is where the truth about your product portfolio shows up. A product-level profit-and-loss statement routinely reveals that a third of your SKUs make no money at all — they exist because nobody ever checked. Inventory on the balance sheet is simply products you've paid for and not yet sold. Development spending may be capitalised as an asset that future sales must justify. Warranty and returns provisions are product promises recorded as financial liabilities. Read your financials with a product lens and you will usually find a decision waiting to be made.Company. The company is the container; the product is the offering. A product must fit the company's identity, capabilities and brand promise — a premium brand selling a cut-price product damages both. The company also carries the legal liability for what the product does, and it owns the product portfolio as a whole. Recall the Company chapter's point about parts working together: the product is the part every other part must line up behind.Management. Management's core job with respect to products is portfolio management: deciding what to fund, what to grow, what to harvest and — hardest of all — what to kill. Roadmaps, stage gates, and the discipline to stop a failing project before it eats the next one are management functions, not product functions. In the Management chapter we saw that managers allocate scarce resources; the product portfolio is where those allocations become visible.Economy. Products have elasticity. Discretionary, big-ticket, borrowed-money products suffer first in a downturn; staples barely notice. Input inflation, interest rates and currency movements all arrive through the product's cost and price. And the economic cycle interacts with the product life cycle: launching a genuinely new category into a recession is brutal, while launching a cheaper alternative into one can be a gift. Great strategists time products, not just design them.Tax. Tax treatment is not uniform across products, and design can follow tax. Excise duties hit alcohol, tobacco and fuel. Sugar taxes have prompted whole reformulation programmes. Sales tax and VAT rates differ by category — basic food versus luxury goods, physical book versus e-book. Tariffs apply to imported components but not to locally made ones, which can make a design decision a tax decision. Research and development tax credits reward the development itself. The Tax chapter's lesson holds: a product that is cleverly structured can be worth more after tax than a better product that is structured badly.Regulations. Compliance is a design input, not an afterthought. Safety standards, labelling, packaging rules, environmental requirements (recyclability, restricted substances, take-back schemes), advertising restrictions and product liability all shape what you are allowed to make and sell. Regulation can also be a moat: if the compliance bar is high, fewer competitors can clear it. Sometimes regulation creates a product category outright — think energy-efficient appliances or low-emission vehicles. And it can remove one just as fast, which is why regulatory horizon-scanning belongs in product planning, not in the legal department's inbox.Northwind is a small roastery with a shop and an online subscription. It wants to sell a canned cold brew in grocery stores. Watch how every factor pushes on one product decision.The company is a craft roaster with a promise of quality — a cheap, syrupy canned drink would contradict it, so the recipe must taste like Northwind. The market is cold coffee drinkers, a young and growing segment, but the competitors are two global brands with shelf power and a lower cost base, which caps the price around $3.50 a can. Raw materials — green beans, water, and aluminium cans — plus suppliers who can guarantee can supply at volume, set the bill of materials. Manufacturing is outsourced to a co-packer with a 20,000-can minimum run, which means Northwind must commit cash before it knows whether the product sells. Labour needs a new production coordinator. Distribution requires refrigerated trucks, and stores will only take the product if it fits a standard shelf-ready case. Sales requires a broker to win the listing. Customer service will field complaints if a can is flat or the shelf life fails. Costs land at $2.10 a can all-in, giving a $1.40 gross margin. Revenue depends on moving 20,000 cans before they expire. Financials show a working-capital hit of tens of thousands before a single dollar comes back. Tax adds deposit-return scheme obligations on the cans and sales tax on the category. Regulations demand nutrition labelling, allergen declarations and food-safety compliance at the co-packer. And the economy decides whether consumers keep paying a premium for a nice-to-have drink when budgets tighten.Change one thing — say, switch to a 12,000-can minimum with a smaller co-packer — and labour, distribution, stores, financials and risk all change with it. That is the whole point of this subsection.The product is the hub the other nineteen factors turn around. On the demand side, Market and Competitors define what the product must be worth, while Distribution, Stores, Sales and Customer Service decide whether it ever reaches a buyer and at what cost. On the supply side, Suppliers, Raw Materials, Manufacturing and Labour are all specified by the product, and Staff give it a voice. Costs, Revenue and Financials turn the product into a profit-and-loss reality — profit = (price − variable cost) × units − fixed costs, every term of which the product touches. Company, Management, Economy, Tax and Regulations form the frame the product must fit inside, and each can be a constraint or an advantage depending on how early you plan for it.The strategic conclusion is simple to state and hard to live by: because the product commits so many other factors, and because it is the hardest decision to reverse, it deserves more of your thinking time than any other single factor. Do the design work carefully, test it against every spoke of the hub, and the rest of the business gets a fair chance to be profitable. Skip that work and you will spend years optimising everything except the thing that was wrong.

item.title: 05-3 The Life Cycle of a Product
item.description:
Part of 05 ProductYour best-selling product will not sell forever. It gets launched, it catches on (or doesn't), it settles into a comfortable groove, and eventually something — a rival, a trend, a new technology, a change in what customers want — starts to pull it downwards. That shape, from launch to fade, is the product life cycle, and understanding it is what stops you from being surprised by your own business.The product life cycle is the pattern a product's sales and profits tend to follow over its life: introduction, growth, maturity, decline. There's also a stage before the beginning — development — where you spend money and sell nothing at all.Here's the whole thing at a glance:
And here's what's actually going on in each stage:Read that table twice, because the middle columns matter more than the sales curve. A product's life cycle is really a story about competition. As a product succeeds, rivals arrive. As rivals arrive, the fight shifts from "can we make enough?" to "why should anyone pick ours?"This is the part people miss. Sales usually peak in maturity — but profit tends to peak earlier, somewhere late in growth.Three things cause the squeeze: Costs per unit fall first, then stop falling. Early on, small volumes mean every bun carries a share of the fixed costs — the oven, the rent, the staff on shift. That links straight back to the Costs chapter: fixed costs spread over few units are painful, and spreading them over many is a gift. But once you're running at capacity, the gift runs out. Prices come under pressure. As rivals multiply, your product stops being the only answer to the customer's need. In the language of the Market chapter, your demand becomes more elastic — a small price rise now costs you more customers than it did two years ago. In the language of the Competitors chapter, your market structure hardens from a crowd of small differentiated sellers into a handful of big ones fighting on everything but price. Selling costs rise. In growth, word of mouth does the work. In maturity, you're paying for it: promotions, loyalty schemes, better packaging, a nicer display. Put those together and you get the classic squeeze: more units sold, less money kept per unit.Priya adds a new product to her bakery — cinnamon buns. Watch it live through a full cycle. (Contribution here means what's left of the price after the ingredients: the money that goes toward rent, wages and profit.)Read the growth and maturity rows together, because that's the lesson in one glance. In maturity she sells more buns than in growth and makes less money doing it.What happened in between? In growth, her bigger volumes let her buy flour and butter in bulk from her supplier at a better price, and 90 buns come out of a single baking session. By maturity, two nearby cafés have copied her, so £3.00 stops working and she drops to £2.60 to hold her spot. She also pays for a new display case and a month of local advertising. Sales are at their highest; profit is quietly going backwards.And it all started with six weeks of recipe testing in development, when the buns sold nothing at all.
Photo by RDNE Stock project on PexelsThe four-stage curve is a pattern, not a law. Real products take several shapes, and mistaking one for another causes expensive mistakes: The fad — a sharp spike and a fast collapse. It never reaches maturity because it was never really about the product; it was about being in on something. If you build a factory for a fad, you own a factory. The fashion — a gentler rise, a real plateau, a gradual fade. Clothing styles, restaurant trends, most "healthy eating" waves. The classic — a long, long maturity, sometimes decades. Bread. Bicycles. A well-run corner shop. These are the ones that pay the bills. The stillborn — a product that never gets past introduction, usually because it solved a problem nobody had, or was priced wrong, or nobody ever heard of it. Two practical points fall out of this. First, the type of product shapes the cycle — a fashion item lives its whole life in months, while a durable tool can sit in maturity for a generation. Second, some products get a second life. Vinyl records were written off as dead and came back as a premium product for a different buyer. A product in decline is not always a product at the end.

Photo by https://kaboompics.com/ on PexelsNothing in strategy says you have to accept the curve as it arrives. Before you let a product slide into decline, you have four levers — and they're not mutually exclusive:
A bakery example of each: selling buns to a café wholesale (new market), promoting them as an after-school snack as well as a breakfast (new use), launching a mini four-pack (product change), or going premium with a hand-rolled, slow-proved version at twice the price (repositioning).Two honest cautions. Extension costs money and, more importantly, it costs management attention — those are the scarce resources from the opening chapter, and every one spent reviving an old product is one not spent on a new one. And a product you keep alive out of sentiment is not a strategy; it's a bill. Read the signals, not the sales figures. Watch competitor entries, repeat-purchase rates, your own price resistance and the trade press. These are the controlling half of the management loop — the check that tells you a stage is turning before the accounts do. Invest ahead of the stage, not after it. Order the second oven while you're still in growth, because you'll wait six weeks for it. Add the extra delivery van, hire the driver, and expand into the wholesale channel before the queue forms. That's planning and organizing, and it's where most product launches are won or lost. Match your other factors to the stage. Distribution widens as you move from introduction to growth; customer service costs climb in maturity as everyone expects support; staffing needs shift from flexible all-rounders to specialists; suppliers get squeezed for better terms once your volumes justify it. The product cycle pulls every other chapter along with it. Mind the cash. Growth eats cash — stock, capacity, credit given to wholesale customers. Maturity throws it off. That's why a healthy company runs a portfolio of products at different stages, with the mature ones funding the launches.
Don't kill a cash cow because it looks boring. A mature product with thin margins may still be paying your rent and bringing customers through the door who then buy other things. Equally, don't cling to a product that's genuinely finished. The question is never "is this old?" — it's "does the money and attention this product consumes earn more here than somewhere else?" The product life cycle runs through development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline — and it's really a story about rivals arriving as your product succeeds. Profit usually peaks before sales do, because unit costs stop falling, rivals force prices down, and selling gets more expensive. The curve is a pattern, not a law: fads spike and collapse, fashions plateau and fade, classics stay mature for decades, and some products die at introduction or come back years later. You can extend a cycle with new markets, new uses, product changes and repositioning — but every extension costs money and management attention. Use the cycle to plan ahead: build capacity and channels before the growth surge, not during it, and check the signals like any other control loop. Run a portfolio — mature products generate the cash that funds the growth products of tomorrow. A product's stage should never be a surprise. If it is, the failure isn't in the product; it's in the managing.

item.title: 05-2 Types of Products
item.description:
Part of 05 ProductYou know what a product is. The next problem is that "product" covers things that behave nothing alike. A chocolate bar and a factory lathe are both products, but they're bought by different people, for different reasons, at different speeds, and they leave wildly different amounts of money behind. Sorting products into types isn't a labelling exercise — the type tells you where to sell, what to charge, how to promote, and how much margin you can realistically expect.Get the type wrong and you'll build a beautiful strategy for the wrong animal. Sell a wedding cake the way you sell a loaf of bread and you'll destroy the margin. Sell a loaf the way you sell a wedding cake and you'll lose the footfall.The single most useful split is between consumer products (bought by individuals for personal use) and business products (bought by organisations to make or sell something of their own). It's sometimes labelled B2C and B2B.The same physical object can be both. A kettle bought for a kitchen is a consumer product; a hundred kettles bought for a hotel chain are a business product. What changed isn't the kettle — it's the buyer's behaviour.That last row is worth pausing on. Derived demand means the demand for a business product comes from the demand for whatever the business is making. A café buys more bread because more people are buying sandwiches. If the café's customers stop coming, the bread order stops too — and no amount of good salesmanship on your part changes it. This is the Market chapter's supply-and-demand machinery, one step further up the chain.
Photo by Eduardo Soares on PexelsMarketers have sorted consumer products by how hard the buyer thinks about the purchase. That one variable predicts almost everything else.
Convenience products are bought often, quickly, and with almost no thought. Milk, bread, chewing gum, a newspaper. The buyer's effort is tiny, so price sensitivity is high, and they'll happily swap to whatever's nearest or cheapest. That means your job is availability and habit, not persuasion: get into as many outlets as possible, keep the packaging instantly recognisable, and don't expect much of a price premium. Convenience goods tend to earn thin margins per unit and make their money on volume and repeat visits. This is why the Distribution and Stores chapters matter so much for them.Shopping products are compared before buying. Shoes, a sofa, a laptop, a family holiday. The buyer actively gathers information, weighs price against quality against style, and often visits two or three places. Here differentiation earns its keep: better service, better design, a clearer guarantee, a nicer shop. You can charge more than the shop next door — but only by as much as the buyer thinks you're genuinely different. Remember the Types of Competition chapter: this is the world of monopolistic competition, where rivals are close substitutes rather than identical goods.Specialty products are the ones the buyer will go out of their way for. A bespoke wedding cake, a particular camera lens, a specialist running shoe, a drug with no alternative. The buyer won't accept a substitute, so demand is inelastic — exactly the elasticity idea from the Market chapter. A modest price rise costs you very few sales. That's why specialty products carry the fattest margins and get sold through few, well-chosen outlets, where the brand and the expertise do the selling.Unsought products are the awkward ones: the buyer isn't looking for them. Life insurance, a will, a fire extinguisher, a dental check-up, a funeral plan. Demand has to be created rather than captured, which makes selling expensive and trust essential. Notice that unsought isn't a comment on quality. Plenty of excellent products sit here. It's a comment on the buyer's state of mind when you reach them.
Photo by Samuel Nuñez on PexelsThere's a second, quieter classification worth knowing: durable goods (used repeatedly over years — a fridge, a bike), non-durable goods (consumed quickly — a sandwich, shampoo) and services (intangible, and cannot be stored — a haircut, a repair, a night in a hotel). Services are perishable: an unsold seat on tonight's class is revenue you can never recover, which is why capacity planning and pricing-by-the-clock matter so much in service businesses.Business products sort differently, by what role they play in the buyer's operation.
Raw materials and parts go into the finished product. Flour for a bakery, steel for a carmaker, a gearbox bought from a supplier. Buyers care about two things above all: reliability of supply and price per unit, because these costs sit directly inside their own margin. This is the Raw Materials and Suppliers chapters in action — and it's why business buyers often sign long contracts rather than shop around each week.Capital items are the big, long-lived purchases: buildings, ovens, delivery vans, IT systems. They're bought rarely, decided by committee, often financed with a loan, and written off over years as depreciation — which is the Financials chapter arriving through the back door. Because the sums are large and the decision is slow, capital goods are sold on negotiation, demonstration and after-sales support, not on a price tag.Supplies and services keep the place running without becoming part of the product: cleaning, stationery, lightbulbs, legal advice, accountancy, IT support. These are routine and mostly chosen on convenience and trust, which is why they're so often outsourced to the same firm for years.Two features tie all three together. Business buyers are fewer but much larger — one café contract may equal two hundred counter customers. And they're professional: they know their numbers, they ask for quotes, and they'll switch suppliers over a two pence difference if everything else is equal.
Photo by J E on PexelsA few more axes are worth keeping in your head, because each one changes the strategy. Commodity vs differentiated. A commodity is interchangeable — nobody cares whose it is, so price is the only lever and margins get squeezed. A differentiated product has a reason to be chosen, which buys pricing power. Most businesses die trying to sell a commodity as if it were differentiated. Physical vs digital. Digital products have almost no cost per extra copy, so extra sales drop straight to the bottom line. That's a completely different economics from baking, where every loaf costs flour. Regulated vs unregulated. Alcohol, medicines, financial products and food all carry licences, labelling rules and extra taxes. The Regulations and Tax chapters are not background noise for these products — they shape the packaging and the price. Branded vs own-label. The same factory output can be sold under a premium brand and under a supermarket's own label at half the price. Same product, different type in the buyer's mind. Pull it together and the classification stops being vocabulary and becomes a decision tool.
| Type | Where buyers expect it | Price | What sells it | Margin | |---|---|---|---|---| | Convenience | Everywhere, near the buyer | Low, compared | Packaging, habit, availability | Thin per unit, volume-driven | | Shopping | A few good outlets | Mid, compared | Service, design, brand | Medium | | Specialty | One exclusive place | High | Story, expertise, prestige | Fat | | Unsought | Wherever you can reach them | Varies | Reassurance, selling effort | Eaten by selling costs | | Business products | Negotiated, direct | Contracted | Reliability, support, price per unit | Depends on scale |Read the columns together and you can see the trap. A convenience product sold through a single boutique will fail on availability. A specialty product discounted heavily "to drive volume" throws away the very thing that made it worth buying. The type sets the rules.Priya's bakery sells six things, and each one is a different type of product needing a different approach.Same ovens, same recipes, six different games. The loaf has to be cheap and everywhere; the wedding cake has to be expensive and rare; the café contract has to be reliable rather than exciting. If Priya managed all six the same way, four of them would lose money.There's a management point here too. Her product mix — how many of each type she sells — is a planning decision, and checking how each one actually performs is the controlling half of the loop. Convenience goods supply the cash flow and the customers; specialty goods supply the margin; business contracts supply predictable volume. A good mix balances all three, and a bad mix looks busy while quietly losing money on half its range.Buyer behaviour defines the type, not your intentions. You can't declare your sandwich a specialty product by pricing it like one. Speak to your own customers: do they compare you, or do they grab and go? Their behaviour, not your label, decides what works.A product can change type. The thing that's specialty today becomes shopping when rivals copy it and convenience when everyone sells it. Types drift, usually in that direction, and the Life Cycle of a Product section picks up exactly where that drift comes from. Products sort first by who buys them: consumer products (individuals, for personal use) or business products (organisations, to make or sell something). Business demand is usually derived — it depends on the buyer's own customers, not on your sales effort. Consumer products come in four types based on how hard the buyer thinks: convenience (fast, cheap, availability-driven), shopping (compared on price and quality), specialty (no substitute accepted, high margin), and unsought (the buyer isn't looking — demand must be created). A parallel split runs by durability: durable goods, non-durable goods, and services, which are intangible and cannot be stored. Business products split into raw materials and parts, capital items, and supplies and services — with very different buying cycles, contract lengths, and financial treatment. Other useful axes: commodity vs differentiated, physical vs digital, regulated vs unregulated, branded vs own-label. The type determines where you sell, what you charge, how you promote, and how fat your margin can be — so it sits underneath decisions in the Distribution, Stores, Revenue, Costs and Customer Service chapters. Get the type right, and your whole mix earns its place: convenience brings footfall, specialty brings margin, business contracts bring volume.
item.guid: Business Management/05 Product/05-2 Types of Products.md

item.title: 05-1 What a Product Really Is
item.description:
Part of 05 ProductMost people, asked what a product is, point at a thing: a loaf of bread, a phone, a can of paint. That answer isn't wrong, it's just the visible tenth of the idea. Get the full definition straight now and a dozen later decisions — what you charge, what it costs to make, who you sell it to, why customers come back — suddenly have a logical place to sit.A product is anything offered to a market that can satisfy a want or need — and what the customer buys is the benefit, not the object.Read that twice. The object is real, and somebody has to make it well. But the customer isn't buying flour, water and yeast bound into a crust. They're buying "something nicer than the supermarket loaf to go with Sunday breakfast", or "a treat that makes the walk to the office worth it". The loaf is the vehicle. The benefit is the purchase.This is why the Market chapter and this one lean on each other. A product only becomes a product when there's a market willing to trade for it. Invent the world's finest left-handed corkscrew in a town where nobody drinks wine and you haven't made a product — you've made an object with costs attached.The word "product" covers a lot more ground than the shelf in a shop: Goods — a bicycle, a jar of honey, a printed book. Services — a haircut, an MOT, a fortnight of accounting. Combinations, which is nearly everything. A delivered pizza is a good and a service. A software subscription is a licence plus support plus updates. “/assets/0596599aeb074814b9a63ec7c0f59bae/product_goods_placeholder.jpg” could not be found. Photo by ready made on PexelsTreat goods and services as two ends of one line rather than two categories. A hand-made chair is mostly good, with a little service — the delivery, the assembly instructions. A taxi ride is mostly service, with a little good — the car. Once you see the line, you stop asking "is this a product?" and start asking "which parts of this do I actually control?"Here's the most useful mental model in this whole chapter. Every product exists at three levels at once.
The core benefit is the need being satisfied. Not "bread" but "a reliable, pleasant lunch". Not "drill" but "a hole in the wall".The actual product is the tangible version: the recipe, the size, the packaging, the label, the flavour, the way it's presented. This is what most businesses spend their time on, and rightly — it's the part you can change.The augmented product is everything wrapped around it: how easy it is to buy, how fast it arrives, whether returns are painless, the guarantee, the support, the reputation of the name on the box. In competitive markets, this is where the fight is actually won, because the actual products have converged. Two loaves of sourdough can be near-identical. One is bought from a shop that opens at 7am with a smile and a paper bag; the other from a shop with no sign and a queue out of the door.Notice how this reaches into other chapters. The augmented product is the Customer Service, Distribution and Stores chapters in disguise. When those sections talk about delivery speed, returns policy or how a shop feels, they're describing product decisions, not afterthoughts.A feature is what your product has. A benefit is what it does for the customer. Businesses fall in love with features because they're the fun part to build. Customers buy benefits and ignore everything else.The translation isn't spin. It's the difference between describing your product and describing your customer's day. If you can't put your product into a single sentence that names a benefit, you don't yet know what you're selling — and neither will anyone else.Priya bakes a sourdough loaf. Follow it through the three levels.Core benefit. Her customer, Sam, isn't solving a flour shortage. She's solving "I want fifteen good minutes and something better than the office vending machine."Actual product. The loaf itself: a 800g sourdough with a dark crust, baked at 5am, sold for £4, wrapped in paper with a hand-stamped label. Recipe, size, price, packaging, name. Every one of those is a decision somebody made.Augmented product. The shop opens at 7am so Sam can buy before work. There's a loyalty card — every tenth loaf free. Staff will slice it if she asks. If a loaf is stale when she gets it home, Priya replaces it without an argument. None of that is bread. All of it is why Sam chooses Priya's over the supermarket meal deal and the café two doors down.Now the strategic part. When Priya raised her price from £4 to £4.40 (see the Prices subsection), she didn't change the core benefit or the recipe. She was testing whether her augmented product — the reputation, the convenience, the relationship — had earned her some pricing power. That's the Competitors chapter and the Costs chapter meeting head-on: what customers will pay depends on how substitutable you are, and how substitutable you are depends on the whole bundle, not the loaf alone.
Read that loop and notice something important: the product is the hinge of the whole business. Every cost you incur — raw materials, labour, manufacturing, storage, distribution — arrives at the product. Every pound of revenue leaves from it. A business is, in a very real sense, a machine for converting inputs into a product and a product into money. Get the product wrong and nothing downstream can save you.Beginners think costs are a separate topic, managed later by someone else. In truth, most of your costs are locked in the moment you define the product.Design a loaf that must be eaten within six hours and you've just signed up for fresh-baked batches, small-scale production, and waste at the end of the day. Design one that keeps for a week and your costs shift to packaging and cold chain. Choose a thick crust and you may need a different oven. Choose a delicate one and you may need different Distribution — a van that doesn't crush it.This is why the Raw Materials and Manufacturing chapters come after this one in the book. They're consequences of product decisions, not independent choices. A good strategist thinks about a product change and immediately asks: what does this do to my cost per unit, my lead times, my supplier list, my storage, and the skills my staff need?Worth separating, because the two get muddled constantly.The product is what actually gets delivered — the loaf, the app, the haircut. The brand is the set of expectations in the customer's head about what the product will be like. The brand is a promise; the product is the keeping of it.A brand can be built in years and destroyed in a week by a product that doesn't deliver. That's why consistency beats occasional brilliance. A bakery whose loaves are superb on Tuesday and mediocre on Friday has a product problem and a brand problem, and the second one is harder to fix. Start from the need, not the idea. Ask what job the customer is hiring your product to do for them. Everything else is downstream. Define the benefit in one sentence. If you can't, you don't yet know what you're selling, and neither will your staff, your suppliers, or your customers. Manage all three levels. The core benefit is settled by the customer's need, but the actual and augmented layers are where you can win. Service, delivery and returns are product decisions — the Customer Service and Distribution chapters are really about this. Remember that a product is never finished. Tastes shift, competitors move, markets shift under you. That's why the next two subsections cover the types of products and the life cycle they pass through — both are tools for deciding what to do next, not just ways of labelling what you already have. Never fall in love with the object. The world is full of beautifully made products that nobody wanted, beaten by average products sold by well-managed businesses. The market rewards the benefit delivered, not the effort spent. A product is anything offered to a market that satisfies a want or need — the customer buys the benefit, not the object. Products include goods, services and combinations; treat them as two ends of one line, not two categories. Every product has three levels: the core benefit (the need), the actual product (the tangible thing), and the augmented product (delivery, service, guarantee, brand). Competition usually happens at the third level. Features describe what you made; benefits describe what the customer gets. Always translate. The product is the hinge of the business — all costs arrive at it, all revenue leaves from it — and most costs are locked in by product decisions made early. A brand is the promise; the product is the keeping of it. Consistency is what keeps the two aligned. The test for any product decision: does this deliver more of what the customer actually needs, at a cost the business can live with?

item.title: 04-4 Market vs. The Other Factors
item.description:
Part of 04 MarketEvery factor in this book is, at heart, a lever. Product, price, staff, stores, suppliers, manufacturing — you decide, you spend, you adjust. The market is different. The market is the verdict. It is the only factor in the whole list that tells you whether pulling all those other levers actually worked, and it is the only one that can change its mind without asking you first.Before we start comparing, one quick recall from earlier in this chapter: a market is not "the shoppers" and it is not "the country." It's a space where buyers and sellers meet and where supply and demand grind out a price. Hold on to those three pieces — buyers, sellers, and the space between them — because almost every comparison below lands on one of them.Here is the loop that ties the whole book together:
Read that left to right and you can see the asymmetry. The market is both the beginning and the end of the chain. Every other factor sits in the middle, doing work on the market's behalf.A company is a machine assembled to serve a market. That sounds obvious until you ask the founding question every strategist eventually asks: what business are we actually in? That question has no answer inside the company. It only has an answer in the market. A firm that thinks it's in the "typewriter business" dies; one that realises it's in the "office document business" survives. The market redefines the company, not the reverse.The relationship runs both ways, though — and this is where strategy gets interesting. A big enough company can shape the market it sells into. Enough marketing, enough distribution reach, enough price power, and you stop responding to demand and start creating it. That's the difference between being a market-taker (you accept the going price) and a market-maker (you help set it). Almost every business starts as a taker. The good ones earn a little market-making power over time — through brand, scale, patents, or sheer ubiquity.Management is the translator in the middle. The market speaks in broad, messy signals — a shift in taste, a new rival, a younger demographic — and management's job is to turn those signals into decisions about the other eighteen factors. Ask yourself what "good management" even means without a market to define it. Efficient at what? Fast at what? The market supplies the target that management aims at. A brilliant management team aimed at the wrong market loses to a mediocre team aimed at the right one.Notice the phrase labour market. It isn't a coincidence. Labour is bought and sold, wages are a price, and that price is set by supply and demand exactly like the price of a coffee. So the market — your market — reaches inside your building and sets what you must pay your people.If your market demands baristas, you're hiring from a shallow, local pool and paying what that pool costs. If it demands machine-learning engineers, you're hiring from a global pool and paying a very different number. The market you serve decides which skills you need; the labour market decides what those skills cost. Those two forces squeeze your margin from opposite sides.Staff are also the market's eyes and ears. Your frontline people hear what buyers complain about, what they ask for, what makes them walk out. A business that treats staff as an internal cost centre throws away its cheapest market research.Here is the sharpest comparison in the book. Financials are the market's report card, written in numbers. Revenue is simply the market's verdict converted into money: demand at a price. Costs are what you spent trying to earn that verdict.The trap is getting the direction of causation backwards. A lot of new business owners build a product, add up what it cost, tack on a margin, and call that the price. The market doesn't care what it cost you. Price is set by supply and demand — by what buyers will pay and what rivals are charging. Your cost structure isn't the source of your price; it's a constraint you must fit underneath it. The market sets the ceiling, and everything in the Costs chapter is about living below it.This is why the same product can be a great business in one market and a terrible one in another. Not because the costs changed, but because the market's willingness to pay did.Suppliers, raw materials and manufacturing are all upstream. They exist because a market somewhere downstream wants something. Suppliers. Your demand for a supplier is derived demand — you only need their cardboard because buyers want your boxes. If the market shrinks, your supplier orders shrink with it, and suddenly your bargaining power with that supplier changes. The supplier chapter's advice about choosing and managing suppliers is really advice about managing market risk upstream. Raw materials. Which materials you use is a market question dressed up as an engineering one. Cotton or polyester? Glass or plastic? The answer depends on what buyers will pay for, what they'll accept, and what regulators will allow — all market-side facts. And when a raw material gets scarce, its price rises, and that rise has to come out of your margin unless the market lets you raise your own price. Usually it won't. Manufacturing. Scale is set by market volume. A factory tooled for 100,000 units is a liability if the market only wants 5,000. On the flip side, manufacturing efficiency can lower your price, and a lower price can expand the market by pulling in buyers who previously couldn't afford you. Manufacturing can therefore create market, not just serve it — one of the few factors with that power. Where your buyers are determines where your stuff has to go. If the market is spread across a continent, you need warehouses and carriers; if it's a two-mile radius, you might need one van. Distribution is geography plus habit, and both of those are market facts.Stores are the most visible expression of this. A shop is a bet on a market: it says "enough buyers who want this, at this price, will pass this spot." Wrong about the market, and no amount of beautiful shopfitting saves you. Right about it, and an ugly shop on a busy corner beats a gorgeous one on a quiet street. The location decision is 80% market analysis and 20% rent.The market defines what a product is — not its ingredients, but its meaning. A watch tells the time; a watch in a certain market means status, or durability, or nostalgia. The same object serves different markets, and the market decides which features are worth paying for and which are worthless gold-plating.Two directions of influence matter here. Normally the market tells you what to build. But occasionally a product creates its own market — nobody was asking for smartphones, streaming, or ride-hailing until they existed. Even then, the market gets the final say: plenty of products that invented a category also failed because the market arrived too early, too late, or never.Competitors are a market phenomenon. No market, no competitors. And the structure of your market — how many buyers, how many sellers, how easy to enter — determines what kind of competition you face. A market with thousands of near-identical sellers and free entry produces brutal price competition and razor-thin margins. A market with three big players produces something else entirely: advertising wars, tacit pricing, and comfortable profits.So when you size up your rivals, you're really reading the market's structure. Market share is a market measurement. Every move a competitor makes changes the space between buyers and sellers that you all live in.Sales is the moment of contact between the market and your business — the handshake where demand turns into revenue. It follows the market rather than leading it: you can't persuade a market that has no need, and you can't sell at a price the market won't pay, no matter how good your closing technique.Customer service works on the market's memory. Service shapes what buyers believe about you, and that belief becomes part of the market's perception of your whole category. Great service turns a one-time buyer into repeat demand and turns buyers into salespeople. Bad service doesn't just lose a customer — in a small market, it shrinks your market.The economy is the market's weather. It sets the total level of demand, the cost of borrowing, and how confident people feel about spending. A recession doesn't change your product or your staff, but it can halve your market overnight. Conversely, a boom can make a mediocre business look brilliant for a few years.The strategist's habit here is to separate the two: how much of my sales is my skill, and how much is just the tide? Businesses that mistake a rising economy for their own genius tend to be the ones that drown when it turns.These two are market-shapers with a legal pen. A tax on a good raises its effective price, which reduces demand — the market shrinks without a single buyer changing their mind. A subsidy does the reverse and can create a market out of nothing (think electric vehicles in their early years).Regulations decide who may sell what, to whom, at what standard, and where. Licensing requirements fence a market off from newcomers. Safety and quality rules can protect existing players or wipe them out. Whole markets have been created and destroyed by a single rule change. This is why the Regulations and Tax chapters sit so close to the Market chapter: they don't just constrain your business, they redraw the arena.And one more comparison worth making: Market vs. market. Your market sits next to other markets, and buyers drift between them. A customer who buys your sandwich today might buy a salad tomorrow. Competitors, substitutes and changing tastes all move the boundaries. The market you're in this year is not guaranteed to be the market you're in next year.Priya makes plant-based ready meals and sells them to office workers in a city centre. Watch how the market drives everything else. Market first. She notices thousands of office workers with 30 minutes for lunch and a growing interest in eating less meat. Buyers exist, sellers are scarce, and the space between them is a short walk from the office. Product follows. She builds meals that reheat in 90 seconds, because the market's constraint isn't taste, it's time. Manufacturing follows. Volume is predictable — weekday lunch, roughly 400 units — so she tooled for that, not for 40,000. Distribution and stores follow. One small unit near the offices beats a bigger, cheaper one two miles away. The market is the location. Suppliers and raw materials follow. She picks ingredients the market recognises and will pay for, from suppliers who can deliver daily. Labour and staff follow. She hires two part-time cooks from the local labour market and pays what that market charges. Costs follow from price. The market will pay about £7. Her cost ceiling is therefore £5-ish, and every cost decision is a negotiation with that ceiling. She did not add up her costs and then declare a price. Sales and service follow. A loyalty card and a friendly face at the counter turn one-off buyers into regulars. Financials and revenue follow. These tell her, monthly, whether her read on the market was right. Now move the market. The economy dips and the offices go hybrid — two days a week, not five. Nothing about her product, staff, suppliers or factory changed, yet her market has shrunk by 60%. That is the whole lesson of this subsection in one paragraph: the market can rewrite your business without touching a single thing inside it.Her strategic options are all market options — find another market (residential neighbourhoods, hospitals), change the product to fit a new market (family-sized meals), change the channel (delivery apps), or exit. Notice she doesn't fix this by being better at manufacturing. Build it and they will come. Building the product before confirming the market. Every other factor is easy to obsess over because it's visible and controllable. The market is invisible and stubborn, which is exactly why it deserves the first look, not the last. Cost-plus pricing. Deriving price from your costs rather than from the market. This works only until a competitor prices below you and the market proves your cost structure was your problem, not its. "Our market is everyone." A market is buyers with a need, money, and access. Everyone is not a market; it's a wish. Narrow markets are where small businesses win, because narrow markets can be understood and served better than anyone else is willing to. The market is the only factor in this book that you mostly can't control, and the only one that gives a verdict rather than taking an instruction. Every other factor is downstream of it: product, manufacturing, distribution, stores, sales and service all exist to satisfy demand the market supplies. Financials, revenue and costs are the market's report card — the market sets the price ceiling, and your cost structure has to fit beneath it. Suppliers, raw materials and labour are themselves markets, which is why the word keeps appearing: anywhere buyers and sellers meet, the same supply-and-demand logic applies. The economy, tax and regulations are the market's weather and its rulebook — they can grow, shrink, create or abolish your market without touching anything inside your business. For profit, the strategist's job is simple to state and hard to do: align every controllable factor to an uncontrollable market, then keep re-reading the market before it re-reads you.
item.guid: Business Management/04 Market/04-4 Market vs. The Other Factors.md

item.title: 04-3 How Supply and Demand Set the Price
item.description:
Part of 04 MarketIn the last subsection you met the cast: buyers, sellers, and the space between them. Price is what fills that space. It's the number that decides whether a seller bothers to open, whether a buyer bothers to walk in, and — as you'll see — whether your business makes money or just makes noise. This subsection is about where that number actually comes from.Here's the short version, and the rest of this page unpacks it: price isn't set by you. It's set by the meeting point between what buyers want and what sellers are willing to provide. Your job as a strategist is not to announce a price but to understand that meeting point well enough to make money inside it.Start with the two sides of the space between buyers and sellers.Demand is the relationship between a price and the quantity buyers will take at that price. It slopes downwards: as the price falls, more people buy, and the people already buying buy more. This isn't a moral statement, it's arithmetic. At £2 a loaf, Sam buys two and freezes one. At £8, she buys none and makes toast at home. Nothing changed about her appetite — only the price.Supply is the relationship between a price and the quantity sellers are willing to offer. It slopes upwards, because making more usually costs more. The first hundred loaves come out of the oven during a normal shift. The next hundred need overtime, a second baker, or flour bought at short notice from a pricier supplier. This is the costs connection: each extra unit has its own cost, and a seller will only supply it if the price covers it.That's why a bakery happily bakes 200 loaves at £4 each and quietly turns the oven off at £2. Turn the price too low and the seller doesn't compete harder — they simply leave.Put the two curves together and something clean happens. At prices that are too high, sellers produce more than buyers want and stock sits unsold. At prices that are too low, buyers want more than sellers care to provide and the shelves empty. Somewhere between the two is a price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. That's the equilibrium price, and at that price the market clears — everything made gets sold, and everyone who wanted one got one.Notice the word clears, not fair. Equilibrium says nothing about whether the price feels reasonable. It only says the two sides match.
Read that loop carefully, because it's the engine of everything that follows. It isn't a committee deciding a price — it's thousands of small decisions correcting each other. Unsold bread gets discounted on Saturday afternoon. A sold-out favourite gets a price rise on Monday, or a bigger batch. The market finds the price by repeatedly overshooting and correcting. Equilibrium is a moving target, not a resting place.
Photo by Rafael Minguet Delgado on PexelsHere's where beginners trip, and where a lot of bad business decisions come from. There are two completely different things that can happen to a market, and people constantly confuse them: A movement along the curve happens when only the price itself changes. Lower the price and buyers take more; that's the same demand, described at a different point. A shift of the whole curve happens when something other than price changes — incomes, costs, tastes, taxes. Now the entire relationship changes, and the market settles at a genuinely new price and quantity. The distinction matters because only a shift creates a new opportunity or a new threat. A discount on Saturday doesn't change the market; a new office block opening down the street does.
On the buyers' side, the curve moves when any of these change: Incomes. When the local economy booms, people buy more of almost everything. That's the Economy chapter showing up in your till. Taste and fashion. Sourdough becomes a status symbol; white sliced becomes a joke. Demand moves for reasons no accountant can predict. Prices of substitutes and complements. This is straight out of the Competitors chapter. If the café across the road raises its prices, your demand rises — you're substitutes. If coffee pods get cheaper, the milk people buy goes up — you're complements. The number of buyers. A new office block, a new housing estate, a cruise ship in port. Expectations. If customers think prices are about to rise, they buy now and borrow demand from next month. On the sellers' side, the curve moves when the cost of supplying changes: Input costs. A bad harvest raises the price of flour. A fuel spike raises delivery costs. Wage rises lift the cost of every hour worked. Here the Raw Materials, Labour and Suppliers chapters all feed directly into price. Technology. A better oven means more loaves from the same hours — supply shifts out, and prices tend to fall. This is one of the quiet engines of long-run prosperity. Taxes and subsidies. A new tax on sugary drinks raises the cost of supplying them; a subsidy on apprentices lowers the cost of labour. That's the Tax chapter, arriving via the supply curve. Regulation. New hygiene rules, labelling rules or licences add cost, and cost is what supply responds to. Straight from the Regulations chapter. The number of sellers. New entrants add supply. When your industry looks profitable, supply arrives and prices sag — which is exactly why good margins attract competitors.
Photo by Markus Winkler on PexelsPriya sells sourdough at £4 a loaf and bakes 100 a day, which sell out by noon. Now two things happen in one month.Shock one: a new office block opens nearby. Three hundred workers now walk past her door at lunchtime. Nothing about her bakery changed — her bread, her costs and her prices are identical. But demand has shifted. At £4, she now has a queue at 11am and sells out at 11:30. She has three options: raise the price to £4.50 and sell the same 100 to the people who really want them; bake more; or keep everything the same and disappoint customers who then try the café next door. The shift in demand gave her a decision to make — that's the whole point.Shock two: a poor harvest pushes flour up 20%. Now supply has shifted. Her cost per loaf has risen, so the price that made 100 loaves worth baking no longer does the job. She can't wish the harvest back. Her realistic choices are to charge more, shrink the loaf, cut other costs, or accept a thinner margin.Notice that neither shock came from her baking. One came from the local economy and the number of buyers; the other from raw materials and her suppliers. That's the honest lesson of supply and demand: the most important movements in your business happen outside your four walls, and the strategist's job is to see them early.There's one more idea worth carrying, because it decides whether a price rise makes you richer or poorer. Elasticity is how much the quantity bought responds to a change in price. Inelastic demand — people barely change what they buy. Insulin, salt, a train ticket to work. Raise the price and sales dip only a little. Elastic demand — people change a lot. Anything with a close substitute: bread from the bakery next door, a mid-range hotel room, a taxi versus a bus. And here's where supply and demand stops being theory and starts being your profit and loss account. Remember from the Costs chapter that each loaf has a variable cost — flour, butter, the bag — and that what's left after paying it is the contribution toward rent, wages and profit.Priya's loaf sells for £4 and costs £1.20 in ingredients. She sells 100 a day: contribution = £2.80 × 100 = £280.She tries a 10% price rise to £4.40, and 15 customers vanish:Both revenue and contribution fell. Her demand was elastic, so the price rise lost more than it gained. On a more inelastic product — say a unique celebration cake nobody else in town makes — the same 10% rise might cost her only two orders, and margin would jump. Same bakery, same arithmetic: elasticity is what decides. Cross-reference this with the Revenue chapter, because revenue is price × quantity, and they move in opposite directions.
Pull it together and a few practical rules fall out. You rarely set the price; you discover it. Nearly every business is a price taker in some markets and a price maker in others. The structural reasons sit in the Types of Competition chapter; the day-to-day version is that a rival's price sets a ceiling above your head. You earn margin by shifting your own cost curve, not by arguing with the market price. In highly competitive markets, the baker who shaves two pence off the cost of a loaf keeps that two pence. Everyone else is stuck. You can change your own elasticity. Differentiate — better service, a location, a brand, a loyalty scheme — and your customers stop treating you as a straight swap for the shop next door. That's how you move away from "price is the only thing that matters". Forecast, then plan, then check. Demand shifts can be anticipated, because they leave traces: job adverts, planning applications, harvest reports, interest rate news. That's the planning and controlling loop from the management chapter applied to price. Watch the whole chain. Your suppliers' costs, your staff's wages, the taxes and rules you pay — every one of them is a supply-side shift waiting to happen.
Photo by Sara Er on Pexels Demand slopes down and supply slopes up; price is where the two meet. Nothing about either curve is a moral judgement — it's just how buyers and sellers respond. The meeting point is the equilibrium price, where the market clears. It's a moving target that markets find by repeatedly overshooting and correcting. Distinguish a movement along a curve (only the price changed) from a shift of the curve (income, costs, tastes, taxes, rivals, regulation changed). Only shifts create new opportunities and threats. Demand shifters: incomes, taste, substitute and complement prices, number of buyers, expectations. Supply shifters: input costs, technology, taxes, regulation, number of sellers. Elasticity decides whether a price rise helps you. Elastic demand means customers leave; inelastic demand means they grumble and stay. The profitability connection is direct: revenue is price × quantity, and profit depends on the contribution left after variable costs. Elasticity and cost control are what you actually control. Strategy in one line: you don't argue with the market price — you lower your costs, sharpen your differentiation, and move your own curves.
